acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q1.body: A car of mass about $2000\ \mathrm{kg}$ travelling at $100\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\approx28\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ has kinetic energy $\tfrac12mv^2=0.784\ \mathrm{MJ}$, so $100\ \mathrm{MJ}$ is unrealistic. An A4 sheet measures $210\ \mathrm{mm}\times297\ \mathrm{mm}$, giving an area of $0.062\ \mathrm{m^2}$ and a mass of about $5.0\ \mathrm{g}$ at $80\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: A laptop can draw about $50\ \mathrm W$, so this is realistic.
perOption.B: Correct. The estimate is over 100 times the example’s kinetic energy.
perOption.C: Standard $80\ \mathrm{g\,m^{-2}}$ A4 paper has a mass of about $5\ \mathrm g$ per sheet.
perOption.D: $500\ \mathrm K$ is about $227\,^\circ\mathrm C$, a plausible temperature for an iron’s heating element.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q2.body: At the top, the vertical velocity is zero and the speed is $u\cos\theta$, where $u$ is the launch speed. The kinetic-energy ratio is $\frac{\tfrac12m(u\cos\theta)^2}{\tfrac12mu^2}=\cos^2\theta$, so the kinetic energy there is $E\cos^2\theta$.

perOption.A: Uses the horizontal speed factor without squaring it.
perOption.B: Uses the vertical launch component, which has fallen to zero at the top.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Keeps the full launch kinetic energy even though the vertical component of velocity has fallen to zero.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q3.body: At $1.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, air resistance balances the downhill component of weight, so $1.4k=(80.0)(9.81)\sin 5^\circ$ and $k=48.857\ \mathrm{N\,s\,m^{-1}}$. At $5.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the air resistance is $(5.5)(48.857)=268.71\ \mathrm N$. The additional downhill force is $268.71-(80.0)(9.81)\sin5^\circ=200\ \mathrm N$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Adds the downhill weight component to the uphill drag magnitude.
perOption.C: Using the full weight in place of its downslope component inflates the calculated drag and the required force.
perOption.D: Using nearly the full weight to infer the drag and then adding gravity instead of subtracting it inflates the result further.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q4.body: At constant speed the compression is $x_1=10.0-7.5=2.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $mg=kx_1$. While the container slows, its acceleration is downward and $mg-kx_2=ma$. Substituting $mg=kx_1$ and dividing by $mg$ gives $a/g=(x_1-x_2)/x_1$, so $x_2=1.99\ \mathrm{cm}\approx2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. The new length is $10.0-2.0=8.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Treats the acceleration as upward and increases the compression.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Adds the reduced compression to the natural length as though the spring were stretched.
perOption.D: Adds an increased compression to the natural length, reversing both the acceleration and the deformation.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q5.body: The angle between the incoming and outgoing velocity vectors is $45^\circ$. The cosine rule gives $(\Delta v)^2=20^2+15^2-2(20)(15)\cos45^\circ$, so $\Delta v=14.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The impulse magnitude is $\Delta p=m\Delta v=(0.140)(14.2)=2.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Uses only the vertical change in momentum.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Adds the two momentum magnitudes as if the velocity reversed along a straight line.
perOption.D: Overstates the vector change, which is bounded by the sum of the initial and final momentum magnitudes of $4.9\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q6.body: For X, Y and Z together, $F=6ma$. For X alone, $F-F_{Y\to X}=ma$, so $F_{Y\to X}=5ma=\tfrac56F$. By Newton’s third law, the force of X on Y has the same magnitude.

perOption.A: Gives the resultant force on X.
perOption.B: Gives the contact force accelerating Z alone.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assigns the entire applied force to the contact even though X also accelerates.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q7.body: Take moments about the point where the beam contacts the wall. For beam length $L$ and weight $W$, the clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance when $(T\cos30^\circ)(L\sin60^\circ)=(T\sin30^\circ)(L\cos60^\circ)+\tfrac12W(L\sin60^\circ)$. With $W=(10)(9.81)\ \mathrm N$, this gives $T=85\ \mathrm N$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Balancing the vertical tension component against the full weight gives about $110\ \mathrm N$ and overlooks the wall’s friction.
perOption.C: This tension gives too large a clockwise moment after both tension components are included.
perOption.D: Uses the full horizontal span as the weight’s lever arm even though the weight acts at the midpoint.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q8.body: Let $r$ be the hemisphere’s radius. Conservation of energy between P and T gives $mgr=\tfrac12m(4.0)^2$, so $gr=8\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. When $75\%$ of the initial gravitational potential energy remains, $mgr=mg(3r/4)+\tfrac12mv^2$. This gives $v^2=gr/2$ and $v=2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the speed at R.

perOption.A: Uses one-quarter of the final speed as though kinetic energy were proportional to speed.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses three-quarters of the final speed even though the remaining fraction refers to gravitational potential energy.
perOption.D: Overlooks that the calculated speed is listed at R.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q9.body: The tape speed is $v=r\omega$. With constant $\omega$ and a radius that decreases at a steady rate, the graph is a straight line with a negative gradient. The speed stays above zero while the radius is positive.

perOption.A: Confuses constant angular velocity with constant tape speed.
perOption.B: Shows the speed dropping more slowly over time, which would require the radius to shrink more slowly.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Shows the speed dropping faster over time, which would require the radius to shrink faster.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q9.issues: The key writes $v\propto r\propto t$, although $r$ decreases linearly with time from a nonzero initial value. The key’s graph and answer are correct.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q10.body: All geostationary satellites have the same orbital radius and angular speed $\omega=2\pi/T$, so they have the same linear speed $v=r\omega$. Equating $mr\omega^2=GMm/r^2$ gives $T^2=4\pi^2r^3/(GM)$. With $T=24\times60\times60\ \mathrm s$ and the given Earth mass, $r=4.231\times10^7\ \mathrm m$. The height above Earth’s surface is $h=r-R$.

perOption.A: A geostationary satellite must stay above a fixed point on the equator.
perOption.B: A geostationary orbit must follow Earth’s eastward rotation.
perOption.C: Uses the orbital radius $4.231\times10^7\ \mathrm m$ as the height without subtracting Earth’s radius.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q11.body: Gravity provides the centripetal force on both stars, so $Md\omega^2=3MD\omega^2=GM(3M)/(d+D)^2$. Comparing the two centripetal expressions gives $d=3D$. Substituting into the equation for the $3M$ star gives $\omega^2=GM/(16D^3)$. The total kinetic energy is $\tfrac12M(d\omega)^2+\tfrac12(3M)(D\omega)^2=6MD^2\omega^2=3GM^2/(8D)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats $3D$ as the separation and applies the single-orbit expression $GM(3M)/[2(3D)]$.
perOption.C: Treats $D$ as the separation and applies the single-orbit expression $GM(3M)/(2D)$.
perOption.D: Adds two single-orbit expressions using $3D$ and $D$ separately as the separation.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q11.issues: The printed letter and the start of the solution are on page 2. Page 3 contains the kinetic-energy calculation and distractor working.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q12.body: All three objects are at the same temperature and are in thermal equilibrium. Their heat capacities differ, and equal temperatures alone do not imply equal internal energies. Energy can still be exchanged in both directions at thermal equilibrium, with zero net transfer.

perOption.A: Assumes equal temperatures guarantee equal internal energies for different materials and masses.
perOption.B: Confuses zero net transfer with the absence of any exchange.
perOption.C: Infers temperature from touch even though all three temperatures are equal.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q12.issues: The key treats different heat capacities as proof of different internal energies. The given information supports only that equal temperature does not guarantee equal internal energy.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q13.body: With the amount of gas and temperature constant, $pV=nRT$ gives $p_1V_1=p_2V_2$. The pressures at the bottom and surface are equivalent to $30\ \mathrm m$ and $10\ \mathrm m$ of water, respectively. Thus $30V_1=10V_2$ and $V_2=3V_1$.

perOption.A: Uses the water pressure alone at the bottom and omits the atmospheric contribution there.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reverses the pressure–volume relation and predicts compression as the bubble rises.
perOption.D: Assumes constant temperature implies constant volume even though pressure decreases.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q14.body: Square the five speeds and take their mean. The root mean square speed is $\sqrt{\frac{250^2+300^2+400^2+100^2+500^2}{5}}=340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Divides by five after taking the square root.
perOption.B: Underestimates the root mean square, which must be at least as large as the arithmetic mean of $310\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Takes the square root of the sum of squares without dividing by five first.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q15.body: At the top of the motion, the downward force equation is $ma=mg-N$. At the limiting amplitude $N=0$, so $m\omega^2x_0=mg$. Hence $x_0=g/\omega^2=g/(2\pi f)^2=9.81/[4\pi^2(2.0)^2]=6.2\ \mathrm{cm}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Chooses an amplitude for which the normal force still remains well above zero at the top.
perOption.B: Sets the limit at a downward acceleration below free fall, so the object still presses on the platform.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Requires a downward acceleration greater than gravity at the top, so the object loses contact.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q16.body: The particle undergoes simple harmonic motion, so $F=-kr$. Equivalently, $F=-\mathrm{d}U/\mathrm{d}r$, and the negative gradient of the potential energy gives a straight force graph through the origin sloping downwards.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Plots the force magnitude and loses its sign.
perOption.C: Copies the potential-energy graph for the force.
perOption.D: Makes the force point away from equilibrium.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q17.body: With transmitted amplitude $A_0$, the receiving aerial measures $A=A_0\sin\theta$. The received power and intensity are proportional to $A^2=A_0^2\sin^2\theta$. The transmitted power and intensity are proportional to $A_0^2=A^2/\sin^2\theta$.

perOption.A: Uses a horizontal projection and applies it again to the received amplitude.
perOption.B: Uses cosine as though the angle were measured from the vertical.
perOption.C: Projects the received amplitude again instead of recovering the transmitted amplitude.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q18.body: Consecutive resonant lengths differ by half a wavelength, so $\lambda/2=0.49-0.15=0.34\ \mathrm{m}$ and $\lambda=0.68\ \mathrm{m}$. Using $v=f\lambda$ gives $330=f(0.68)$ and hence $f=490\ \mathrm{Hz}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Implies an 85 cm wavelength, larger than twice the measured resonance spacing.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Rounds the calculated frequency too coarsely.
perOption.D: Treats the first 15 cm length as exactly one quarter wavelength.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q19.body: Glass has a higher refractive index than air, so the light travels more slowly and has a shorter wavelength inside the glass. The block therefore contains more wavelengths than the same thickness of air. The central maximum shifts upwards, where the shorter geometric path from $S_1$ compensates for the extra phase delay.

perOption.A: Uses the wavelength in glass to predict the fringe spacing on the screen.
perOption.B: Treats the delay from the thin glass block as varying from fringe to fringe.
perOption.C: Confuses the phase delay with an improvement in the balance of the two beam intensities.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q20.body: To the left of $-Q$ the two fields oppose each other. Let $x$ be the charge separation and $y$ the distance to $-Q$. Equating field magnitudes gives $\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0y^2}=\frac{4Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(x+y)^2}$, hence $x+y=2y$ and $y=x$, as at B.

perOption.A: At A the field from $+4Q$ is stronger.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: At C the field from $-Q$ is stronger.
perOption.D: At D the larger charge is also closer, so its field dominates.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q20.issues: The key defines x as the distance to +4Q, but its equation uses x as the separation between the charges.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q21.body: The particle can be positively or negatively charged, so it can deflect upwards or downwards. Deflection begins at entry, as shown by paths 1 and 3. The equipotentials for equal potential intervals are closer together in region P, indicating a stronger electric field.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Delays the initial deflection and selects the region with wider equipotential spacing.
perOption.C: Identifies the possible paths but selects the region with wider equipotential spacing.
perOption.D: Identifies the stronger field region but delays the initial deflection.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q22.body: Density is $d=m/(AL)$, so $A=m/(dL)$. Substituting into $R=\rho L/A$ gives $R=\rho L^2d/m$, hence $m=\rho L^2d/R$. Since $L$ and $R$ are equal, $m_{\mathrm{Al}}/m_{\mathrm{Cu}}=(2/1)(1/3)=0.67$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Inverts the resistivity ratio.
perOption.B: Uses the density ratio alone, assuming equal cross-sections.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives the copper-to-aluminium mass ratio.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q23.body: At $0.20\ \mathrm{A}$ the graph gives $2.0\ \mathrm{V}$ for A and $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$ for B. Using $R=V/I$ gives $10\ \Omega$ for A and $15\ \Omega$ for B, so B has 50% more resistance.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: A dissipates $0.40\ \mathrm{W}$ and B dissipates $0.60\ \mathrm{W}$, a factor of 1.5.
perOption.C: The parallel currents add to $0.30+0.20=0.50\ \mathrm{A}$.
perOption.D: At the common current of $0.20\ \mathrm{A}$, A has $2.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and B has $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$ across it.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q23.issues: The key prints A correctly but swaps the resistance labels. The graph gives A = 10 Ω and B = 15 Ω at 0.20 A.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q24.body: The Earth and solenoid fields are perpendicular, so $\tan68^\circ=B_{\mathrm{solenoid}}/B_{\mathrm{Earth}}$. Thus $B_{\mathrm{solenoid}}=(2.0\times10^{-5})\tan68^\circ=4.95\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$. Substituting into $B_{\mathrm{solenoid}}=\mu_0nI$ gives $4.95\times10^{-5}=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(20/0.15)I$, so $I=0.30\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the field components in the tangent ratio.
perOption.B: Uses the Earth’s field in place of the solenoid field.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses 20 turns per metre instead of 20 turns over 15 cm.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q25.body: Sliding the rod induces an e.m.f. across it and produces currents in opposite senses in the two loops. Increasing the magnetic flux density increases the outward flux linkage through the frame. By Lenz’s law the induced field points into the page, so the current around the frame is clockwise.

perOption.A: A decreasing outward flux induces an outward field and an anticlockwise current.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Sliding left produces opposite circulation in the two loops, with clockwise circulation only in the right loop.
perOption.D: Sliding right produces opposite circulation in the two loops, with clockwise circulation only in the left loop.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q25.issues: The intended answer reads “through the frame” as circulation around the entire perimeter. Either rod motion gives clockwise circulation in one subloop.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q26.body: The period is $T=1/f=1/50=0.020\ \mathrm{s}$ and spans two horizontal divisions, giving a time-base of $10\ \mathrm{ms\,div^{-1}}$. The $2.8\ \mathrm{V}$ peak spans 1.4 vertical divisions, so the Y-gain is $2.8/1.4=2.0\ \mathrm{V\,div^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the peak-to-peak height with the peak voltage.
perOption.B: Uses a half-cycle for the period and the peak-to-peak height for the peak voltage.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a half-cycle for the period.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q27.body: The cut-off wavelength is the shortest wavelength present. Since $E=hc/\lambda$, it corresponds to the most energetic photon released.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Braking radiation from decelerating electrons produces the continuous spectrum with a short-wavelength cutoff.
perOption.C: Outer-shell electrons can emit X-rays when they fill vacancies in inner shells.
perOption.D: The sharp peaks arise from transitions between discrete energy levels in tungsten.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q28.body: These uncertainties arise from the wave nature of matter and persist regardless of the equipment. Reducing the position spread raises the lower bound on the corresponding momentum spread, so equipment cannot make both spreads arbitrarily small together.

perOption.A: Exact position and its corresponding momentum component cannot be achieved simultaneously.
perOption.B: The uncertainty relation pairs position and momentum components along the same axis.
perOption.C: This statement is also false as written because the standard-deviation bound is $\Delta x\,\Delta p_x\ge h/(4\pi)$, allowing the product to be below $h$.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q28.issues: D is the intended answer, but C is also false as written. The strict lower bound for standard deviations is h/(4π), even though the syllabus gives an order-of-magnitude relation.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q29.body: Subtract the total product mass from the total reactant mass to get $\Delta m=[(235.04393+1.00866)-(140.91440+91.92617+3\times1.00866)]\ \mathrm{u}$. This is $3.088\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{kg}$. The energy released is $E=(\Delta m)c^2=2.78\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Reports the mass difference in kilograms as an energy in joules.
perOption.B: Multiplies the mass difference by the speed of light only once.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Omits the three outgoing neutrons from the product mass.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q30.body: The graph of $\ln C$ against $t$ is linear, with gradient $(0-5.20)/(26.0-0)=-0.20\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The gradient is $-\lambda$, so $t_{1/2}=\ln 2/\lambda=\ln 2/0.20=3.5\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Reports the magnitude of the gradient, which is the decay constant in inverse seconds.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reads the time for the logarithm of the count rate to halve.
perOption.D: Reads the time intercept, where the count rate is one count per second.

acjc-2022-prelim-p1-q30.issues: The key labels the negative gradient λ and then uses a positive λ in the calculation. The gradient equals −λ.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q1.body: Electromotive force is energy supplied per unit charge, so its unit is the joule per coulomb. Since $\mathrm{J}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$ and $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{A\,s}$, this gives $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. It uses kilogram, metre, second and ampere.
perOption.B: Momentum has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, which use three base units.
perOption.C: From $B=F/(IL)$ for a perpendicular conductor, the metre cancels and the unit is $\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}\,A^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: Power is energy per time, with units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}}$.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q2.body: Assuming the force acts along the initial motion, $a=F/m$ gives the gradient of the speed–time graph. The speed stays constant at first, rises with an increasingly steep gradient as the force grows, and stays constant at its new value once the force drops to zero.

perOption.A: Correct. It shows a progressively steeper rise followed by constant speed.
perOption.B: Its straight rising segment implies constant force.
perOption.C: Its final decline requires a backward force after the applied force ends.
perOption.D: Its instantaneous speed jump requires a finite impulse delivered in zero time.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q2.issues: The force direction relative to the initial velocity is unspecified. The keyed graph assumes a force parallel to and in the same direction as the initial motion.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q3.body: Distance is the area under the speed–time graph. The triangle from 5 to 10 s has half the base and half the height of the whole triangle, so it covers one quarter of the total area. The first 5 s therefore account for three quarters of the total distance, giving a ratio of $4/3\approx 1.3$.

perOption.A: It underestimates the contribution of the last 5 s.
perOption.B: Correct. The first 5 s cover three quarters of the total distance.
perOption.C: It overestimates the last 5 s by treating its distance as half the first interval’s.
perOption.D: It assigns almost as much distance to the last 5 s as to the first despite the much lower speed.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q4.body: The force changes the velocity by a vector of magnitude $Ft/m=(1.5)(2.0)/3.0=1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The final speed is smallest when this change opposes the initial velocity and largest when it points along it. It can range from $1.0$ to $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so $0.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is impossible.

perOption.A: Correct. It is below the minimum final speed.
perOption.B: This is possible when the force opposes the initial velocity.
perOption.C: This is possible with a force angled so the final velocity has the original magnitude.
perOption.D: This is possible when the force points along the initial velocity.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q5.body: The component of weight down the slope is $mg\sin30^\circ$. The block slides down the slope, so both tension and friction act uphill. Newton’s second law gives $a=(5.0g\sin30^\circ-2.0-3.0)/5.0=3.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ down the slope.

perOption.A: Correct. Both tension and friction reduce the downhill resultant.
perOption.B: Adds friction downslope while subtracting tension.
perOption.C: Adds both friction and tension to the downhill weight component.
perOption.D: Uses the perpendicular weight component $mg\cos30^\circ$ in the along-slope equation.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q6.body: In diagram 1 both moments are anticlockwise, so $M=2F(r/2)=Fr$. In diagram 2 the top force produces a clockwise moment $Fr$, and the left force produces an anticlockwise moment $3Fr/4$. The clockwise moment is larger, leaving a net moment of $Fr/4=M/4$ clockwise.

perOption.A: Reverses the sense of the larger moment.
perOption.B: Correct. The clockwise moment exceeds the anticlockwise moment by $M/4$.
perOption.C: Uses a ratio of moment arms for the magnitude and reverses the direction.
perOption.D: Uses a ratio of moment arms in place of subtracting the opposing moments.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q7.body: Taking right and up as positive, the resultant has components $R_x=40+50\sin45^\circ-70\sin72^\circ=8.78\ \mathrm{N}$ and $R_y=50\cos45^\circ+70\cos72^\circ=57.0\ \mathrm{N}$. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{R_x^2+R_y^2}=57.7\ \mathrm{N}$, at about $9^\circ$ clockwise from P. The balancing force points in the opposite direction, at $189^\circ$ clockwise from P.

perOption.A: Gives the direction of the original resultant.
perOption.B: Correct. It gives the equal and opposite balancing force.
perOption.C: Adds the leftward component as if it pointed right and reports the resulting direction without reversing it.
perOption.D: Reverses a resultant calculated by adding the leftward component as if it pointed right.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q7.issues: The question omits the angle convention. The keyed angle is measured clockwise from line P.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q8.body: At constant power $P$, the upward pulling force at speed $v$ is $P/v$. As the block speeds up, the pull decreases while its weight $mg$ stays constant, so the upward acceleration decreases. The speed approaches $P/(mg)$ as the pull approaches the weight.

perOption.A: Shows constant acceleration followed by a sudden drop to zero.
perOption.B: Shows constant acceleration throughout the rise.
perOption.C: Correct. The gradient gradually decreases as the pull approaches the weight.
perOption.D: Shows increasing acceleration while the pulling force is falling.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q9.body: The masses share the disc’s angular speed $\omega$ while they rotate with it. Static friction supplies the required centripetal force $mr\omega^2$, which is greatest at $6R$. For identical masses on the same surface, the maximum static friction is the same, so the outermost mass reaches that limit first.

perOption.A: At fixed angular speed, the required centripetal force increases with radius.
perOption.B: Correct. The mass at $6R$ requires the greatest static friction.
perOption.C: All three masses complete the same number of revolutions per unit time while co-rotating.
perOption.D: Kinetic energy scales with the square of linear speed, giving a factor of nine.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q10.body: The stars exert equal gravitational forces on each other and have the same angular speed $\omega=2\pi/T$, so $M_A r_A\omega^2=M_B r_B\omega^2$. Thus $r_B=0.2r_A$, and $r_A+r_B=d$ gives $r_A=5d/6$. The force on B equals the force on A, $M_A r_A\omega^2=10\pi^2 dM_A/(3T^2)$.

perOption.A: Correct. Both the orbital radius and force magnitude agree.
perOption.B: Uses the mass of B with the larger orbital radius of A.
perOption.C: Uses the full separation for A’s orbital radius.
perOption.D: Uses the full separation for A’s orbital radius and pairs B’s mass with the force coefficient for A’s radius.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q11.body: For a planet of mass $m$ orbiting the Sun, $GM_\odot m/r^2=4\pi^2mr/T^2$, so $T^2$ is proportional to $r^3$. Saturn therefore takes $9.5^{3/2}$ Earth years, or about $29$ years.

perOption.A: Applies too small a power to the orbital radius ratio.
perOption.B: Correct. The period scales as $r^{3/2}$.
perOption.C: Squares the radius ratio, giving about 90 years.
perOption.D: Cubes the radius ratio without taking the square root.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q12.body: At constant temperature, the molecules’ mean kinetic energy stays constant. The ice absorbs latent heat during melting, and its microscopic potential energy increases as its structure changes. The internal energy therefore increases, making A the incorrect statement.

perOption.A: Correct. Melting increases internal energy.
perOption.B: Constant temperature keeps the mean molecular kinetic energy constant.
perOption.C: Ice contracts on melting, so the surroundings do positive pressure–volume work on it.
perOption.D: The energy absorbed is $mL_f$ for the $30\ \mathrm{g}$ sample, while $L_f$ is energy per unit mass.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q13.body: Using the intended mean-energy criterion, equate $\tfrac32 kT$ to the escape energy $GMm/r$ for a helium-4 atom. With $r=3.4\times10^6\ \mathrm{m}$ and $m\approx6.65\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$, this gives $T=2GMm/(3kr)\approx4.03\times10^3\ \mathrm{K}$. This puts the school’s keyed value, $4.1\times10^3\ \mathrm{K}$, near the estimate, but the estimate rounds to option C at the stated precision.

perOption.A: Using the diameter as the radius halves the result to about $2.0\times10^3\ \mathrm{K}$.
perOption.B: This is near the half-value obtained by using the diameter in the escape-energy expression.
perOption.C: This is the two-significant-figure result of the mean-energy calculation.
perOption.D: Correct. This is the keyed estimate, though the calculation rounds to C.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The school key and keyAnswer both give D. The intended mean-energy calculation gives about 4030 K, which rounds to C. An ideal gas has a distribution of speeds, so this criterion gives a characteristic temperature rather than a strict minimum for individual atoms to escape.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q14.body: After heating and leakage, the gas is at $1050\ \mathrm{K}$ and pressure $2P$. During cooling, assume no further gas escapes, so $p/T$ is constant at fixed volume. The final pressure is $2P(150/1050)=0.29P$.

perOption.A: Correct. It scales the post-leak pressure by $150/1050$.
perOption.B: Uses the temperature rise of $900\ \mathrm{K}$ as the hot temperature.
perOption.C: Assumes a pressure decrease by a factor of two even though the absolute temperature falls by a factor of seven.
perOption.D: Assumes the original pressure returns when the original temperature returns, overlooking the loss of gas.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q15.body: The block completes several oscillations while viscous forces dissipate its mechanical energy. Its amplitude decreases until it is effectively at rest, which is characteristic of light damping.

perOption.A: Critical damping returns the block to equilibrium without repeated oscillations.
perOption.B: Heavy damping gives a slower, nonoscillatory return to equilibrium.
perOption.C: Correct. Oscillations persist while their amplitude decreases.
perOption.D: Without damping, the oscillations would continue at constant amplitude.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q16.body: In steady state, the periodic driver sets the frequency of the spring–mass system. The natural frequency governs free oscillation and helps determine where the driven amplitude peaks.

perOption.A: The amplitude can fall as the driving frequency moves above resonance.
perOption.B: A larger driving amplitude can produce a larger response.
perOption.C: The natural frequency governs free oscillation.
perOption.D: Correct. The steady-state motion follows the driving frequency.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q17.body: The travel-time difference is $3.5-3.0=0.5\ \mathrm{s}$. Each cycle is $2\pi$ radians, so the phase difference is $2\pi f\Delta t=2\pi(0.40)(0.5)=2\pi/5$ radians.

perOption.A: Uses $\pi$ radians for a full cycle.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This is the numerical value of the period in seconds, $5/2$, multiplied by $\pi$.
perOption.D: Uses the numerical value of the period, 2.5, as the number of cycles in the phase calculation.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q18.body: For the second order, $d\sin31^\circ=2\lambda$. Since $\sin\theta\leq 1$, the order satisfies $m\leq d/\lambda=2/\sin31^\circ\approx3.88$. The allowed orders are $0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3$, giving seven maxima.

perOption.A: Counts only the three nonzero orders on one side.
perOption.B: Counts the central maximum and the orders on just one side.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Rounds the order limit up and counts a fourth-order maximum on each side.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q19.body: The air column has a displacement node at the water surface and an antinode near the open end. Successive resonances occur at effective lengths that differ by $\lambda/2$, so $x=\lambda/2$ and $\lambda=2x$.

perOption.A: Halves the measured separation even though it is already half a wavelength.
perOption.B: Treats the separation as one full wavelength.
perOption.C: The factor $3/2$ misstates the relation between successive resonances.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q20.body: Every point on PO is equidistant from A and D and from B and C, so the opposite-charge contributions to electric potential cancel in pairs. Thus $\Delta U=q\Delta V=0$. The proton’s kinetic energy is constant, so $W_{\mathrm{ext}}=\Delta K+\Delta U=0$.

perOption.A: Assumes a rise in potential even though the potentials at P and O are both zero.
perOption.B: Assigns opposite signs to external work and the potential energy change at constant speed.
perOption.C: Assumes a drop in potential even though the opposite charges cancel in pairs at both endpoints.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q21.body: The voltage across the plates is $630\ \mathrm{V}$ and their separation is $0.020\ \mathrm{m}$, giving $E=630/0.020=3.15\times10^4\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. The force magnitude is $eE=5.0\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{N}$, directed toward the positive plate.

perOption.A: Multiplies by the plate separation when calculating the field.
perOption.B: Multiplying the local potential of $472.5\ \mathrm{V}$ by the electron charge gives an energy.
perOption.C: Multiplying the full plate voltage by the electron charge gives an energy.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q22.body: Closing A gives a direct path from the junction of $R_1$ and $R_2$ to Y, so $R_1=12\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$. With A open, closing B bypasses $R_3$, so the resistance drops from $24$ to $20\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $R_3=4\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$. Hence $R_1/R_3=3.0$.

perOption.A: Inverts the requested ratio to obtain $R_3/R_1$.
perOption.B: Divides $R_3$ by $R_2$, whose resistance is $20-12=8\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$.
perOption.C: The other two resistors total $12\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ in series, but $R_3$ alone is $4\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q23.body: The voltmeter measures the potential drop from X, so its reading starts near zero and increases along the paper. The narrow region has greater resistance per unit length, so the same current produces a steeper potential drop there. As the paper widens, the graph becomes less steep.

perOption.A: Starts above zero and treats the measured drop from X as a decreasing quantity.
perOption.B: Starts above zero and treats the uniform-width sections as having no resistance per unit length.
perOption.C: Makes the slope larger where the paper is wider and has less resistance per unit length.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q24.body: ST is parallel to the field and experiences zero magnetic force. The two vertical sides each experience a force of magnitude $BIy$, in opposite directions perpendicular to the loop. They form a couple with separation $x$, giving a moment of $BIxy$.

perOption.A: Applies $BIl$ to a side parallel to the field, for which $\sin\theta=0$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The equal and opposite forces on the vertical sides cancel in the net force.
perOption.D: The vertical sides each experience a magnetic force because they are perpendicular to the field.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q25.body: At each instant, the resistor dissipates power $I^2R$, so halving the current amplitude reduces the mean power to $P/4$ before rectification. An ideal diode removes one of the two equal contributions from the half-cycles, giving a mean power of $P/8$ over a full cycle.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Accounts for halving the current amplitude but ignores the blocked half-cycle.
perOption.C: Accounts for the blocked half-cycle alone.
perOption.D: Leaves the mean power unchanged despite the reduced current amplitude and the blocked half-cycle.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q26.body: The coil normal is at $30^\circ$ to the field. With $A=20\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, the flux linkage is $N\Phi=NBA\cos30^\circ=15(0.50)(20\times10^{-4})\cos30^\circ=1.3\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

perOption.A: Makes the converted area a factor of 100 too small.
perOption.B: Uses $\sin30^\circ$ even though $30^\circ$ is the angle to the coil normal.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Converts the area with a factor of $10^{-2}$ instead of $10^{-4}$.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q27.body: Higher intensity at the same frequency delivers more photons per second, so more photoelectrons are emitted per second and the saturation current increases. Photon energy $hf$ and maximum photoelectron kinetic energy $hf-\phi$ stay the same, so the stopping potential is unchanged. Curve A shows both features.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows a higher saturation current but also makes the stopping potential more negative.
perOption.C: Shows a lower saturation current and a more negative stopping potential.
perOption.D: Keeps the stopping potential the same but makes the saturation current smaller.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q28.body: The highest-energy X-ray photon can receive the electron’s entire kinetic energy, so $hc/\lambda_{\min}=p^2/(2m_e)$ in the nonrelativistic model. Doubling $p$ quadruples that energy and gives a new minimum wavelength of $\lambda_0/4$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats maximum photon energy as proportional to the electron’s momentum, or uses the electron’s de Broglie wavelength.
perOption.C: Makes wavelength increase linearly with electron momentum.
perOption.D: Correctly obtains a fourfold increase in energy but makes wavelength increase with it.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q29.body: Most alpha particles passed through the thin foil with little or no deflection. The rare large deflections show that the region producing strong scattering occupies very little of each atom, so most of the atom is empty space.

perOption.A: Alpha particles are positively charged.
perOption.B: The positive charge of the incident alpha particles was already known.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The observation that most particles pass through does not determine gold’s exact proton number.

acjc-2023-prelim-p1-q30.body: The energy released is the increase in total binding energy, and free neutrons contribute zero binding energy. For the two product nuclei and the original uranium nucleus, this gives $92(8.70)+141(8.33)-235(7.59)=191.28\ \mathrm{MeV}$, or $191\ \mathrm{MeV}$ to three significant figures.

perOption.A: Accounts for only part of the change in binding energy, which requires both product nuclei and the full uranium contribution.
perOption.B: Leaves out part of the net increase in binding energy across the two product nuclei.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Using 234 instead of 235 for the uranium nucleon count gives this value.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q1.body: Because $k$ is dimensionless, $P$ and $\rho Av^n$ have the same base units. This gives $(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}})(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})=(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}})(\mathrm{m^2})(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})^n$, so $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}}=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3+2+n}\,s^{-n}}$. Matching the powers of seconds gives $n=3$.

perOption.A: Gives a time factor of $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ for power.
perOption.B: Gives a time factor of $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$ for power.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives a time factor of $\mathrm{s^{-4}}$ for power.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q2.body: The gradient of the displacement–time graph gives velocity. Its gradient changes most rapidly in interval A, so A has the greatest magnitude of acceleration.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The gradient is nearly constant, so the velocity changes little.
perOption.C: The constant gradient represents constant velocity and zero acceleration.
perOption.D: The horizontal segment represents zero velocity throughout the interval.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q3.body: Use $s=ut+\frac12at^2$ with $u=0$ at release. Subtracting the two displacements gives $h=\frac12a(t_2^2-t_1^2)$, so $a=\frac{2h}{t_2^2-t_1^2}$. Since $a=g\sin\theta$, $g=\frac{2h}{(t_2^2-t_1^2)\sin\theta}$.

perOption.A: Gives the acceleration along the incline.
perOption.B: Uses $(t_2-t_1)^2$ as if the block started from rest at the first sensor.
perOption.C: Uses $\cos\theta$, the factor for the component perpendicular to the slope.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q4.body: The rate of change of momentum is $v\frac{\Delta m}{t}$, where $v$ is the water speed relative to the nozzle. In time $t$, a column of water of length $h$ passes through the nozzle, giving $\Delta m=\rho\pi r^2h$. Since $h/t=v$, the momentum rate is $\rho\pi r^2v^2=1000\pi(0.012)^2(10)^2\approx45\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Using the radius directly in place of $\pi r^2$ and counting the speed only once gives 120 but has the wrong units.
perOption.C: Uses $\pi r$ in place of the nozzle area $\pi r^2$.
perOption.D: Uses the circumference $2\pi r$ in place of the nozzle area $\pi r^2$.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q5.body: Take rightward as positive and conserve momentum for Charlie and the ball during the throw. From $0=(1.5)(2.5)+60u$, Charlie recoils at $u=-0.0625\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. When Charlie catches the returning ball, $(60)(-0.0625)+(1.5)(-2.5)=(61.5)v$. This gives $v=-0.122\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so Charlie's speed is $0.12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Treats the returning ball's momentum as opposite to Charlie's recoil momentum.
perOption.B: Uses Charlie's speed immediately after the throw.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses Charlie's mass alone for the final moving mass, giving a speed of $0.125\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ before rounding.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q5.issues: The key uses −0.0626 m/s in the catch equation after deriving −0.0625 m/s, and its symbolic throw equation has an inconsistent sign convention. The rewrite uses one signed velocity throughout.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q6.body: Vertical equilibrium gives $T\cos18^\circ=W$, so $T=520/\cos18^\circ\approx550\ \mathrm{N}$. Horizontal equilibrium gives $R=T\sin18^\circ=(520/\cos18^\circ)\sin18^\circ\approx170\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Calculates the tension by multiplying the weight by the cosine, leaving its vertical component too small.
perOption.B: Uses a tension smaller than the weight and assigns the cosine component to the horizontal reaction.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Sets the horizontal reaction equal to the weight, which balances the vertical component.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q7.body: Taking moments about the pivot gives $P(30)=Q(70)$. The required ratio is therefore $P/Q=7/3$, which is satisfied by $P=21\ \mathrm{N}$ and $Q=9.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the required load ratio.
perOption.B: Uses a ratio of 7 and drops the factor of 3 from the shorter arm.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a ratio of 3, making the moment from P too large.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q8.body: The useful power for lifting the water is $P=mg\Delta h/\Delta t=\rho Vg\Delta h/\Delta t$. Substituting gives $P=\frac{1000(0.20)(9.81)(10)}{5\times60}=65.4\ \mathrm{W}$. At 40% efficiency the required input power is $65.4/0.40=163.5\ \mathrm{W}$, which rounds to $160\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies the useful lifting power by the efficiency.
perOption.B: Gives the useful lifting power before converting to input power.
perOption.C: Correct. This is the required input power.
perOption.D: Uses 5 seconds for the lifting time.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q8.issues: The key interprets “power generated by the motor” as required input power (C). If the phrase means useful mechanical output under the key's energy model, the result is 65 W (B).

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q9.body: The hour hand takes $T=12\times60\times60\ \mathrm{s}$ to complete one revolution. Its angular speed is $\omega=2\pi/T\approx1.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses a six-hour period, doubling the angular speed.
perOption.C: Uses the one-hour period of the minute hand.
perOption.D: Implies roughly a one-minute period, treating the hour hand as a seconds hand.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q10.body: The linear speed is $v=r\omega$ and the centripetal acceleration is $a=\omega^2r$. With radius $r/2$ and angular speed $2\omega$, the new linear speed is $(r/2)(2\omega)=v$. The new centripetal acceleration is $(r/2)(2\omega)^2=2a$.

perOption.A: Ignores the doubled angular speed in the speed calculation and misses the doubling of acceleration.
perOption.B: Accounts for the smaller radius alone when calculating the linear speed.
perOption.C: Treats the acceleration as constant because the linear speed stays constant, overlooking the halved radius.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q11.body: The gravitational field strength due to a planet of mass $M$ is proportional to $M/r^2$. The key places the neutral point at B, close to Planet 1, where the short distance helps its field compete with the fields of the more massive planets. At A, on the line joining Planets 1 and 2, their fields can balance each other, but Planet 3 adds an off-axis field.

perOption.A: Considers only the balance of the two fields along the line joining Planets 1 and 2.
perOption.B: Correct. B lies near Planet 1 and off the line joining Planets 1 and 2.
perOption.C: Places the balance farther from Planet 1, where the key expects its field to be too weak.
perOption.D: Places the balance still farther from the least massive planet, weakening its contribution further.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q11.issues: B is the intended qualitative choice. Mass ratios and an unscaled sketch do not determine the exact neutral point or justify rejecting C and D by distance alone.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q12.body: The ideal gas equation $pV=nRT$ gives $1/p=V/(nRT)$. Halving both $n$ and $T$ reduces $nRT$ to one quarter of its original value, so the gradient becomes four times as large. This is line A.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Doubles the gradient by accounting for only one of the two changes.
perOption.C: Halves the gradient as if it were directly proportional to only one of the changed quantities.
perOption.D: Quarters the gradient as if it were directly proportional to the product of amount and temperature.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q13.body: Add the energy to warm the ice, melt it, and warm the resulting water. This gives $Q=(mc\Delta\theta)_{\mathrm{ice}}+ml_f+(mc\Delta\theta)_{\mathrm{water}}$. Substituting gives $Q=2.1(2108)(4.5)+2.1(334\times10^3)+2.1(4190)(96)\approx1.57\ \mathrm{MJ}$.

perOption.A: Counts the warming and melting of the ice but leaves out the warming of the water.
perOption.B: Counts only the two temperature increases, omitting the latent heat of fusion.
perOption.C: Omits the energy needed to warm the ice to its melting point.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q14.body: The kinetic theory assumes that the molecules together occupy a negligible fraction of the container's volume. Option C instead treats the volumes as comparable.

perOption.A: Random molecular motion is part of the model.
perOption.B: The model allows a distribution of molecular speeds.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Perfectly elastic collisions are part of the model.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q15.body: With critical damping, the system returns to equilibrium quickly without oscillating. Graph D shows the displacement approaching zero on that short timescale.

perOption.A: Shows undamped oscillations with constant amplitude.
perOption.B: Shows a slower nonoscillatory approach to equilibrium, characteristic of overdamping in the comparison.
perOption.C: Shows underdamping because the system still oscillates as its amplitude falls.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q15.issues: The graphs label signed displacement as amplitude. The intended B–D distinction is the relative return time shown schematically.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q16.body: In simple harmonic motion, $v=\pm\omega\sqrt{A_0^2-x^2}$. At $x=A_0/2$, the squared speed is $\omega^2[A_0^2-(A_0/2)^2]=\tfrac34 v_{\max}^2$. Since the total energy equals the maximum kinetic energy, the ratio is $\tfrac34=0.75$.

perOption.A: Treats the kinetic energy fraction as linear in displacement.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the speed ratio instead of its square.
perOption.D: Assumes all the energy is kinetic, as it is at equilibrium.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q17.body: One wavelength is the distance between adjacent compressions. The $100\ \mathrm{m}$ span contains five wavelengths, so $\lambda=100/5=20\ \mathrm{m}$. Using $v=f\lambda$ gives $350=20f$, so $f\approx18\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Uses twice the compression-to-compression spacing as the wavelength.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the compression-to-rarefaction spacing as a full wavelength.
perOption.D: Implies a sub-metre wavelength, whereas adjacent compressions are 20 m apart.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q18.body: The wavelength is $\lambda=v/f=36/400=0.090\ \mathrm{m}$. Using $\Delta x/\lambda=\Delta\phi/(2\pi)$ gives $\Delta\phi=[0.18/(36/400)](2\pi)=4\pi$. This is equivalent to the listed phase difference of $2\pi$, since both describe points in phase.

perOption.A: $0.50\pi$ represents a quarter-cycle phase offset.
perOption.B: This gives half a cycle, whereas the two points are in phase.
perOption.C: Correct. It is equivalent to the calculated two complete cycles.
perOption.D: $2.5\pi$ leaves a quarter-cycle offset after one full cycle is removed.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q18.issues: The unwrapped result is 4π rad and the principal phase difference is 0 rad. Neither is listed, but C is the only equivalent option.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q19.body: By Rayleigh’s criterion, $\theta\approx\lambda/b$. Doubling the slit width gives $\theta_{\mathrm{new}}/\theta_{\mathrm{old}}=b_{\mathrm{old}}/b_{\mathrm{new}}=0.5$. The new angular resolution is $2.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Assumes inverse-square dependence on slit width.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Assumes direct rather than inverse proportionality.
perOption.D: Assumes angular resolution grows as the square of slit width.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q20.body: Electric potential is a scalar. The charges at P and R are equal and opposite and equidistant from Q, so their potentials cancel. Only S contributes to the net potential at Q, giving $V_Q=\frac{1}{4\pi(8.85\times10^{-12})}\frac{100\times10^{-6}}{20\times10^{-2}}=+4.5\ \mathrm{MV}$.

perOption.A: Cancels the contributions from P and R but omits S.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses 10 cm instead of 20 cm for the distance from S to Q.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitude of the negative contribution from P as if it were positive.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q20.issues: The key uses A, B, C and D for the points labelled P, Q, R and S in the question.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q21.body: Field lines point away from a positive charge, and the potential due to that charge decreases with distance from it. In general, the field points in the direction of decreasing potential. Whether the field strength itself increases or decreases depends on how the spacing between field lines changes along the path.

perOption.A: Reverses the direction of change of potential.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The field weakens along an outward field line from a positive charge.
perOption.D: The field strengthens along an inward field line toward a negative charge.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q21.issues: The key says distance from the field line where the argument needs distance from the positive charge, and explicitly discusses only a positive source.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q22.body: The central wires form a single node, and the loops connected only to that node carry no current. The circuit reduces to two pairs of parallel resistors in series. The effective resistance is $2(1/R+1/R)^{-1}=R$.

perOption.A: Counts only one of the two parallel pairs.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Counts a single two-resistor path and ignores its parallel alternatives.
perOption.D: Follows four outer resistors in series and overlooks the central connections.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q23.body: Along JML the same current $I$ flows through $R$ and $2R$, so the total drop is $3IR$. Since L is earthed, $V_L=0$ and $V_J=3IR$. The drop is $IR$ along JM and $2IR$ along ML, so the equal-length second segment is twice as steep.

perOption.A: Reverses which wire has the greater potential drop.
perOption.B: Shows constant potential along each resistive wire and leaves L above zero.
perOption.C: Gives both equal-length wires the same potential drop.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q24.body: A vertical magnetic field would initially deflect a positive particle into the page or a negative particle out of the page. The observed deflection is downwards, so the field is electric. The particle is positive because its deflection is in the direction of the electric field.

perOption.A: A negative charge in the electric field would deflect upwards.
perOption.B: A negative charge in the magnetic field would initially deflect out of the page.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: A positive charge in the magnetic field would initially deflect into the page.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q25.body: At speed $v$ down the slope, the induced e.m.f. is $BLv\cos\theta$, so $I=BLv\cos\theta/R$. The magnetic force has magnitude $BIL$ and its component up the slope is $BIL\cos\theta$. At terminal speed, $mg\sin\theta=B(BLv\cos\theta/R)L\cos\theta$. Solving gives $v=\frac{mgR\tan\theta}{B^2L^2\cos\theta}$.

perOption.A: Uses the plane width and loses one factor of $\cos\theta$.
perOption.B: Uses the rod length but loses one factor of $\cos\theta$.
perOption.C: Uses the plane width for the conductor length.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q26.body: Over the first half-period, $V(t)=(2V_0/T)t$, and the other half has the same mean square. Thus $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{T}\int_0^{T/2}\frac{4V_0^2}{T^2}t^2\,dt}$. Evaluating gives $\sqrt{\frac{8V_0^2}{T^3}\frac{T^3}{3\times8}}=\frac{V_0}{\sqrt3}$.

perOption.A: Uses the average voltage, which is zero.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the RMS value for a sinusoidal waveform.
perOption.D: Uses the RMS value for an alternating voltage of constant magnitude $V_0$.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q27.body: The photoelectric equation is $hf=\Phi+eV_s$, with $\Phi=hf_m$. Thus $V_s=(h/e)f-\Phi/e$. A smaller work function lowers the threshold frequency while the gradient remains $h/e$, so the line shifts left and stays parallel to the original.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Keeps the original threshold and makes the line steeper.
perOption.C: Keeps the original threshold and makes the line shallower.
perOption.D: Keeps the slope but shifts the threshold to a higher frequency.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q27.issues: The key prints the wrong sign in the photoelectric equation and omits division by e in the intercept for Vₛ. Its graph reasoning and letter A are correct.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q28.body: Decreasing the tube voltage gives the electrons less energy, so the cutoff wavelength $\lambda_1$ increases. The target material is the same, so the characteristic wavelength $\lambda_2$ stays fixed.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the cutoff as fixed and the characteristic wavelength as voltage-dependent.
perOption.C: Reverses the effect of tube voltage on the cutoff.
perOption.D: Reverses the cutoff shift and assumes the characteristic wavelength also decreases.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q28.issues: The characteristic wavelength stays fixed provided the reduced voltage still allows that line to be excited.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q29.body: Most alpha particles still pass through with negligible deviation because atoms are mainly empty space. The heavier isotope has the same nuclear charge, and the chance of a nearly head-on encounter is approximately unchanged. The scattering pattern therefore shows no significant change.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Extra neutrons leave the nuclear charge and the chance of near-head-on scattering essentially unchanged.
perOption.C: The higher nuclear mass does not substantially strengthen the Coulomb repulsion responsible for large deflections.
perOption.D: Changing the isotope does not appreciably change the chance of an encounter that deflects an alpha particle.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q30.body: The fission products Y and Z are more stable than X. Each therefore has a higher binding energy per nucleon than X, so both ratios in row A exceed 1.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Both products have greater binding energy per nucleon than X, so the second ratio also exceeds 1.
perOption.C: Y has greater binding energy per nucleon than X, so the first ratio exceeds 1.
perOption.D: Reverses the binding-energy-per-nucleon comparison for the parent and its fission products.

acjc-2024-prelim-p1-q30.issues: The printed phrase 'total binding energy per nucleon of Y and Z' is ambiguous. For the usual heavy-nucleus fission assumed by the key, both the sum of the two values and the combined binding energy per nucleon exceed the value for X.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q1.body: The speed is constant, so $|\mathbf v_f|=|\mathbf v_i|$. Draw $\Delta\mathbf v=\mathbf v_f+(-\mathbf v_i)$ by adding the down-right final velocity to the leftward reverse of the initial velocity. The resultant points steeply down and left.

perOption.A: Points down and right even though the horizontal velocity decreases.
perOption.B: Points up and left even though the vertical change is downward.
perOption.C: Correct. The vector difference points steeply down and left.
perOption.D: Reverses the direction of the velocity change.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q1.issues: If the uniform field supplies the sole force, its fixed direction is incompatible with a curved path at constant speed. C follows from the stipulated endpoint velocities.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q2.body: On the way up, both weight and air resistance act downward, so the object slows at a rate greater than $g$. On the way down, air resistance opposes weight, so the downward acceleration is less than $g$. Over the same height interval the descent therefore takes longer, so $t_{\mathrm d}>t_{\mathrm u}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Drag adds to weight during the ascent and opposes it during the descent.
perOption.B: At the same height the object is slower on the way down because drag has dissipated energy.
perOption.C: Reverses the force comparison because drag reduces the resultant on descent.
perOption.D: Ignores the upward drag during descent and incorrectly infers a shorter descent time.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q3.body: Treat carts 3 and 4 as one system of mass $800\ \mathrm{kg}$. The bar tension $T$ is the only external horizontal force on this system. By $F=ma$, $T=800(2.0)=1600\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: Uses the mass of one cart as the force without applying the acceleration.
perOption.B: Uses the mass of only one trailing cart in $F=ma$.
perOption.C: Uses $600\ \mathrm{kg}$ in $F=ma$ even though the two trailing carts total $800\ \mathrm{kg}$.
perOption.D: Correct. The tension accelerates both trailing carts.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q4.body:
For balls of mass $m$, the initial momentum is $mv$, so the final momentum must also be $mv$. Options A and B give $mv$, while C gives $\tfrac12mv$ and D gives zero.

An elastic collision has equal relative speeds of approach and separation. A gives a separation speed of $v$, whereas B gives zero and fails to conserve kinetic energy.

perOption.A: Correct. Both momentum and the relative speed are conserved.
perOption.B: Conserves momentum but gives zero relative speed of separation, so kinetic energy is lost.
perOption.C: Gives a total final momentum of $\tfrac34mv-\tfrac14mv=\tfrac12mv$.
perOption.D: Gives zero total final momentum because the two momenta cancel.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q5.body: The object starts and finishes at the same height, so its gravitational potential energy is unchanged. The spring energy becomes kinetic energy and work done against friction, so $\tfrac12kx^2=(K_{\mathrm f}-K_{\mathrm i})+fd$. Since $K_{\mathrm i}=0$, $K_{\mathrm f}=\tfrac12kx^2-fd$.

perOption.A: Correct. Subtract the energy dissipated by friction from the initial spring energy.
perOption.B: Subtracts $mgH$ even though the object finishes at its starting height.
perOption.C: Adds $fd$ even though friction removes mechanical energy.
perOption.D: Adds the frictional loss and treats the dip as a net drop in height.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q6.body: At the bottom, the inward direction is upward, so $N-mg=mv^2/r$. Hence $N=mg+mv^2/r=0.52(9.3^2/1.3+9.81)=39.7\ \mathrm N\approx40\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: Equates the normal force to the weight, giving zero upward acceleration.
perOption.B: Subtracts the weight from the required inward resultant.
perOption.C: Gives the inward resultant alone and omits the downward weight.
perOption.D: Correct. The normal force supplies the inward resultant and balances the weight.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q7.body:
Each mass is a distance $r=\sqrt{10^2+10^2}\ \mathrm m$ from P. The horizontal field components cancel, so the resultant is $2(6.67\times10^{-11})(30)\cos45^\circ/r^2=1.4\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$ upward.

The two potentials add as scalars, giving $\phi=-2(6.67\times10^{-11})(30)/r=-2.8\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Add the upward field components and both negative potentials.
perOption.B: Incorrectly cancels the two equal negative scalar potentials.
perOption.C: Adds the full field magnitudes without resolving them.
perOption.D: Adds the full field magnitudes and incorrectly cancels the scalar potentials.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q8.body: At radius $r$, the orbital kinetic energy is $E_{\mathrm k}=GMm/(2r)=3.2\ \mathrm{MJ}$. The potential energy there is $E_{\mathrm p}=-GMm/r=-6.4\ \mathrm{MJ}$. At $2r$ it is $E_{\mathrm p}=-GMm/(2r)=-3.2\ \mathrm{MJ}$.

perOption.A: Divides the given kinetic energy by four using inverse-square scaling and gives it a negative sign.
perOption.B: Halves the given kinetic energy and changes its sign, missing the factor of two between the energy magnitudes at a given radius.
perOption.C: Correct. Doubling the radius halves the magnitude of the initial potential energy.
perOption.D: Gives the potential energy at $r$ without scaling it to $2r$.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q9.body: The key treats the two portions as initially at the same temperature, as they would be if they contained equal amounts of gas at the given pressure and volume. With the portions initially at the same temperature, removing the partition leaves the temperature and pressure unchanged, so the final pressure is $P$.

perOption.A: Accounts for expansion into twice the volume but counts only the gas from one half.
perOption.B: Correct. Both halves contribute to the final pressure.
perOption.C: Counts one half’s original pressure in full and halves only the other half’s contribution.
perOption.D: Adds the two original pressures without allowing each portion to spread through twice its original volume.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q9.issues: Equal initial pressure and volume imply equal NT, not equal T unless the amounts are equal. B is still valid for the intended same ideal gas with constant heat capacity, by conservation of internal energy.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q10.body: At the same temperature, both gases have the same mean molecular kinetic energy $\tfrac12m\langle c^2\rangle$. Thus $\langle c^2\rangle\propto1/m$, and $c_{\mathrm{rms},X}/c_{\mathrm{rms},Y}=\sqrt{m_Y/m_X}=\sqrt{1/2}=0.71$.

perOption.A: Uses the inverse mass ratio directly without taking its square root.
perOption.B: Correct. RMS speed scales as the inverse square root of mass.
perOption.C: Reverses the mass ratio under the square root.
perOption.D: Uses the direct mass ratio and omits the square root.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q11.body: Use $\Delta U=Q+W$, where $W$ is work done on the gas. Along path 1, $\Delta U=10+(-4)=+6\ \mathrm J$. The endpoints are the same for path 2, so $6=Q+(-2)$ and $Q=+8\ \mathrm J$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the work done by the gas from the internal energy increase when solving for heat input.
perOption.B: Correct. Path 2 requires $6\ \mathrm J$ for the internal energy increase and $2\ \mathrm J$ for work done by the gas.
perOption.C: Adds the work for path 2 to the heat input for path 1, instead of to the common internal energy change.
perOption.D: Treats work done by the gas in path 1 as positive in $\Delta U=Q+W$.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q12.body: Heavy damping prevents the system from oscillating after release. The resistance to motion is large, so the object approaches equilibrium slowly.

perOption.A: Correct. Heavy damping gives a slow approach to equilibrium.
perOption.B: An exponentially decaying oscillation is characteristic of light damping.
perOption.C: Heavy damping prevents repeated oscillations, so there is no oscillation amplitude that decays linearly.
perOption.D: Critical damping gives the fastest return without overshoot.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q13.body: For simple harmonic motion, $a_0=\omega^2x_0$. The graph gives $6.0=\omega^2(0.30)$, so $\omega=\sqrt{6.0/0.30}=4.47\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\approx4.5\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Divides displacement by acceleration and leaves the result unsquared-rooted.
perOption.B: Multiplies $6.0$ by $0.30$ instead of dividing and taking the square root.
perOption.C: Correct. The angular frequency is the square root of the gradient magnitude.
perOption.D: Gives the magnitude of the gradient, which equals $\omega^2$.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q14.body: P and S are at the centres of compressions, while T is at the centre of a rarefaction. A compression centre and a rarefaction centre differ in phase by $\pi\ \mathrm{rad}$, so P and T have that phase difference.

perOption.A: P and S are both compression centres, so they are in phase.
perOption.B: Correct. P is at a compression centre and T is at a rarefaction centre.
perOption.C: Mistakes the relatively wide spacing between Q and R for a half-cycle separation.
perOption.D: R is between a rarefaction centre and the compression centred at S, so the pair is less than half a cycle apart.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q15.body: One full cycle spans $4.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ on the screen, giving $T=4(4.0\times10^{-5})=1.6\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm s$. The frequency is $f=1/T=6250\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Hence $\lambda=v/f=330/6250=5.3\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Uses one horizontal division for a whole cycle.
perOption.B: Uses two horizontal divisions, which span only half a cycle.
perOption.C: Reads the width of a cycle on the screen as a physical wavelength in air.
perOption.D: Correct. The full-cycle time gives a wavelength of $5.3\ \mathrm{cm}$.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q16.body: The double-slit relation is $\lambda=ax/D$, so $x=\lambda D/a$. Fringe separation is directly proportional to wavelength, and the plotted range starts at $400\ \mathrm{nm}$, where the separation is already positive.

perOption.A: Treats the left edge of the graph as zero wavelength.
perOption.B: Correct. The spacing rises linearly from a positive value at 400 nm.
perOption.C: Makes the spacing decrease linearly as wavelength increases.
perOption.D: Makes the spacing decrease nonlinearly as wavelength increases.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q17.body: The limiting angle is $\theta\approx\lambda/b$, where $b$ is the dish diameter. By the small-angle approximation, $x/D\approx\theta$, so $x=\lambda D/b=(0.40\times10^{-6})(2.8\times10^{25})/5.1=2.2\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Halves the full source separation found from the limiting angle.
perOption.B: Correct. The minimum separation is the distance multiplied by the limiting angle.
perOption.C: Inverting the limiting angle and then halving the resulting distance gives this value.
perOption.D: Divides the source distance by the limiting angle instead of multiplying.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q18.body: The receiver travels $33.5/12.0=2.79$ wavelengths. Since X is an antinode, the nodes occur $0.25\lambda$, $0.75\lambda$, $1.25\lambda$, $1.75\lambda$, $2.25\lambda$ and $2.75\lambda$ from X, so six minima are detected.

perOption.A: Counts only complete wavelengths, missing the nodes spaced half a wavelength apart.
perOption.B: Counting just the nodes at quarter-wavelength plus whole-wavelength offsets skips every second node.
perOption.C: Counting only complete half-wavelength intervals misses the sixth node at $2.75\lambda$.
perOption.D: Correct. Six nodes lie within the distance travelled.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q19.body: The electric field $E$ between the parallel charged plates is uniform. The force $F=qE$ on the $\alpha$-particle is therefore constant throughout the gap.

perOption.A: The force must stay at the same nonzero value throughout the uniform field.
perOption.B: The fixed charge and uniform field require a horizontal force graph.
perOption.C: Correct. The force is constant between the plates.
perOption.D: The field is uniform, so the force cannot vary with position.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The question PNG cuts off all four option graphs. C is supported by the worked key, but the graph labels and distractor shapes could not be independently verified.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q20.body: Moving along a field line takes you from one equipotential to another. The potential therefore changes in both an electric field and a gravitational field.

perOption.A: Electric potential is work done per unit charge, and gravitational potential is work done per unit mass.
perOption.B: For point sources, both potentials vary as $1/r$.
perOption.C: The electric potential of a positively charged object can be positive.
perOption.D: Correct. A field line crosses equipotentials.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q21.body: From $I=nevA$, the drift speed is $v=I/(neA)$. Since $I$, $n$ and $e$ are the same for both wires, $v\propto1/A\propto1/d^2$. Hence $v_Y/v_X=d_X^2/d_Y^2=d^2/(2d)^2=0.25$.

perOption.A: Correct. Quadrupling the area quarters the drift speed.
perOption.B: Uses inverse diameter instead of inverse cross-sectional area.
perOption.C: Treats drift speed as directly proportional to diameter.
perOption.D: Treats drift speed as directly proportional to cross-sectional area.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q22.body: Between $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ and $9.0\ \mathrm{V}$, the ratio $I/V$ increases as $V$ increases. Its reciprocal, $V/I$, decreases, so the resistance decreases.

perOption.A: Correct. The ratio $V/I$ falls as the voltage rises over this interval.
perOption.B: Calculates $I/V$, which gives conductance in siemens.
perOption.C: Uses the inverse slope $\Delta V/\Delta I$ instead of the point ratio $V/I$.
perOption.D: Zero current at a nonzero voltage indicates effectively infinite resistance.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q23.body: When Q blows, the effective resistance of the right-hand part of the circuit increases. By the potential divider principle, S receives a larger share of the cell voltage and brightens, while P and R receive a smaller share and dim.

perOption.A: P receives a smaller potential difference and becomes dimmer.
perOption.B: Correct. S receives a larger share of the cell voltage.
perOption.C: S still has a complete path through the left-hand parallel pair.
perOption.D: The voltage across the P–R pair falls, so both lamps dim.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q24.body: Use the right-hand grip rule at each wire and add the four field contributions at each midpoint. The resultant points down at P, right at Q, up at R and left at S.

perOption.A: Correct. The four resultant directions are different.
perOption.B: P and Q have perpendicular fields, as do R and S.
perOption.C: P and R have opposite fields, as do Q and S.
perOption.D: The resultant changes direction from one midpoint to the next.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q25.body: The magnetic force on the electron points out of the page and has magnitude $F_B=Bev\sin\theta$. To keep the electron undeflected, the electric force must have the same magnitude, so $E=F_E/e=Bv\sin\theta$. The electric force points into the page, so the electric field points out of the page because the electron is negatively charged.

perOption.A: Keeps the charge rather than the speed in the field magnitude and reverses the required field direction.
perOption.B: Keeps the charge rather than the speed after dividing the magnetic force by $e$.
perOption.C: Assigns the electric force direction to the field even though the electron is negatively charged.
perOption.D: Correct. The field is $Bv\sin\theta$ out of the page.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q26.body: In one rotation, the spoke sweeps an area $A=\pi r^2$, so the flux swept is $BA$. The rotation period is $T=2\pi/\omega$, so the induced e.m.f. is $BA/T=\tfrac12 Br^2\omega$. Substituting gives $\tfrac12(0.23)(0.65)^2(120)=5.8\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Halving the flux rate again gives half the e.m.f. across one spoke.
perOption.B: Correct. The spoke sweeps flux at a rate of $5.8\ \mathrm{Wb\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Uses the rim speed along the whole spoke, giving twice the correct e.m.f.
perOption.D: Uses $B\omega r$, omitting the additional length and the factor of one-half from the swept-area calculation.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q27.body: The diode rectifies the square wave so the resistor sees $V_0$ for half a period $T$ and zero for the other half. Thus $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{V_0^2(T/2)/T}=V_0/\sqrt{2}$. The mean power is $P_{\mathrm{ave}}=V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/R=V_0^2/(2R)$.

perOption.A: Squares the mean voltage $V_0/2$ rather than taking the mean of the squared voltage.
perOption.B: Correct. The resistor dissipates peak power for half the cycle.
perOption.C: Applies the RMS factor $1/\sqrt{2}$ to only one of the two voltage factors in the power calculation.
perOption.D: Treats the resistor as dissipating peak power throughout the cycle.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q28.body: A photon of wavelength $650\ \mathrm{nm}$ has energy $E=hc/\lambda=(6.63\times10^{-34})(3.0\times10^8)/(650\times10^{-9})$, which converts to $1.9\ \mathrm{eV}$. The transition from $E_3$ to $E_2$ releases the same energy, $20.6-18.7=1.9\ \mathrm{eV}$.

perOption.A: This transition releases $2.7\ \mathrm{eV}$, exceeding the photon energy.
perOption.B: This transition releases $20.6\ \mathrm{eV}$, exceeding the photon energy.
perOption.C: This transition releases $4.6\ \mathrm{eV}$, exceeding the photon energy.
perOption.D: Correct. The level difference is $1.9\ \mathrm{eV}$.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q29.body: Increasing the accelerating potential difference gives the electrons more kinetic energy, increasing the maximum energy of the emitted X-rays. This reduces the cutoff wavelength. The target is unchanged, so its characteristic wavelengths stay the same.

perOption.A: Treats the characteristic wavelengths as voltage-dependent even though the target's energy gaps are unchanged.
perOption.B: Correct. The cutoff decreases and the characteristic wavelengths stay fixed.
perOption.C: Reverses the cutoff shift and incorrectly makes the characteristic wavelengths depend on voltage.
perOption.D: Higher maximum photon energy corresponds to a shorter cutoff wavelength.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q30.body: The key selects the large drop in count rate over $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ of air because alpha radiation has a short range in air. Beta and gamma radiation are more penetrating, so the key uses the short-distance drop as the distinguishing observation.

perOption.A: Correct. Alpha radiation has a short range in air.
perOption.B: A lead block can shield alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
perOption.C: Both alpha and beta particles are charged and deflect in a perpendicular electric field.
perOption.D: A magnetic field parallel to the beam leaves alpha, beta and gamma radiation undeflected.

acjc-2025-prelim-p1-q30.issues: A is the intended and best available option, but none of the options establishes exclusive alpha emission. A significant drop is compatible with an alpha-dominated mixture that also emits beta or gamma, and a change in detector distance can reduce count rate through geometry alone.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body:
A hydrogen nucleus is about $10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$ across and light travels at about $10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (order of magnitude).

Time $\approx \dfrac{10^{-15}}{10^{8}} = 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Far too long: light covers tens of metres in $10^{-7}$ s.
perOption.B: This is the size of the nucleus in metres, not the crossing time.
perOption.C: Uses the size of a whole atom (~$10^{-10}$ m) instead of the nucleus.
perOption.D: Correct. Nuclear diameter divided by the speed of light.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body:
For equilibrium, the resultant torque about the support must be zero.

Since the body is balanced on a single support, the line of action of its weight must pass through the support.

perOption.A: Equal masses on each side do not give zero torque for a non-uniform body; moments depend on distances too.
perOption.B: For a non-uniform body the centre of gravity need not be at the geometric centre.
perOption.C: Correct. The weight then has zero moment about the support.
perOption.D: The force by the body on the support and the support's reaction are a Newton's third law pair acting on different bodies; they don't explain the body's equilibrium.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
By symmetry, the tension $T$ in both strings is the same.

The vertical components balance the weight: $2T\sin\theta = W$, where $\theta$ is the small angle each string makes with the horizontal.

Since the strings are almost horizontal, $\sin\theta$ is very small, so $T = \dfrac{W}{2\sin\theta}$ must be greater than $W$.

perOption.A: $T$ can never be less than $W/2$; two strings must at least share the weight.
perOption.B: Only true if both strings were vertical.
perOption.C: Would need $\theta \ge 30^\circ$; nearly horizontal strings give much larger tension.
perOption.D: Correct. Small $\sin\theta$ makes $T \gg W$.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body:
By conservation of energy, loss in GPE = gain in elastic potential energy:

$mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, so $x = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mgh}{k}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(0.22)(9.81)(0.40)}{350}} = 7.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: This is $x^2$: forgets to take the square root.
perOption.B: About what you get with $h = 0.40$ cm taken as $0.004$ m (factor-of-100 error in $h$).
perOption.C: Omits $g$ from $mgh$.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body:
As air resistance is negligible, the acceleration ($g$) does not depend on mass, so it does not change.

The time of flight remains the same, and with the same horizontal velocity, the horizontal displacement also remains the same.

perOption.A: Correct. Motion is independent of mass without air resistance.
perOption.B: Horizontal velocity and time are unchanged, so the distance cannot decrease.
perOption.C: A heavier ball does not fall faster; vertical acceleration is $g$ for all masses.
perOption.D: Assumes heavier objects fall faster; both time and distance are unchanged.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body:
For vertical equilibrium, $F_y = mg$. For horizontal motion, $F_x = ma = 0.50\,mg$.

$F = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2} = \sqrt{(0.50mg)^2 + (mg)^2} = 1.1\,mg$.

perOption.A: Only the horizontal component $F_x$; ignores supporting the weight.
perOption.B: Only the vertical component $F_y$; ignores the acceleration.
perOption.C: Correct. Vector sum of the two perpendicular components.
perOption.D: Adds the components as scalars instead of as vectors.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body:
$a_c = r\omega^2 = r\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2$.

With $T$ unchanged, $a_c \propto r$, so doubling $r$ gives $a_{\text{new}} = 2a_c$.

perOption.A: Treats $a = v^2/r$ as $\propto v^2$ only, forgetting that $r$ also doubles in the denominator.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses $a = v^2/r$ with $v$ held constant, but $v = 2\pi r/T$ doubles.
perOption.D: Ignores the dependence on $r$ at fixed period.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body:
$g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$ and $M = \rho\left(\tfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3\right)$, so $g = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi G\rho R$.

With the same density, $g \propto R$, so $g_A : g_B = 2 : 1$.

perOption.A: Uses $g \propto 1/R^2$ with the same mass, but the mass is not the same.
perOption.B: Inverts the ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the mass ratio ($M \propto R^3$) and forgets the $1/R^2$ factor.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body:
Total energy in orbit is $-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, so

$\Delta TE = -\dfrac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(6.0\times10^{24})(690)}{2}\left[\dfrac{1}{7.2\times10^{6}} - \dfrac{1}{6.5\times10^{6}}\right] = +2\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Or: $\Delta KE = \tfrac{1}{2}(690)[(7.5\times10^{3})^2 - (7.9\times10^{3})^2] = -2.13\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$ and $\Delta GPE = -GMm\left[\dfrac{1}{7.2\times10^{6}} - \dfrac{1}{6.5\times10^{6}}\right] = +4.13\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$, giving $\Delta TE = +2\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The satellite gains total energy moving to a higher orbit.
perOption.B: This is only the gain in GPE; it ignores the loss of KE.
perOption.C: This is only the change in KE; the GPE gain is larger.
