perOption.D: Treats both the KE and GPE changes as losses ($-2.1 - 4.1 \approx -6\times10^{9}$ J).

perOption.A: Uses $\omega = f$ instead of $\omega = 2\pi f$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Omits the factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
perOption.D: Uses an amplitude of 5.0 cm instead of 5.0 mm.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body:
The cork vibrates with maximum amplitude at resonance, when the wave period equals the cork's natural period, $T = 0.12$ s.

$v = \sqrt{gd} = \dfrac{\lambda}{T}$, so $\lambda = T\sqrt{gd} = 0.12\sqrt{9.81\times0.30} = 0.206\ \mathrm{m} \approx 0.21\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Does not follow from $\lambda = vT$ with $v = \sqrt{gd}$.
perOption.B: Does not follow from $\lambda = vT$ with $v = \sqrt{gd}$.
perOption.C: Correct. Resonance: wave period equals the natural period.
perOption.D: Forgets the square root: $Tgd \approx 0.35$ m.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body:
Intensity $\propto$ amplitude$^2$, so twice the intensity means the amplitude is $\sqrt{2}$ times larger.

Half the frequency means the period is doubled, so the graph shows half as many cycles.

perOption.A: Doubles the amplitude, as if intensity were proportional to amplitude.
perOption.B: Correct. Amplitude $\times\sqrt{2}$ and period doubled.
perOption.C: Doubles the amplitude and doubles the frequency instead of halving it.
perOption.D: Correct amplitude, but the frequency is doubled instead of halved.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body:
The first polariser transmits half of the unpolarised light: $\tfrac{1}{2}I_0$.

By Malus' law, $I = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}I_0\right)\cos^2 60^\circ = \tfrac{1}{8}I_0$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Applies $\cos^2 60^\circ$ but forgets the first polariser halves unpolarised light.
perOption.C: Uses $\sin^2 60^\circ$ instead of $\cos^2 60^\circ$.
perOption.D: Ignores the effect of the second polariser.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body:
$\sin\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$. Since the slit-screen distance $D$ is much greater than the slit width, the angle is small.

$\theta = \dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}x}{D} = \dfrac{\lambda}{b}$, so $x = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{b}$.

New width: $x' = \dfrac{2(2\lambda)D}{b/2} = \dfrac{8\lambda D}{b} = 4x$.

perOption.A: Wrong proportionality; $x \propto \lambda/b$, so both changes widen the pattern.
perOption.B: Assumes the two changes cancel, but doubling λ and halving b both increase the width.
perOption.C: Accounts for only one of the two changes.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body:
$\sin\theta_1 = \dfrac{(1)\lambda}{d}$ and $\sin\theta_2 = \dfrac{(2)\lambda}{d}$, so $\sin\theta_2 = 2\sin\theta_1$.

The rate of increase of $\sin\theta$ decreases as $\theta$ increases from 0 to 90°, so $\theta_2 > 2\theta_1$.

At higher orders, since the distance travelled by the light increases, intensity decreases, so the second order is dimmer.

perOption.A: Assumes $\theta \propto n$, but it is $\sin\theta$ that is proportional to $n$; also intensity is not the same.
perOption.B: Assumes $\theta \propto n$; it is $\sin\theta$ that doubles.
perOption.C: Angle relation is right, but higher orders are dimmer.
perOption.D: Correct.

perOption.A: Uses 200 m instead of 200 km for the orbital height.
perOption.B: Introduces an extra factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a lens diameter of 3.5 cm instead of 35 cm.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body:
When a molecule collides elastically with a wall, its velocity reverses, so the magnitude of its change in momentum is twice its momentum before the collision. This change is not negligible; it is what produces the pressure.

So D is not a valid assumption.

perOption.A: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.
perOption.B: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.
perOption.C: This is a valid kinetic theory assumption.
perOption.D: Correct. The momentum change $2mu$ per collision is what causes the pressure.

perOption.A: Does not follow from $p \propto T/V$; mishandles the temperature or volume ratio.
perOption.B: Uses Celsius temperatures instead of kelvin.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Multiplies by the volume ratio instead of dividing (treats $p \propto V$).

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body:
Movement along an equipotential surface involves zero work done, so only the radial parts of each path matter.

Paths Y and Z both end on the same (middle) equipotential, so $W_Y = W_Z$. Path X ends on the inner equipotential, closer to Q, so $W_X$ is larger.

perOption.A: Assumes longer paths need more work, but work depends only on the start and end potentials.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Path X ends at a higher potential than Y and Z, so more work is needed.
perOption.D: Inverts the comparison; X goes closer to Q, so it needs more work.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: Electric field strength at a point is equal to the negative potential gradient at that point: $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dx}$ at P.

perOption.A: $V/D$ is not the field; field depends on the gradient of $V$, not the ratio.
perOption.B: Still uses the ratio $V/D$ rather than the gradient.
perOption.C: Missing the negative sign; $V$ decreases with $x$, so $dV/dx$ is negative while $E$ points outward.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: Current is $I=dQ/dt$. In the first three hours, $Q=(0.60)(3\times60\times60)=6480\ \mathrm{C}$. In the fourth hour the mean current is half the initial current, giving $Q=\tfrac12(0.60)(60\times60)=1080\ \mathrm{C}$. The total is $6480+1080\approx7.6\times10^3\ \mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Uses a time scale of minutes without converting it to seconds.
perOption.B: Uses the fourth-hour mean current for all four hours.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Keeps the current at 0.60 A throughout the fourth hour.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: Resistance is $R=V/I$. The initial straight line through the origin gives a constant $V/I$. As graph D bends over, $I/V$ falls and $V/I$ increases.

perOption.A: The resistance increases from the start.
perOption.B: The resistance falls as the voltage rises.
perOption.C: The resistance is initially constant and then falls.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The three parallel resistors have an equivalent resistance of $R/3$ and a potential difference of $3.0\ \mathrm{V}$. The series resistor has three times that resistance, so its potential difference is $3\times3.0=9.0\ \mathrm{V}$. The battery e.m.f. is $3.0+9.0=12.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Uses only the voltage across the parallel group.
perOption.B: Reverses the series voltage ratio, assigning 1.0 V to the single resistor.
perOption.C: Assumes the two series sections have equal voltage drops.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: The force is $F=BIL\sin\theta=(3.4\times10^{-2})(3.7)(0.050)\sin70^\circ=5.9\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{N}$. By Fleming’s left-hand rule, the leftward field and downward current component give a force into the paper.

perOption.A: Uses the component parallel to the field to calculate the force.
perOption.B: Uses the parallel component and reverses the force direction.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Reverses the force direction.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: The magnetic force has magnitude $B|q|v=(2.0\times10^{-3})(1.60\times10^{-19})(3.0\times10^6)=9.6\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{N}$. It provides the centripetal force for uniform circular motion, so speed and kinetic energy stay constant. The velocity changes direction, so the momentum changes.

perOption.A: Omits statement 2 even though the kinetic energy stays constant.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Includes statements 1 and 2 only.
perOption.D: Includes the false statement 3 and omits both true statements.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: Faraday’s law gives the magnitude of the average induced e.m.f. as $\mathcal{E}=NA|\Delta B|/\Delta t$. Substitution gives $\mathcal{E}=\frac{5\pi(0.060)^2}{0.42}(0.75-0.18)=0.0767\ \mathrm{V}$, or $77\ \mathrm{mV}$.

perOption.A: Calculates the e.m.f. for one turn.
perOption.B: Uses a flux-density change smaller than 0.57 T or an equivalent underestimate of the flux-linkage change.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overestimates the ratio of the flux-linkage change to the elapsed time.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: The secondary current is $I_s=V_s/R=80/100=0.80\ \mathrm{A}$. For the ideal transformer, $I_p/I_s=N_s/N_p$, so $I_p=(1000/200)(0.80)=4.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Inverts the current ratio.
perOption.B: Uses the secondary current as the ammeter reading.
perOption.C: Divides by the peak-to-r.m.s. factor even though the given a.c. voltage is already r.m.s.
perOption.D: Correct.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.issues: The key’s second equation labels the numerical current as the current ratio. The ratio is 5, and the primary current is 4.0 A.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The key compares how spread out the probability density $|\psi|^2$ is. In A, equally high peaks recur across the graph, while B, C and D are concentrated near the centre. Using the position–momentum uncertainty principle, the key takes A’s greater spread in position to indicate the smallest spread in momentum.

perOption.A: Correct. This is the key’s choice based on the broad spatial spread.
perOption.B: Its probability density is concentrated more strongly near the centre than A’s.
perOption.C: Its probability density is concentrated near the centre, so the key rejects it on the basis of spatial extent.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.issues: Printed key and keyAnswer both give A. The uncertainty relation only sets a lower bound on momentum spread. Taken literally as a real sinusoid, A has opposite momentum components at ±ℏk, while C’s broad, smooth, nonoscillating profile suggests a narrower distribution around zero momentum. C is the better choice on that reading, though the sketches do not specify full wavefunctions.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Compare the positions of each element’s emission lines with the lines in the nebula spectrum. All the lines shown for helium and hydrogen match. Nitrogen and krypton each have lines missing from the nebula spectrum.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Includes krypton even though some of its lines are missing.

acjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: For radioactive decay, $A=A_0e^{-\lambda t}$. At three years, $A_0/3=A_0e^{-3\lambda}$, so $\lambda=\ln(1/3)/(-3)=0.36620\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. At six years, $A=A_0e^{-0.36620(6)}\approx0.11A_0$.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q1.body: One joule is $1\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Substituting into $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ cancels the kilogram and leaves $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}\,K^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses only one factor of length in the joule.
perOption.B: Correct.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q2.body: The factor of $3$ cancels when the absolute uncertainty of $3X$ is divided by $3X$, leaving $x$. Squaring $Y$ gives a fractional uncertainty of $2y$, and the fractional uncertainties add for the quotient, giving $x+2y$.

perOption.B: Multiplies the fractional uncertainty of $X$ by 3 and subtracts the denominator's contribution.

perOption.D: Subtracts the denominator's fractional uncertainty.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q3.body: Before braking, $v$ is constant. During braking, $v^2=u^2+2as$, with $a$ constant and negative and $s$ measured from the start of braking. Thus $v=\sqrt{u^2+2as}$, which falls increasingly steeply as the car comes to rest.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q4.body: The object starts from rest, where air resistance is negligible, so the initial velocity–time gradient is the same as in vacuum, $g$. As speed increases, air resistance increases and the gradient falls.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q5.body: The horizontal change in momentum is $p\cos\theta-p\cos\theta=0$, so the average horizontal force is zero. Taking upward as positive, the vertical change is $p\sin\theta-(-p\sin\theta)=2p\sin\theta$. Dividing by the contact time gives an average resultant force of magnitude $2p\sin\theta/t$.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q6.body: About the bottom-left corner of the book, its weight acts with horizontal lever arm $x/2$, producing a clockwise moment $Wx/2$. For rotational equilibrium the net moment about that corner is zero, so the student supplies an anticlockwise moment $Wx/2$.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q7.body: The rate of increase of kinetic energy is the net mechanical power, $F_{\mathrm{net}}v$. With $F_{\mathrm{net}}=ma$, this gives $(250000)(0.90)(5.0)\ \mathrm{W}\approx1.1\ \mathrm{MW}$.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q8.body: Convert the radius to $1.22\times10^9\ \mathrm{m}$ and the period to $(15.9)(24)(3600)\ \mathrm{s}$. Using $a=r\omega^2$ gives $a=(1.22\times10^9)\left[\frac{2\pi}{(15.9)(24)(3600)}\right]^2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\approx2.55\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Omits one factor of $2\pi$ in the squared angular-speed term.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q9.body: All points on the record have the same constant angular speed $\omega$. Since $v=r\omega$, linear speed is directly proportional to radius and the graph is a straight line through the origin.

At a height $2R_{\mathrm E}$ the radius is $3R_{\mathrm E}$, giving $v_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{1.1\times10^4}{\sqrt3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx6.4\times10^3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q11.body: A geostationary satellite stays above a fixed point on the equator by matching Earth's angular velocity, including its west-to-east direction. Its orbital radius is greater than the equatorial radius, so its linear speed is greater.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q12.body: For container X, $p_X=n_X R(2T)/(2V)=n_XRT/V$. For container Y, $p_Y=n_YRT/V$. The tube connects the gases, so $p_X=p_Y$ and hence $n_X/n_Y=1$.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q13.body: The same heat input gives $Q=mc_{\mathrm w}\Delta T_{\mathrm w}=mc_{\mathrm i}\Delta T_{\mathrm i}$. Hence $\Delta T_{\mathrm i}/\Delta T_{\mathrm w}=c_{\mathrm w}/c_{\mathrm i}>1$. Both start at the same temperature, so iron ends up warmer.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q14.body: The clockwise cycle gives net work done by the gas equal to the enclosed triangular area, $\frac12(4-1)\times10^{-3}(8-4)\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}=60\ \mathrm{J}$. The net work done on the gas is therefore $-60\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Includes only the work done on the gas during expansion.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q15.body: Under light damping the amplitude of oscillation decreases exponentially. The energy associated with that amplitude scales with its square, so the total energy decreases along a curve that gradually flattens.

perOption.B: Shows energy being lost at a constant rate.
perOption.C: Shows no energy loss despite damping.
perOption.D: Shows total energy periodically increasing even though damping removes mechanical energy.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q16.body: P is at a crest and its transverse speed is zero. The displacement of Q varies sinusoidally with time. At the trough R the speed is zero, so its kinetic energy is zero. At S the displacement is greatest in magnitude, and $a=-\omega^2x$ gives the greatest acceleration magnitude.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q17.body: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. The bright fringe has $I_o\propto(2A+A)^2$ and the dark fringe has $I\propto(2A-A)^2$. Thus $I/I_o=(A/3A)^2=1/9$.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q18.body: Using $s=r\theta$, the angular separation is $\theta=25/(335\times10^3)=7.46\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}$, or $7.5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}$. The minimum angle of resolution is $\theta_m\approx\lambda/b=(500\times10^{-9})/(200\times10^{-3})=2.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad}$. The images are resolved because the angular separation exceeds this minimum.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q19.body: The electric force on P must initially act upwards to balance its weight, so the upper plate is at lower potential than the lower plate. Reducing the voltage makes P fall towards the higher-potential plate, so its electric potential energy increases during the fall. Its gravitational potential energy decreases as it loses height.

perOption.A: During the fall the positive charge moves towards higher electric potential.
perOption.B: Correct. The fall raises electric potential energy and lowers gravitational potential energy.
perOption.C: During the rise the positive charge moves towards lower electric potential.
perOption.D: After the voltage change the two forces have different magnitudes and do unequal amounts of work over the same displacement.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The key describes the motion after adjusting the voltage. Comparing the electric potential energy across the voltage adjustment itself would require a common reference for the plate potentials.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q20.body: Electric field strength is the negative potential gradient, $E=-\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}x$. From P to the $0\ \mathrm{V}$ line, successive drops of $100\ \mathrm{V}$ occur over increasing distances, so the field weakens. From the centre towards Q the distances for the same potential drops decrease, so the field strengthens.

perOption.A: Correct. The field is weakest at the centre.
perOption.B: This misses the strengthening field where the equipotentials close up near Q.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q21.body: The metal wire at constant temperature has constant resistance, giving straight line Y. The filament lamp’s resistance rises with potential difference, giving Z. The diode begins conducting appreciably at about $0.3$–$0.7\ \mathrm{V}$ in forward bias, after which the current rises steeply as in X.

perOption.A: This assigns the diode’s threshold to the metal wire and the straight line to the lamp.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q22.body: No current flows through the ideal voltmeter, so $I_1=I_2$ and the ammeter reads $I_2$. The voltmeter measures the drop across $R_1$, which equals the drop across the parallel branch containing $R_2$. The loop rule gives $V=I_2R_1=I_3R_2=E-I_4R_3$.

perOption.A: $I_1$ is a valid current reading, but $I_4R_3+I_3R_2$ gives the full battery e.m.f.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q23.body: The magnetic force on XY must be downwards to balance the moment of the rider’s weight. With the current flowing from X to Y, Fleming’s left-hand rule gives a field directed to the right.

perOption.A: A downward field gives a sideways force.
perOption.B: The leftward field gives an upward force.
perOption.C: An upward field gives a sideways force.
perOption.D: Correct. The rightward field gives a downward force.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q24.body: The induced e.m.f. is $E=Blv$, where $v$ is the horizontal component of the rod’s velocity. From P to Q the rod moves parallel to the field and $E=0$. From Q to R the constant component of weight along the slope makes the horizontal speed increase at a constant rate, so $E$ rises linearly. After R the rod is in projectile motion with constant horizontal velocity, so $E$ stays constant while it is in the field.

perOption.A: This drops the e.m.f. to zero at launch even though the rod retains horizontal velocity in the field.
perOption.B: Correct. The e.m.f. follows the horizontal velocity through all three stages.
perOption.C: This continues the horizontal acceleration after launch, when gravity acts vertically.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q24.issues: The key idealises the transition to rolling at Q. The impact transient and eventual exit from the field are outside the model used for the best-fit graph.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q25.body: The first source gives $V_{\mathrm{rms}}=150/\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{V}$. Using $P=V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/R$ gives $13=150^2/(2R)$, so $R=865\ \Omega$ and the series resistance is $2\times865\ \Omega$. The total power is $240^2/(2\times865)\approx33\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Treating the first peak voltage as r.m.s. doubles the inferred resistance and halves the final power.
perOption.B: Correct. The series pair dissipates 33 W.
perOption.C: The calculation requires the square of the r.m.s. voltage divided by the full series resistance.
perOption.D: This applies the full mains voltage to just one resistor.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q26.body: The voltage ratio gives $V_s/V_p=5/1$, so $V_s=5\times240=1200\ \mathrm{V}$. The secondary current is $I_s=1200/1000=1.2\ \mathrm{A}$. Since $I_p/I_s=5/1$, the primary current is $I_p=5\times1.2=6.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: This can result from reversing the current ratio or applying the primary voltage directly to the load.
perOption.B: This is the secondary current through the load.
perOption.C: Correct. The primary current is five times the secondary current.
perOption.D: This overstates the current multiplication, which is a factor of five applied to 1.2 A.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q27.body: The electron emission rate at maximum current is $I/e=(2.0\times10^{-6})/(1.6\times10^{-19})=1.25\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The incident photon rate is $P/E_\gamma=(3.1\times10^{-3})/(3.11\times1.6\times10^{-19})=6.23\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The ratio is $(1.25\times10^{13})/(6.23\times10^{15})=2.0\times10^{-3}$.

perOption.A: This uses the current directly without converting it to electrons per second.
perOption.B: Correct. About two electrons are emitted per thousand incident photons.
perOption.C: This assumes that every incident photon ejects an electron.
perOption.D: This omits the electronvolt-to-joule conversion for the photon rate.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q28.body: Use the syllabus estimate $\Delta p_x\Delta x\gtrsim h$, with $\Delta p_x=m\Delta v$ and $\Delta x=0.25\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$. Substitution gives $(5.30\times10^{-26}\Delta v)(0.25\times10^{-3})\gtrsim6.63\times10^{-34}$. The closest offered velocity uncertainty scale is $10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. This is the closest offered uncertainty scale.
perOption.B: Using the diameter in millimetres as though it were in metres lowers the estimate by a factor of a thousand.
perOption.C: This assigns too little momentum spread for confinement to an alveolus.
perOption.D: This would require a much larger confinement length for a molecule of the given mass.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q28.issues: The key’s use of h gives 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ m/s before rounding. A is the closest offered choice. The exact standard-deviation bound uses ℏ/2.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q29.body: Most alpha particles pass through the foil undeflected, so $n$ peaks sharply at $0^\circ$. Very few particles are deflected through large angles, so the count rate stays low at large positive and negative angles.

perOption.A: This puts the highest rates near backscattering angles and misses the strong undeviated beam.
perOption.B: This gives backscattering peaks comparable to the forward peak even though backscattering is rare.
perOption.C: Correct. A narrow forward peak dominates the low counts at large angles.
perOption.D: The broad peak implies too many particles are scattered through intermediate angles.

asrjc-2022-prelim-p1-q30.body: Two days is very short compared with the 33-year half-life, so the activity is effectively constant. Activity is the number of decays per unit time, giving $N_{\mathrm{decay}}\approx At=(4.0\times10^5)(2\times24\times3600)=6.912\times10^{10}$ decays.

perOption.A: This undercounts the decays by using an effective duration far shorter than two days.
perOption.B: This is close to what results from using the number of minutes in two days as the number of seconds.
perOption.C: Correct. The activity times the elapsed seconds gives about 69 billion decays.
perOption.D: This would require a much larger activity or a much longer time than given.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q1.body: The train starts from rest. Take $60\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$, or about $17\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, as a representative speed reached after about $15\ \mathrm{s}$. This gives $a\approx 17/15\approx 1.1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, so $1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ is a reasonable estimate. This is below $g=9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: At this acceleration the train would take about 170 s to reach the estimated speed.
perOption.B: Correct. It matches the estimated speed gain per second.
perOption.C: This would bring the train to the estimated speed in less than 2 s.
perOption.D: This is about ten times gravitational acceleration.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q1.issues: The key gives 1.111 for 17/15, which is about 1.13. The estimate and answer are unaffected.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q2.body: The speed is $v=(s_2-s_1)/(t_2-t_1)$. Add the absolute uncertainties within each difference, then add the fractional uncertainties for the quotient. This gives $\Delta v/v=(1+1)/270+(0.02+0.02)/2.00=2/270+0.04/2.00$.

perOption.A: Correct. Both differences and the quotient use the appropriate uncertainty rules.
perOption.B: Subtracts the fractional time uncertainty even though the fractional uncertainties add.
perOption.C: Uses single-reading uncertainties and multiplies the fractions.
perOption.D: Uses single-reading uncertainties and divides the fractions.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q3.body: Let $t$ be the time spent accelerating from rest. The distance is the trapezium area under the velocity–time graph, so $100=\frac{11.0+(11.0-t)}{2}\times10$. This gives $t=2.0\ \mathrm{s}$ and $a=10/t=5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: This acceleration would take 20 s to reach the stated speed, longer than the race.
perOption.B: Divides the speed gain by the full 11.0 s, including the constant-speed phase.
perOption.C: This implies almost 6 s of acceleration and gives only about 81 m in 11.0 s.
perOption.D: Correct. The speed increases by 10 m/s over 2.0 s.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q4.body: The gradient of a displacement–time graph gives velocity. In D, the speed rises from zero to a constant maximum, shown by the final straight section.

perOption.A: The slope flattens towards zero, so the sphere slows towards rest.
perOption.B: The slope keeps getting steeper without reaching a constant value.
perOption.C: The final horizontal section represents rest.
perOption.D: Correct. The final slope is constant and nonzero.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q5.body: The blocks stay in contact, so they have the same acceleration $a$. If $F_{YX}$ is the magnitude of the backward contact force on X, then $a=(F-F_{YX})/m_X$. Since X accelerates forward, $F_{YX}<F$. Newton’s third law gives $F_{XY}=F_{YX}$ in magnitude, so X exerts a force smaller than $F$ on Y.

perOption.A: This treats F as the resultant on X and ignores the backward contact force.
perOption.B: If X exerted F on Y, Y would exert an equal opposing force on X, giving X zero acceleration.
perOption.C: Correct. The contact force is smaller than the applied force.
perOption.D: The two contact forces form a Newton’s third-law pair and have equal magnitudes.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q6.body: By Newton’s second law, $F_{\mathrm{net}}=\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}t$, the gradient of the momentum–time graph. As the force magnitude increases, the graph must get steeper. In B the slope becomes increasingly negative, so the magnitude of the force opposing the motion increases.

perOption.A: Its positive gradient becomes less steep, so the force magnitude decreases.
perOption.B: Correct. The magnitude of the negative slope increases.
perOption.C: Its negative gradient becomes less steep, so the force magnitude decreases.
perOption.D: Its constant gradient represents a constant force.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q6.issues: B is correct if “increased” refers to force magnitude. Its signed gradient becomes more negative. The key’s comment about C should refer to the decreasing magnitude of its gradient.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q7.body: Constant velocity means the forces balance, so $X=Y+Z$. The bubble’s weight is tiny, making it the shorter downward arrow $Y$. The upward force $X$ is upthrust, leaving the downward force $Z$ as viscous drag.

perOption.A: Correct. Upthrust balances the bubble’s weight and drag.
perOption.B: The inequality implies upward acceleration.
perOption.C: It assigns the bubble’s small weight to the larger downward arrow.
perOption.D: It swaps weight and drag and implies an upward resultant.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q8.body: The frictionless ground exerts only a vertical upward normal force $R$. The weight $W$ acts vertically downwards. At the rough wall, upward friction and the horizontal normal force combine to give the upward-angled contact force $P$.

perOption.A: Weight should point vertically downwards.
perOption.B: Correct. The force directions match both contact surfaces and gravity.
perOption.C: The tilted ground reaction implies ground friction, and the horizontal wall force omits wall friction.
perOption.D: The tilted ground reaction implies friction at the icy ground.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q9.body: Efficiency is useful output power divided by input power, expressed as a percentage. Over the same time interval, the power ratio equals the energy ratio, giving $\frac{U}{E_{\mathrm{in}}}\times100\%$.

perOption.A: Correct. It uses useful output energy over total input energy.
perOption.B: It gives the percentage of input energy wasted.
perOption.C: It divides useful output by wasted energy.
perOption.D: It counts both useful and wasted energy as useful output.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q10.body: Before the jump the jumper is stationary and the cord is slack. On the way down before the cord extends, its elastic potential energy is still zero. When the net force is zero on the way down, the jumper is above ground and moving, and the cord is stretched, so all three energies are nonzero. At maximum extension the jumper is momentarily at rest.

perOption.A: The stationary jumper and slack cord give zero kinetic and elastic potential energy.
perOption.B: The cord is still slack, so its elastic potential energy is zero.
perOption.C: Correct. The jumper is moving above ground with the cord stretched.
perOption.D: The jumper momentarily stops, so kinetic energy is zero.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q10.issues: The key assumes the ground is the zero level for gravitational potential energy.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q11.body: The hour hand turns through $2\pi$ radians in 12 hours. Its average angular velocity has magnitude $\omega=\theta/t=2\pi/(12\times3600)=1.45\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses one revolution as one radian, omitting the factor of 2π.
perOption.B: Uses a 24-hour period for the hour hand.
perOption.C: Correct. It uses one full turn in 12 hours.
perOption.D: Uses the minute hand’s one-hour period.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q13.body: The gravitational force is $F=\frac{G(2M)M}{(3x)^2}=\frac{2GM^2}{9x^2}$. Comparing this with $\frac{kGM^2}{x^2}$ gives $k=2/9=0.22$.

perOption.A: Correct. Both stellar masses and the full separation are used.
perOption.B: Uses the larger orbital radius, 2x, as the separation.
perOption.C: Uses the separation factor 3 without squaring it.
perOption.D: Uses the smaller orbital radius, x, as the separation.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q14.body: For a satellite in a circular orbit, $E_k=GMm/(2r)$ and $E_{\mathrm{p}}=-GMm/r$. As the orbital radius increases, kinetic energy decreases and gravitational potential energy increases because it becomes less negative.

perOption.A: The potential energy increases, but the kinetic energy falls as the radius grows.
perOption.B: It reverses both trends with increasing radius.
perOption.C: Correct. The kinetic energy falls and the potential energy becomes less negative.
perOption.D: It treats the decrease in the magnitude of potential energy as a decrease in potential energy itself.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q16.body: At $t=0$ the mass passes through equilibrium, where its speed and kinetic energy are greatest. The displacement–time graph is a sine curve, so $v=\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t$ varies as a cosine. Since $E=\tfrac12mv^2$, kinetic energy follows a cosine-squared curve.

perOption.A: It places zero kinetic energy at the initial equilibrium crossing.
perOption.B: It shows only one peak and misses the repeated maxima at later equilibrium crossings.
perOption.C: It places kinetic energy maxima at the displacement extrema, where the mass is stationary.
perOption.D: Correct. Kinetic energy peaks at each equilibrium crossing.

asrjc-2023-promo-p1-q17.body: With more damping, the response amplitude is lower at nonzero driving frequencies. At zero driving frequency, the response amplitude still equals the driver’s, so the curve starts at the same height as X.

perOption.A: It exceeds the original response at some nonzero frequencies.
perOption.B: Correct. It starts at the same amplitude as X and lies below X at nonzero frequencies.
perOption.C: It incorrectly reduces the zero-frequency amplitude.
perOption.D: It starts below X, so it incorrectly reduces the zero-frequency amplitude.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q13.body: A single speed bump transfers energy to the rear-view mirror once, so it provides no periodic driving force. In the other examples, resonance can occur when the driving frequency matches a natural frequency of the system.

perOption.A: Correct. A single bump gives the mirror a one-off disturbance.
perOption.B: The vibrating reed can excite a resonance of the clarinet’s air column.
perOption.C: Wind gusts can drive a bridge mode if the forcing has a component near its natural frequency.
perOption.D: The speaker note can drive the ornament at its natural frequency.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q14.body: Amplitude is the maximum magnitude of a particle’s displacement from its rest position. Compare the positions of corresponding bars in the two rows and take the largest shift.

perOption.A: Halves a displacement already measured from equilibrium.
perOption.B: Uses half the spacing between particles as if it were half a peak-to-peak displacement.
perOption.C: Correct. This is the maximum displacement from equilibrium.
perOption.D: Measures separation between particles instead of displacement from each particle’s rest position.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q15.body: From $x=\lambda D/a$, the wavelength is $\lambda=(0.008)(0.0001)/2.0=4.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$. The slit sources are in phase, so dark fringes occur at path differences $(n+\tfrac12)\lambda$ with $n=0,1,\dots$. The second dark fringe has $n=1$, so its path difference is $1.5\lambda=6.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\lambda/2$, which gives the first dark fringe.
perOption.B: Uses $\lambda$, which gives the first bright fringe away from the centre.
perOption.C: Correct. The second dark fringe has a path difference of one and a half wavelengths.
perOption.D: Uses $2\lambda$, which gives the second bright fringe away from the centre.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q16.body: The node at the mouthpiece and the antinode at the open end allow only odd harmonics. Their frequencies follow $(2n+1)f$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots$, with $f=92\ \mathrm{Hz}$, giving $92$, $276$, $460$, $644$ and $828\ \mathrm{Hz}$ as the first five.

perOption.A: Includes frequencies such as 138 Hz that are not odd integer multiples of the fundamental.
perOption.B: Includes even harmonics such as 184 Hz.
perOption.C: Correct. These are the first five odd harmonics.
perOption.D: Successive tripling skips allowed harmonics such as 460 Hz.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q16.issues: D also consists entirely of allowed odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 9th, 27th and 81st) under the stated model. C uniquely lists the first five, but the question does not ask for consecutive or lowest frequencies.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q17.body: For wire X, $n=I/(vAq)=3.0/[(2.8\times10^{-2})\pi(5.0\times10^{-5})^2(1.6\times10^{-19})]=8.526\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Both wires are copper, so they have the same free-electron number density. For wire Y, $v=I/(nAq)=2.0/[(8.526\times10^{28})\pi(1.0\times10^{-4})^2(1.6\times10^{-19})]=4.7\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats twice the radius as twice the area, though the area increases fourfold.
perOption.C: Underestimates the effect of the larger cross-sectional area on the drift speed.
perOption.D: Scales by the current alone, treating the two cross-sectional areas as equal.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q18.body: Each wire has resistance $R=\rho l/A$, so its potential drop is $IR=I\rho l/A$. The current and resistivity are the same throughout, giving a constant drop per unit length $I\rho/A$ within each wire. The narrowest wire has the steepest drop, and the potential reaches zero at Y.

perOption.A: Correct. The downward slope gets steeper at each reduction in area.
perOption.B: Makes the potential drop per unit length smaller as the wire gets narrower.
perOption.C: Places the voltage drops at discrete steps even though each length of wire has resistance.
perOption.D: Treats the wires as equipotential stretches with drops only at steps.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q19.body: The central horizontal and vertical wires form a single node. The two-resistor paths in the upper-right and lower-left corners each begin and end at this node, so they carry no current. The remaining circuit is two parallel pairs in series, giving $R_{PQ}=R/2+R/2=R$.

perOption.A: Treats all eight resistors as parallel across P and Q.
perOption.B: Counts only one parallel pair and omits the second in series.
perOption.C: Correct. Both parallel pairs contribute to the total.
perOption.D: Takes one resistor from each side in series and overlooks their parallel partners.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q20.body: As the thermistor heats up, its resistance falls, so its share of the $10\ \mathrm{V}$ supply falls and the potential difference across the fixed resistor rises. When that potential difference exceeds the diode’s forward threshold (about $0.3$–$0.7\ \mathrm{V}$ in the key), current can flow down through the diode and lamp to light it.

perOption.A: Correct. Heating raises the voltage across the forward-oriented lamp branch.
perOption.B: Takes the lamp-branch voltage across the thermistor, where it falls as temperature rises.
perOption.C: The diode is reverse biased even when the voltage across the fixed resistor exceeds its forward threshold.
perOption.D: The reversed diode blocks lamp current, and the branch voltage falls as the thermistor heats.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q21.body: The electric field at X is tangent to the field line and points left, the direction of the force on a positive test charge. An electron is negatively charged, so its force is in the opposite direction, to the right.

perOption.A: Points along the field, which is the force direction for a positive charge.
perOption.B: Gives the force a downward component even though the field-line tangent at X is horizontal.
perOption.C: Gives the force a downward component even though the field-line tangent at X is horizontal.
perOption.D: Correct. The force points right.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q22.body: The equal and opposite charges contribute scalar potentials that cancel at the midpoint, so the potential is III or IV. Between the charges, both fields point from the positive charge toward the negative charge, so the signed field keeps the same sign. Since $E=-\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}r$, the negative field in II requires the rising potential in IV.

perOption.A: Graph I gives a nonzero midpoint potential, and graph IV would make the field reverse direction.
perOption.B: Graph II gives a nonzero midpoint potential, and graph III would make the field reverse direction.
perOption.C: The falling potential in III requires a positive field, whereas II shows a negative field.
perOption.D: Correct. The rising potential gives a negative axial field.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q22.issues: The key interprets electric field strength as the signed axial component between the charges. If read as a nonnegative magnitude, graph I is required for the field and no listed pair is valid.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q23.body: The field lines around each conductor are concentric circles, so its field at O is tangent to the circle through O. By the right-hand grip rule, a current into the page at P gives a field toward S. With currents into the page at R and S and out of the page at P and Q, the vertical components cancel and the rightward components add.

perOption.A: Reverses all the currents in D, producing a leftward field.
perOption.B: Produces a downward field because the horizontal components cancel.
perOption.C: Pairs equal currents at opposite corners, so the fields cancel at O.
perOption.D: Correct. The resultant points right.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q24.body: As the wire approaches the coil at constant speed, its field $B=\mu_0 I/(2\pi d)$ grows at an increasing rate as $d$ shrinks. The flux linkage therefore changes faster, increasing the induced e.m.f. and hence the coil current.

perOption.A: Correct. The rate of change of flux linkage increases.
perOption.B: Assumes the flux linkage changes more slowly as the wire moves closer.
perOption.C: Assumes constant speed gives a constant rate of flux change despite the inverse-distance field.
perOption.D: Assumes a reversal even though the flux through the coil keeps increasing in the same direction.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q25.body: For perpendicular motion in a uniform magnetic field, the induced e.m.f. is $E=Blv$. With $B$ and $l$ fixed, $E$ is proportional to the speed, given by the gradient of the $s$–$t$ graph. The gradient is initially small and constant, then larger and constant, and finally falls to zero and stays there, as shown in C.

perOption.A: Shows a falling e.m.f. while the rod initially moves at a constant speed.
perOption.B: Follows the shape of the distance graph and leaves a nonzero e.m.f. after the rod stops.
perOption.C: Correct. The e.m.f. follows the gradient of the distance–time graph.
perOption.D: Shows the e.m.f. rising during deceleration and staying nonzero after the rod stops.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q26.body: The diode passes only one half-cycle, and the peak current is $100\ \mathrm{V}/(100\ \Omega)=1.0\ \mathrm{A}$. A current of $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$ for half a period and zero for the other half would average $0.5\ \mathrm{A}$. The rectified sinusoid stays below $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$ except at its peak, so its mean is less than $0.5\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The conducting half-wave averages less than its peak.
perOption.B: Treats the current as being at its peak throughout the conducting half-cycle.
perOption.C: Uses the approximate r.m.s. current of the unrectified sine wave as the mean.
perOption.D: Uses the peak current as the mean.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q27.body: The shortest wavelength corresponds to the highest photon frequency, and the photon energy $hf$ equals the energy difference between the levels. For each atom, the largest possible drop is from the highest level reachable with energy $W$ down to the ground state. Atom B has the largest such energy difference.

perOption.A: A’s level above $W$ cannot be reached, and its accessible excited level gives a smaller drop than B’s.
perOption.B: Correct. B has the greatest accessible energy drop.
perOption.C: C’s highest accessible level is below B’s, so its maximum photon energy is smaller.
perOption.D: D’s highest level is farther below the energy limit, so its maximum drop is smaller.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q28.body: In the non-relativistic model, the gain in kinetic energy is $e\Delta V=p^2/(2m)$, so $p=\sqrt{2me\Delta V}$. The de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda=h/p=h/\sqrt{2me\Delta V}$. Both electrons have the same mass and charge magnitude, so $\lambda_0/\lambda_1=\sqrt{100/1}=10$.

perOption.A: Inverts the wavelength ratio.
perOption.B: Treats the two momenta as equal despite the different accelerating voltages.
perOption.C: Correct. The ratio is the square root of the inverse voltage ratio.
perOption.D: Uses the voltage ratio directly and misses the square root.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q28.issues: The key uses non-relativistic momentum. Relativistic momentum gives a ratio of about 10.5, so C remains the closest choice.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q29.body: The combined rest mass of the proton and neutron exceeds that of the deuteron, so the reaction needs an energy input. The mass difference is $(1.0086+1.0097-2.0150)\ \mathrm{u}=0.0033\ \mathrm{u}$. Using $E=\Delta mc^2$ gives about $3.07\ \mathrm{MeV}$, rounded to $3\ \mathrm{MeV}$ in the key.

perOption.A: Photon emission takes energy away from a reaction that requires energy input.
perOption.B: Even a 3 MeV emitted photon would carry energy away from the breakup.
perOption.C: A 2 MeV photon supplies less than the binding energy.
perOption.D: Correct under the key’s rounding to whole MeV.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q29.issues: The key rounds 3.07 MeV to 3 MeV and omits the eV-to-MeV conversion factor in its printed expression. Taken literally with the supplied masses, a 3 MeV photon is below threshold and no option is physically valid. D is the intended rounded choice.

asrjc-2024-prelim-p1-q30.body: Alpha decay decreases the proton number by 2, beta-minus decay increases it by 1, and gamma emission leaves it unchanged. One alpha emission followed by two beta-minus emissions gives a net change of $-2+1+1=0$.

perOption.A: Two alpha emissions and one beta-minus emission give a net change of −3.
perOption.B: Correct. The changes cancel.
perOption.C: One alpha and one beta-minus emission give a net change of −1, and gamma emission leaves it unchanged.
perOption.D: Two beta-minus emissions raise the proton number by 2, and gamma emission leaves it unchanged.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q1.body: A typical small car has a mass of about $1500\ \mathrm{kg}$. Its kinetic energy is $\frac12(1500)(30)^2\approx0.68\times10^6\ \mathrm{J}$, so $10^6\ \mathrm{J}$ is the closest estimate.

perOption.A: This energy at the stated speed would require a mass below 1 kg.
perOption.B: This energy corresponds to a mass of only about 22 kg.
perOption.C: Correct. It is the closest estimate.
perOption.D: This energy would require a mass of about 220 tonnes.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q1.issues: The key calls the change from 0.68 × 10⁶ J to 1 × 10⁶ J rounding to one significant figure. It is a choice of the closest listed power of ten.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q2.body: For a fixed resistor, $V/I=R$ is constant, so the expected $I$–$V$ line passes through the origin. The nonzero current intercept indicates a systematic error. All the points lie on the best-fit line, so there is no visible random scatter.

perOption.A: Random error would produce scatter about the line and does not explain the consistent offset.
perOption.B: Correct. The data show a systematic offset.
perOption.C: The offset is systematic, and the points show no visible scatter.
perOption.D: The nonzero intercept indicates a systematic error.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q3.body: Use $s=ut+\tfrac12at^2$ with $u=0$ and constant $a$, so $s\propto t^2$. If $x$ is the distance fallen in $0.50T$, then $x/L=(0.50T)^2/T^2=0.25$, giving $x=0.25L$.

perOption.A: Keeps an extra factor of one-half when taking the ratio, although that factor cancels.
perOption.B: Correct. Halving the time quarters the distance.
perOption.C: The distance is fixed by the squared time ratio, which gives $0.25L$.
perOption.D: Assumes constant speed and takes the distance to be proportional to time.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q4.body: The horizontal section shows that the stone reaches terminal velocity in water. The area under the graph in air is larger than the area in water, so the stone travels farther in air. The gradient in air decreases with time, so the acceleration in air also decreases.

perOption.A: The air section still has a positive slope at water entry.
perOption.B: The area under the water section is smaller than the area under the air section.
perOption.C: Correct. The slope decreases during the fall through air.
perOption.D: A constant rate of change would give a straight line in air.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q5.body: A Newton’s third-law pair consists of forces of the same type that act in opposite directions on different bodies. $P$ is the upward contact force of Earth on the box, and $R$ is the downward contact force of the box on Earth.

perOption.A: Both act on the box, and one is a contact force while the other is gravitational.
perOption.B: Both point upward and come from different interactions.
perOption.C: Correct. They are the mutual contact forces.
perOption.D: Pairs a contact force with a gravitational force.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q6.body: The mass flow rate is $90\ \mathrm{kg\,min^{-1}}=1.5\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$. The horizontal rate of momentum transfer is $F=v\,\Delta m/\Delta t=20(1.5)=30\ \mathrm{N}$. The person applies this force in the direction of the jet to balance the backward reaction.

perOption.A: Correct. The jet carries away momentum at a rate of 30 N.
perOption.B: A force of 270 N would require a mass flow of 13.5 kg per second at the stated jet speed.
perOption.C: Uses 90 kg per minute as though it were 90 kg per second.
perOption.D: A force of 10,800 N would require using 540 kg per second, 360 times the actual mass flow.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q7.body: The rod is in equilibrium, so $\sum\tau=0$ about $O$. The triangle has equal sides $PO$ and the rod, both $2L$, so the rod is at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. Taking moments about $O$ gives $T(2L\sin30^\circ)=20g(\frac{L}{2}\cos60^\circ)+30g(\frac{3L}{2}\cos60^\circ)$. Hence $T=269.78\ \mathrm{N}\approx270\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the combined moment, giving a value close to the moment of B alone with its weight placed at the junction.
perOption.B: Using the junction as the point of action of B’s weight shortens its moment arm and gives about 196 N.
perOption.C: Omitting the moment from A gives about 221 N, close to this choice.
perOption.D: Correct. Both weights contribute to the moment about the pivot.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q8.body: The key estimates the work done stretching the band as $\tfrac12(0.5)(35)\approx9\ \mathrm{J}$ and the energy recovered as $\tfrac12(0.6)(20)=6\ \mathrm{J}$. The net work in one cycle is about $9-6=3\ \mathrm{J}$. Counting about six squares between the curves also gives $(5\times0.1)\times6=3\ \mathrm{J}$, the quantity the key calls the energy remaining.

perOption.A: The unloading area gives about 6 J of recovered energy.
perOption.B: Correct in the key’s intended sense of net work over the cycle.
perOption.C: Net work is the loading area minus the unloading area, about 3 J.
perOption.D: The loading area gives about 9 J of work during stretching.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q8.issues: The loop area is about 3 J of net mechanical work dissipated by hysteresis. The graph cannot establish how much of that energy remains in the rubber band as internal energy after unloading. B is intended, but its literal claim is unsupported and no other option fits.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q9.body: A constant force gives a constant acceleration $a$. Since the body starts from rest, $v=u+at=at$. Thus $P=Fv=Fat$, so power increases linearly from zero.

perOption.A: Assumes constant force gives constant power even while speed increases.
perOption.B: Correct. Power increases linearly from zero.
perOption.C: The increasing slope would require an increasing acceleration with constant force.
perOption.D: The decreasing slope would require a decreasing acceleration with constant force.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q10.body: At the top of the path, the vertical component is the centripetal acceleration and points down toward the centre. The horizontal component points to the right, along the velocity, because the drone is speeding up. The resultant therefore points down and to the right.

perOption.A: Shows only the centripetal component, so the speed is instantaneously constant.
perOption.B: The leftward component is opposite the velocity and would slow the drone down.
perOption.C: Shows only tangential acceleration and omits the inward component needed to turn.
perOption.D: Correct. Both inward and forward components are shown.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q11.body: On P, $g_P=W_P/m=1.0/1.0=1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. On Q, $g_Q=10g_P=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and the mass is still $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$. The weight on Q is therefore $W_Q=1.0(10)=10\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the field-strength ratio and divides the weight by ten.
perOption.B: Correct. The same mass weighs 10 N in the stronger field.
perOption.C: Scales up the mass even though the weight is correctly estimated.
perOption.D: Scales up both the mass and field strength, applying the same factor twice.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q12.body: From kinetic theory, $P=\frac13(Nm/V)\langle c^2\rangle=\frac13\rho\langle c^2\rangle$. Substitution gives $1.0\times10^5=\frac13(1.2)\langle c^2\rangle$. Therefore $\sqrt{\langle c^2\rangle}=500\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Using $3/2$ in place of the factor 3 when solving for mean square speed gives about this value.
perOption.B: Correct. This is the square root of $3P/ho$.
perOption.C: A speed of 3700 m/s would imply a pressure far above the one given.
perOption.D: Reports the mean square speed and omits the square root.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q13.body: Over a full cycle, the change in internal energy is zero. Using $\Delta U=Q+W$, with $W$ the work done on the gas, $0=Q+[-4.2+(1.0\times10^5)(20.0-5.0)\times10^{-6}]$. The heat gain is $Q=2.7\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Assigns the wrong sign to the expansion work when finding the net work on the gas.
perOption.B: Reports the net work done on the gas as the heat gain.
perOption.C: Correct. The gas gains $2.7\ \mathrm{J}$ of heat.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes of the expansion and compression work.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q14.body: The bob starts at equilibrium, $x=0$, with amplitude $50\ \mathrm{mm}$ and period $2.0\ \mathrm{s}$. At the end of the exposure, $x=25\ \mathrm{mm}$, so $25=50\sin(2\pi t/2.0)$. The shutter is open for $t=0.17\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The bob reaches half its amplitude in one twelfth of a period.
perOption.B: Treats half the amplitude as half the time from equilibrium to an extreme.
perOption.C: Uses the full quarter-period needed to reach the extreme.
perOption.D: Uses a half-period, which would return the bob to equilibrium.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q14.issues: The key prints “x = 0 s” in one line. The starting displacement is 0 mm.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q15.body: The air molecules undergo simple harmonic motion. Wave intensity is proportional to the square of the displacement amplitude $x_0$, so raising the intensity increases $x_0$ and hence the maximum molecular speed $v_0=(2\pi f)x_0$. The speed of sound is set by the properties of the air, which are unchanged.

perOption.A: Assumes greater intensity also makes the wave travel faster.
perOption.B: Correct. The molecular speed increases and the wave speed stays fixed.
perOption.C: Keeps molecular speed fixed despite the larger amplitude and incorrectly increases wave speed.
perOption.D: Overlooks the increase in molecular speed at fixed frequency.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q16.body: The phase difference at P is the source phase difference plus $2\pi$ times the path difference divided by the wavelength. Zero intensity requires destructive interference, for which the waves arrive with a phase difference of an odd multiple of $\pi$.

perOption.A: Correct. The phase difference is $2\pi+\pi=3\pi$.
perOption.B: The phase difference is $\tfrac12(2\pi)+\pi=2\pi$, giving constructive interference.
perOption.C: The phase difference is $2\pi+\tfrac{\pi}{2}=\tfrac{5\pi}{2}$, which does not give cancellation.
perOption.D: The phase difference is $2\pi+0=2\pi$, giving constructive interference.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q17.body: The grating equation is $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$. Both maxima have the same $d$ and $\theta$, so $3\lambda_X=2\lambda_{\mathrm{red}}=2(720\times10^{-9})\ \mathrm{m}$. Thus $\lambda_X=480\ \mathrm{nm}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Both orders have the same product of order and wavelength.
perOption.B: Uses a wavelength ratio of three quarters instead of two thirds.
perOption.C: Makes the third-order wavelength larger even though the order–wavelength product is fixed.
perOption.D: Reverses the order ratio, giving about $1100\ \mathrm{nm}$.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q18.body: The electric force is $F=qE$, so $ma=qE$ and $a=qE/m$ is constant. From $v^2=u^2+2ax$ with $u=0$, we get $v^2=2ax$. Therefore $E_{\mathrm K}=\tfrac12 m(2ax)$ is proportional to $x$.

perOption.A: Shows nonzero initial kinetic energy and no gain from the electric force.
perOption.B: Shows an increasing energy gain per unit distance even though the force is constant.
perOption.C: Shows a decreasing energy gain per unit distance even though the force is constant.
perOption.D: Correct. The energy increases linearly from zero.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q19.body: By definition, $V=W/Q=(W/t)/(Q/t)=P/I$. Using $R=V/I$ gives $P=IV=I^2R=V^2/R=W^2/(Q^2R)$. Hence $R=W^2/(PQ^2)$, so D is the invalid relationship.

perOption.A: This relationship is valid because $I=P/V=PQ/W$.
perOption.B: This relationship is valid because $Q=W/V=W/(IR)$.
perOption.C: This relationship is valid because $P=V^2/R$.
perOption.D: Correct. $W/(PQ)=1/I$.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q20.body: Closing S adds a parallel path, which lowers the effective external resistance and raises the current measured by the ammeter. The larger current increases the potential difference across the internal resistance, so the terminal potential difference measured by the voltmeter falls.

perOption.A: Correct. The voltmeter reading falls as the ammeter reading rises.
perOption.B: Assumes a second parallel branch reduces the total current.
perOption.C: Overlooks the increased potential difference across the internal resistance.
perOption.D: Reverses the change in current and therefore the change in terminal potential difference.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q21.body: The $2\ \Omega$ and $4\ \Omega$ resistors form a potential divider across the cell. The voltmeter reads the share across the $4\ \Omega$ resistor, so $V_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{4}{2+4}E$ and $V_{\mathrm{out}}/E=2/3$.

perOption.A: Uses the wrong resistance fraction for the $4\ \Omega$ resistor in the divider.
perOption.B: Gives the share across the $2\ \Omega$ resistor.
perOption.C: Treats the unequal series resistors as sharing the cell voltage equally.
perOption.D: Correct. The voltmeter measures two thirds of the cell e.m.f.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q22.body: The potential gradient of XY is $k=V_{XY}/\ell_{XY}=\frac{[0.50/(0.50+0.50)](1.5)}{0.96}=0.781\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. At balance, $E=k\ell_{XZ}=(0.781)(0.64)=0.50\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The unknown e.m.f. equals the potential difference along XZ at balance.
perOption.B: Uses the potential difference along the entire wire XY.
perOption.C: Applies the length fraction to the full driving e.m.f., overlooking the internal resistance.
perOption.D: Overestimates the driving voltage available along XZ by undercounting the drop elsewhere in the circuit.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q23.body: The key’s diagram places P at the end of a current-carrying solenoid. In the marked region just outside that end, the field lines curve inwards and point towards P, matching the pattern in the question.

perOption.A: Places the coil’s axis perpendicular to PQ even though the central field shown runs along PQ.
perOption.B: Correct. The lines curve into the solenoid end at P.
perOption.C: A straight wire produces concentric field lines around PQ.
perOption.D: A south pole at Q would draw field lines towards Q.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q24.body: Fleming’s left-hand rule gives a force out of the page. As $\theta$ tends to $0^\circ$, the wire becomes perpendicular to the field and the force is greatest. Each half contributes a perpendicular length $(L/2)\cos\theta$, so $F=BI(2)(L/2)\cos\theta=BIL\cos\theta$.

perOption.A: Correct. The force is out of the page and depends on the perpendicular length.
perOption.B: Reverses the force direction given by Fleming’s left-hand rule.
perOption.C: Uses the length component parallel to the field.
perOption.D: Uses the parallel length component and reverses the force direction.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q25.body: Split the frame into its triangular front and rectangular rear. As the triangular section enters or leaves the field, the area crossing the boundary per unit time grows, so the magnitudes of the rate of flux change, induced e.m.f. and induced current all rise. While the rectangular section crosses, the rate of flux change and the induced current magnitude are constant. The current is zero while the frame is wholly inside and reverses for exit because the flux then decreases.

perOption.A: Shows a constant exit current first, although the triangular tip reaches the exit boundary first.
perOption.B: Gives entry and exit the same current direction despite opposite flux changes.
perOption.C: Treats the rectangular section as crossing first at both boundaries.
perOption.D: Correct. Each crossing gives a ramp and a plateau, with opposite current directions.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q26.body: In one period, the current is $-I_0$ for two time units and $2I_0$ for one time unit. Squaring, averaging over the period and taking the square root gives $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_0^2+(2I_0)^2}{3}}=\sqrt{2}\,I_0$.

perOption.A: Correct. It is the square root of the time-weighted mean square.
perOption.B: Applies the sinusoidal formula to the lower current magnitude.
perOption.C: Underestimates the mean square by failing to account for the interval at twice the current magnitude.
perOption.D: Uses the peak current in place of the root-mean-square current.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q27.body: Violet light has a frequency of about $7\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$, or a wavelength of roughly $400\ \mathrm{nm}$. Using $E=hf$, the photon energy is $(6.63\times10^{-34})(7\times10^{14})\approx5\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$ to one significant figure.

perOption.A: Overestimates the photon energy, which is about $3\ \mathrm{eV}$.
perOption.B: Overestimates the photon frequency into the ultraviolet range.
perOption.C: Underestimates the photon frequency, giving an energy closer to that of red light.
perOption.D: Correct. It gives the violet photon’s energy to one significant figure.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q28.body: Using $\Delta x\Delta p\ge h$, halving $\Delta x$ gives $(1.00\times10^{-20})\Delta p\ge6.63\times10^{-34}$. The minimum $\Delta p$ is $6.63\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. The change is $\frac{6.63-4.00}{4.00}\times100\%\approx66\%$.

perOption.A: A 100% reduction would make the momentum uncertainty zero.
perOption.B: Reverses the sign even though the new minimum exceeds the original uncertainty.
perOption.C: Correct. The new minimum is about 66% higher.
perOption.D: Assumes the initial momentum uncertainty was already at its lower bound.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q28.issues: The key uses the syllabus-scale bound with $h$. For the exact standard-deviation bound $h/(4\pi)$, no increase is required and no option expresses that.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q30.body: The key tracks the charged products using $\vphantom{X}{}^{a}_{b}\mathrm{X}\to{}^{a-4}_{b}\mathrm{Y}+{}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}+2\,{}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$. X and Y have the same proton number and different neutron numbers, so Y is an isotope of X.

perOption.A: A beta-minus electron is produced when a neutron in the nucleus becomes a proton.
perOption.B: Alpha emission lowers the daughter nucleus's nucleon number by four.
perOption.C: Correct. Y has the same proton number and four fewer neutrons.
perOption.D: The products carry kinetic energy, so their total rest mass is smaller.

asrjc-2025-prelim-p1-q30.issues: The key's equation omits the two electron antineutrinos.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: For $N$ oscillations, $T=t/N$, so $\Delta T/T=\Delta t/t$. Timing more oscillations increases $t$ while the absolute timing uncertainty $\Delta t$ stays about the same, reducing the fractional uncertainty.

perOption.A: The key assumes the diameter’s fractional uncertainty is set by the instrument, so averaging readings leaves it unchanged.
perOption.B: A best-fit gradient reduces the effect of random error without eliminating it.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: A zero error is systematic.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.issues: Option A can also be valid when independent random errors contribute to the uncertainty of the mean. C is the intended answer under the key’s implicit assumption for A.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: Place the two $1\ \mathrm{N}$ force vectors head to tail so that they and the resultant form an equilateral triangle. The angle between the forces when drawn tail to tail is $180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ$, and the resultant is $1\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: An acute angle between the two 1 N forces gives a resultant greater than 1 N.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The 1 N force has a positive component along the 2 N force, so the resultant exceeds 2 N.
perOption.D: A 1 N resultant from 2 N and 1 N requires the forces to be exactly opposite.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
Vertically the bomb starts with zero velocity: $500 = \tfrac{1}{2}(9.81)t^2$, so $t = 10.1\ \mathrm{s}$ to reach sea level.

In that time the bomb moves $138 \times 10.1 = 1394\ \mathrm{m}$ horizontally, while the ship moves $12 \times 10.1 = 121\ \mathrm{m}$ further away.

So the bomb must be released when the horizontal separation is $1394 - 121 \approx 1270\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses the bomb's horizontal range minus the ship's motion incorrectly (too small a separation).
perOption.B: Correct. Bomb's horizontal range minus the distance the ship moves during the fall.
perOption.C: Ignores the ship's motion: this is just the bomb's horizontal range of about 1390 m.
perOption.D: Adds the ship's displacement instead of subtracting it, though the ship moves in the same direction as the bomb.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.issues: Explanation written by the orchestrator from the school's worked solution (Codex declined this item).

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: Treat the two blocks as one system. At rest, the ground’s upward force balances their combined weight. When the system accelerates upward in (3), the applied force must exceed that combined weight.

perOption.A: The ground supports the same combined weight in (1) and (2).
perOption.B: The third-law partner is the copper block’s force on the wooden block in (1), in the same configuration.
perOption.C: In (3), the wood’s upward force on the copper must exceed the copper’s weight, so the copper pushes down harder on the wood than in (2).
perOption.D: Correct.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: Take the ball’s initial direction as positive and let $m$ and $M$ be the masses of the ball and foot. With the ball stopped after impact, momentum conservation gives $mu+Mv=Mv_1$, where $v_1$ is the foot’s final velocity. The elastic collision gives equal relative speeds of approach and separation, so $u-v=v_1$. Substituting gives $2Mv=(M-m)u$, so for $M\gg m$, $v\approx u/2=6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the ball’s original direction.

perOption.A: Reverses the direction and uses the full approach speed instead of half.
perOption.B: Reverses the direction of the required foot velocity.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses far less than half the ball’s initial speed.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: At constant speed, the motor torque balances the total torque from air resistance. Each of the four carriages experiences $85.0\ \mathrm{N}$ of air resistance at a radius of $3.20\ \mathrm{m}$. The required torque is $4(85.0)(3.20)=1088\ \mathrm{N\,m}\approx1090\ \mathrm{N\,m}$.

perOption.A: Grossly underestimates the torque from the four 85.0 N forces acting at a radius of 3.20 m.
perOption.B: Counts the torque from one carriage only.
perOption.C: Counts only two carriages, or one opposing pair.
perOption.D: Correct.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.issues: The key calls the motor torque the resultant torque and gives its unit as N. The resultant torque is zero and the motor torque is measured in N m.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: The ball falls at constant speed, so its kinetic energy remains constant. The resistive force is constant, and the ball falls equal distances in equal times, so its gravitational potential energy decreases linearly.

perOption.A: Shows the gravitational potential energy decreasing at a changing rate.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Shows kinetic energy increasing even though the speed is constant.
perOption.D: Shows kinetic energy increasing even though the speed is constant.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: The old lamp’s useful light output is $60(100-95)/100=3.0\ \mathrm{W}$. The modern lamp produces the same light output with a $4.0\ \mathrm{W}$ input, so its efficiency is $(3.0/4.0)\times100\%=75\%$.

perOption.A: Uses the old lamp’s efficiency.
perOption.B: Divides the modern lamp’s input power by the old lamp’s input power.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the fraction of the old lamp’s input converted to heat.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: Let $r$ be the cord length. The drop to P converts gravitational potential energy into kinetic energy, so $mgr=\tfrac12 mv^2$ and $v=\sqrt{2gr}$. At P, $T-mg=mv^2/r=2mg$. Hence $T=3mg$.

perOption.A: Assumes the cord has no tension at the bottom of the swing.
perOption.B: Balances the weight and leaves no inward resultant.
perOption.C: Uses the inward resultant force as the tension.
perOption.D: Correct.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: At X the fields point in opposite directions, each towards its source mass. Their magnitudes are $g_P=Gm/d^2$ and $g_Q=G(2m)/(2d)^2=Gm/(2d^2)$, so the net field is $Gm/(2d^2)$ towards P. Gravitational potential is scalar, so $\phi=-Gm/d-G(2m)/(2d)=-2Gm/d$.

perOption.A: Assumes the fields cancel and counts only one potential contribution.
perOption.B: Gives the correct potential but counts only P’s field.
perOption.C: Assumes the fields cancel and overlooks that Q is twice as far from X as P.
perOption.D: Correct.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.issues: The solution starts on page 2 and continues on page 3.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The molecules rebound from the inward-moving piston faster than they approached it. Their average kinetic energy increases, so the gas temperature rises.

perOption.A: The insulation prevents heat transfer, but the piston can still do work on the gas.
perOption.B: For a fixed amount of ideal gas, $pV$ is proportional to temperature.
perOption.C: More frequent intermolecular collisions supply no extra kinetic energy.
perOption.D: Correct. The molecules rebound faster from the moving piston.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: During compression the work done on the gas is $-p(V_f-V_i)=-(1.0\times10^5)(2-5)\times10^{-4}=30\ \mathrm{J}$. During expansion it is $-(1.5\times10^5)(5-2)\times10^{-4}=-45\ \mathrm{J}$. The net work done on the gas is $30-45=-15\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the work sign and understates the magnitude by a factor of ten.
perOption.B: Understates the magnitude by a factor of ten when applying the axis scales.
perOption.C: Gives the net work done by the gas.
perOption.D: Correct. The negative work during expansion has the greater magnitude.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: At half the amplitude $x_0$, the speed is $v=\omega\sqrt{x_0^2-x_0^2/4}$. This simplifies to $v=(\sqrt{3}/2)\omega x_0=(\sqrt{3}/2)v_0$.

perOption.A: Uses the squared displacement fraction as the speed fraction.
perOption.B: Assumes halving the displacement halves the speed.
perOption.C: Uses the fraction of squared speed without taking its square root.
perOption.D: Correct. The speed is $\sqrt{3}/2$ times its maximum.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: At P, the displacement curve crosses zero with a negative slope. As the curve shifts right, the displacement at P becomes positive, so the particle is moving in the positive $x$-direction.

perOption.A: P is at a compression, where the pressure is maximum.
perOption.B: This is a progressive wave, so it has no stationary-wave antinodes.
perOption.C: At Q, the particle passes through equilibrium in a rarefaction at maximum speed.
perOption.D: Correct. The particle at P moves in the positive $x$-direction.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: The open tube has fundamental wavelength $2L$, so $v=f_0\lambda_0=(256)(2L)=512L$. With one end closed the longest resonant wavelength is $4L$, giving $f_1=512L/(4L)=128\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The next wavelength is $4L/3$, giving $f_2=512L/(4L/3)=384\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Includes the even harmonic at 256 Hz, which the tube with one closed end cannot support.
perOption.B: Correct. These are the fundamental and third harmonic.
perOption.C: Gives the third and fifth harmonics and skips the 128 Hz fundamental.
perOption.D: Both frequencies are even multiples of the new fundamental.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: For the third order, $d\sin45^\circ=3\lambda$. At the limiting angle of $90^\circ$, $d\sin90^\circ=n\lambda$. Combining these gives $n=4.24$ at the limit, so the highest allowed integer order is 4.

perOption.A: Stops at the observed order even though the fourth fits within the angular limit.
perOption.B: Correct. Four is the largest allowed integer order.
perOption.C: The fifth order would require $\sin\theta>1$.
perOption.D: The sixth order would also require $\sin\theta>1$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: The total charge is $Q=It=(20\times10^{-3})(5.0)=0.10\ \mathrm{C}$. Dividing by the magnitude of the electron charge gives $N=0.10/(1.6\times10^{-19})=6.3\times10^{17}$.

perOption.A: Gives the transferred charge in coulombs before dividing by the elementary charge.
perOption.B: Fails to convert the current-time product into an electron count using the elementary charge.
perOption.C: Correct. Divide the transferred charge by the charge magnitude per electron.
perOption.D: This many electrons would carry far more than the transferred $0.10\ \mathrm{C}$.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: The potential difference across $R$ is $IR$, so $IR=E-Ir$. The measurements give $3.0=E-1.0r$ and $4.8=E-0.4r$. Solving simultaneously gives $r=3.0\ \Omega$ and $E=6.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Predicts too small a terminal voltage change for the measured current change.
perOption.B: Correct. This resistance satisfies both readings with the same e.m.f.
perOption.C: Confuses the numerical value of the e.m.f. in volts with the internal resistance in ohms.
perOption.D: Predicts too large a terminal voltage change for the measured current change.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: The right-hand network has equivalent capacitance $(1/C+1/C)^{-1}+C=1.5C$. It is in series with X, so it also carries $6\ \mu\mathrm{C}$ and has voltage $V_{\mathrm{right}}=(6\ \mu\mathrm{C})/(1.5C)$. The lower branch has capacitance $C/2$, giving charge $(C/2)V_{\mathrm{right}}=2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$. The two series capacitors in that branch carry equal charge, so Y stores $2\ \mu\mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Y carries the charge of the lower series branch.
perOption.B: Splits the charge equally between parallel branches with different capacitances.
perOption.C: Gives the charge on the single capacitor in the upper branch.
perOption.D: Treats Y as directly in series with X and ignores the upper branch.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: The time constant is $\tau=RC=4700\times2200\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s}$. Since $E=\tfrac12 CV^2$, $E_0/E_t=(V_0/V_t)^2=8$ and $V_0/V_t=\sqrt{8}$. Substitution into $V_t=V_0e^{-t/\tau}$ gives $1/\sqrt{8}=e^{-t/\tau}$, so $t=10.8\ \mathrm{s}\approx11\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The voltage falls to $V_0/\sqrt{8}$.
perOption.B: At 16 s the energy has already fallen below one-eighth of its initial value.
perOption.C: Uses one-eighth as the voltage fraction, leaving one-sixty-fourth of the initial energy.
perOption.D: Treats the energy decrease as requiring three full $RC$ time constants.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The field pushes positive charges to the right and negative charges to the left. In B, the forces on each horizontal pair are equal, opposite and collinear. The net force is zero and the clockwise and anticlockwise moments about the centre balance.

perOption.A: The net rightward force on the top row and net leftward force on the bottom row produce moments in the same sense.
perOption.B: Correct. The resultant force and resultant moment are both zero.
perOption.C: The top and bottom charges experience unequal leftward forces, so their opposing moments do not cancel.
perOption.D: The rightward top forces and leftward bottom forces turn the square in the same sense.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The electric force must act upwards to balance the weight, so the upper plate is at lower potential. When $V$ is decreased, the particle falls towards the higher-potential lower plate. During that fall, the positive particle gains electric potential energy and loses gravitational potential energy.

perOption.A: During the fall, the positive particle moves towards higher electric potential.
perOption.B: Correct. During the fall, electric potential energy rises and gravitational potential energy falls.
perOption.C: During the rise, the positive particle moves towards lower electric potential.
perOption.D: After the voltage changes, the electric force and weight differ, so the energy changes need not have equal magnitudes.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.issues: The key compares positions during motion after the voltage adjustment. If the comparison includes the adjustment itself, the electric potential change depends on how the individual plate potentials are changed relative to a fixed reference.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The electron is negatively charged, so its electric force points along B. The magnetic force must point along D for the beam to remain undeflected. Fleming's left-hand rule, with conventional current opposite to the electron beam, gives magnetic field direction C.

perOption.A: This field reverses the magnetic force, making it reinforce the electric force.
perOption.B: The magnetic force would be perpendicular to B and could not oppose the electric force along B.
perOption.C: Correct. Field direction C produces a magnetic force along D.
perOption.D: The magnetic force would be perpendicular to D, although the required force is along D.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: By Lenz's law the coil end X becomes a north pole when north approaches and a south pole when south approaches, reversing the current and the needle deflection. At half the speed, the flux linkage changes more slowly, so the induced e.m.f. and current are smaller.

perOption.A: Accounts for the smaller deflection but misses the reversal caused by switching poles.
perOption.B: Correct. The needle moves less than 10 units to the right.
perOption.C: Misses both the current reversal and the decrease in magnitude.
perOption.D: Gets the reversal right but treats slower insertion as producing a larger current.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: Treat PQ as a straight conductor moving in the magnetic field. Fleming's right-hand rule gives conventional current from P to Q along the disc. The rotating disc acts as a source, so current flows internally from lower to higher potential and P is at lower potential than Q.

perOption.A: Correct. The disc drives current from P to Q with Q at higher potential.
perOption.B: Gets the polarity right but reverses the current inside the source.
perOption.C: Reverses both the induced current and the polarity.
perOption.D: Gets the current direction right but applies a resistor's potential drop to the source.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: Over one period, $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{(4^2\times1+2^2\times2+0\times1)/4}=2.45\ \mathrm{A}$. The average power is $I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2R=2.45^2\times11=66\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Uses the zero mean current, although power depends on the mean squared current.
perOption.B: Uses the 2 A level alone and ignores the other parts of the waveform.
perOption.C: Correct. The period average of $I^2R$ is 66 W.
perOption.D: Counts the 4 A pulse but omits the power from the negative-current interval.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: The de Broglie equation is $\lambda=h/p$. Therefore $\lambda p=h$, where $h$ is Planck's constant.

perOption.A: Correct. The product is Planck's constant.
