perOption.B: Makes wavelength directly proportional to momentum.
perOption.C: Substitutes kinetic energy for momentum, although the two are not proportional.
perOption.D: Makes wavelength increase with kinetic energy, although it decreases as momentum increases.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The graph of $\lvert\psi\rvert^2$ shows the position probability density. D has the narrowest peak, centred near $x=1.5$, and hence the smallest position uncertainty $\Delta x$. This gives the largest lower bound on $\Delta p$, which is the key's basis for choosing D.

perOption.A: The flat density spreads the particle across the region shown, giving weak localisation.
perOption.B: The probability is distributed across many peaks, giving a large position uncertainty.
perOption.C: The broad packet from about $x=0.0$ to $3.2$ gives a larger position uncertainty than D.
perOption.D: Correct. D is the most tightly localised in position.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.issues: The key treats the uncertainty bound as an inverse equality. For standard deviations the bound is $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$. The graphs omit the wavefunction phase, so the densities alone cannot establish a ranking of momentum uncertainties. D is the intended answer.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Let R be the intermediate nucleus. Beta decay gives $\phantom{}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{P}\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{R}+{}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$, followed by gamma decay $\phantom{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{R}\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}\mathrm{Q}+\gamma$. The neutron number in Q is $A-(Z+1)=A-Z-1$.

perOption.A: Correct. The neutron count drops by just one.
perOption.B: Alpha decay removes two neutrons and gamma emission leaves the neutron count unchanged.
perOption.C: Alpha decay removes two neutrons and beta-minus decay converts one more into a proton.
perOption.D: Each beta-minus decay converts a neutron to a proton, so the count drops by two.

asrjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: Let $C$ be the initial count rate due to the source alone. After two half-lives it has fallen by $3C/4$, so $3C/4=324-108$ and $C=288\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$. The background count rate is $324-288=36\ \mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Quarters the later reading even though it includes a constant background contribution.
perOption.B: Correct. The background contributes 36 counts per minute.
perOption.C: Halves the later reading even though the half-life applies only to the source contribution.
perOption.D: Gives the remaining source count rate after two half-lives.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q1.body: The absolute uncertainty is $47.12\times10\%=4.71\ \Omega$, which rounds to $5\ \Omega$ to one significant figure. Round the reading to the same place to obtain $(47\pm5)\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Correct. Both values are reported to the nearest ohm.
perOption.B: Uses an uncertainty much smaller than the stated 10%.
perOption.C: Keeps two significant figures in the uncertainty under the school's one-significant-figure convention.
perOption.D: Keeps hundredths of an ohm when the uncertainty is rounded to whole ohms.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q2.body: Let $t$ be the time in seconds since Train B starts. Using $s=ut+\frac12at^2$, Train A travels $\frac12(0.30)(t+120)^2$ and Train B travels $\frac12(0.50)t^2$. Equating the displacements at catch-up gives $\frac12(0.30)(t+120)^2=\frac12(0.50)t^2$, so $t\approx410\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: This time is far too short for B to erase A's 120 s head start.
perOption.B: This is when the trains have equal speeds, while A is still ahead.
perOption.C: At 210 s, B's displacement from the station is still smaller than A's.
perOption.D: Correct. Both trains have travelled the same distance.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q2.issues: Printed key letter D differs from keyAnswer A (answer-missing placeholder).

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q3.body: With air resistance neglected, horizontal acceleration is zero, so horizontal velocity is constant. The vertical acceleration is a constant $9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ downward, so the upward velocity decreases uniformly as the stone rises.

perOption.A: Assumes the horizontal velocity decreases despite zero horizontal acceleration.
perOption.B: Assumes horizontal acceleration and treats downward gravity as increasing the upward velocity.
perOption.C: Treats downward gravity as increasing the upward component.
perOption.D: Correct. Horizontal velocity is constant and upward velocity decreases uniformly.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q3.issues: Printed key letter D differs from keyAnswer A (answer-missing placeholder).

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q4.body: Take right as positive. Conservation of momentum gives $(0.5)(2.0)+(0.4)(-3.0)=(0.5+0.4)v$. Thus $v=-0.22\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so the blocks move left.

perOption.A: Correct. The combined velocity is negative with right taken as positive.
perOption.B: Reverses the direction of the net initial momentum.
perOption.C: Adds the magnitudes of opposing momenta and assigns the result to the left.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes of opposing momenta and assigns the result to the right.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q5.body: The key takes the impulse to be the ball's change in momentum. With upward positive, $m(v_f-v_i)=0.060[14-(-21)]=2.1\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the speed magnitudes despite the reversal in direction.
perOption.B: Correct. It gives the net impulse used by the key.
perOption.C: Divides the momentum change by contact time, giving the mean net force in newtons.
perOption.D: Uses 60 as the mass in kilograms instead of converting 60 g to 0.060 kg.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q5.issues: Printed key letter B differs from keyAnswer A (answer-missing placeholder). Printed B is the net impulse. The ground's impulse is $2.1+0.060(9.81)(0.30)\approx2.28\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ upward, so none of the options is strictly correct. B is the intended and closest choice.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q6.body: By Hooke's law, $F=ke$, with extension $e=0.10\ \mathrm{m}$. The stored energy is $\frac12ke^2=\frac12Fe=\frac12(2)(0.10)=0.1\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The energy is half the final force times the extension.
perOption.B: Uses the final force over the full extension and misses the factor of one-half.
perOption.C: Multiplies the final force by the unstretched length.
perOption.D: Multiplies the final force by the stretched length.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q7.body: When floating, the upthrust equals the block's weight, $\rho_{\mathrm{b}}Vg$, where $V$ is the block's volume. When fully submerged, the upthrust equals the weight of displaced water, $\rho_{\mathrm{w}}Vg$. Their submerged-to-floating ratio is $\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{w}}Vg}{\rho_{\mathrm{b}}Vg}=\frac{1000}{700}=1.43$.

perOption.A: Places the decimal point one place too far left in the density ratio.
perOption.B: Divides the floating upthrust by the fully submerged upthrust.
perOption.C: Correct. The ratio equals the water density divided by the wood density.
perOption.D: The densities differ by a factor of about 1.4, so a sevenfold increase is too large.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q7.issues: Printed key letter C differs from keyAnswer A (answer-missing placeholder).

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q8.body: The rod's weight acts at its centre, initially $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ left of the pivot. Taking moments gives $(Mg)(0.30)=(mg)(1.2)$, so $M/m=4$. After moving the pivot right and doubling the hanging mass, $(Mg)(0.30+x)=(2mg)(1.2-x)$. Thus $\frac{2(1.2-x)}{0.30+x}=4$, giving $x=0.20\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The two moments balance at the new pivot.
perOption.B: Increases the rod's moment arm too far, so the rod's moment dominates.
perOption.C: Moves the pivot far enough right to give the rod a larger moment than the doubled mass.
perOption.D: Shortens the doubled mass's moment arm to 0.40 m, making its moment too small.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q9.body: At constant speed the resultant force is zero, so the driving force balances friction, $F=kv^2$. Using $P=Fv=kv^3$ gives $\frac{100}{30^3}=\frac{200}{v^3}$. Hence $v=2^{1/3}(30)=37.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Doubling power multiplies speed by the cube root of two.
perOption.B: Uses square-root scaling and misses the extra speed factor in power.
perOption.C: Overestimates the speed increase and would require about five times the original power.
perOption.D: Doubles the speed as though power were directly proportional to speed.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q10.body: Since $W=\int F\,\mathrm{d}s$, the force is the gradient of the work–displacement graph. The gradient starts at zero, increases, is briefly approximately constant, then falls to zero at the maximum work. The work then decreases, so the force is negative.

perOption.A: Shows an initially constant positive force even though the work gradient starts at zero and increases.
perOption.B: Correct. The force follows the gradient and becomes negative after the maximum.
perOption.C: Omits the negative force needed for work to decrease.
perOption.D: Copies the work curve and stays positive where the gradient is negative.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q10.issues: Printed key letter B differs from keyAnswer A (answer-missing placeholder). The question PNG cuts off options C and D. Their full graphs appear on page 9 of the key.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q11.body: The speed $v$ remains constant in uniform circular motion. With fixed radius $r$, the magnitude $a_{\mathrm{c}}=v^2/r$ stays constant, so its variation over a revolution is zero.

perOption.A: Correct. The magnitude stays constant throughout the revolution.
perOption.B: Confuses gravity's effect on the rod force with a change in centripetal acceleration magnitude.
perOption.C: Gives the constant magnitude itself.
perOption.D: Uses the difference between opposite acceleration vectors when the question asks about changes in magnitude.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q11.issues: The key refers to constant linear velocity, although its calculation requires constant speed and the direction changes.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q12.body: Geostationary satellites have a period of one day, giving them the same angular velocity. Their common orbital radius also gives them the same centripetal acceleration. Their kinetic energies may differ because kinetic energy depends on satellite mass.

perOption.A: All geostationary satellites share Earth's angular velocity.
perOption.B: Their common orbital radius and angular speed give the same centripetal acceleration.
perOption.C: Correct. Satellite masses may differ.
perOption.D: Each geostationary orbit has the same period as Earth's rotation.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q12.issues: Printed key letter C differs from keyAnswer A (answer-missing placeholder).

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q13.body: The mass starts at maximum displacement, so $x=x_0\cos(3.14t)$. At equilibrium $x=0$, which occurs for $3.14t=\pi/2,3\pi/2,5\pi/2,\ldots$. Hence $t=0.50,\ 1.50,\ 2.50,\ldots\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Halves both the first crossing time and the interval between crossings.
perOption.B: Uses the correct interval but starts the crossings too early.
perOption.C: Counts the turning point at 1.00 s as an equilibrium crossing.
perOption.D: Correct. Crossings start at 0.50 s and repeat every 1.00 s.

cjc-2022-promo-p1-q13.issues: Printed key letter D differs from keyAnswer A (answer-missing placeholder).

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: For $x=ab^2/c$, the fractional uncertainty is $\Delta x/x=\Delta a/a+2\Delta b/b+\Delta c/c$. In percentage terms, option A gives $(4+2(2)+4)\%=12\%$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $20\%$.
perOption.C: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $9\%$.
perOption.D: Doubling the contribution from $b$ gives $14\%$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: The velocity of P relative to Q is $\mathbf v_P-\mathbf v_Q=\mathbf v_P+(-\mathbf v_Q)$. Add the $1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ westward vector to the tip of the $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ northward vector to obtain the steep northwest arrow.

perOption.A: Points southeast and understates the north–south component.
perOption.B: Points northwest but understates the northward component relative to the westward component.
perOption.C: Reverses the relative velocity and shows Q moving relative to P.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: The complete sheet and the cut-out have centres $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ below M, respectively. Subtract the cut-out's first moment from the complete sheet's, giving $\rho tg[(4.0)(4.0)(2.0)-(1.0)(2.0)(3.0)]=26\rho tg$, using centimetres throughout. The remaining weight times its distance $y$ below M is $14\rho tg\,y$, so $y=26/14=1.857\ \mathrm{cm}\approx1.9\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Shifts the centre too far upward for a cut-out of area $2.0\ \mathrm{cm^2}$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Shifts the centre toward the cut-out, as if the removed metal added weight.
perOption.D: Shifts the centre downward despite the removal of metal below the original centre.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.issues: The key labels the calculation as torques about M. The weights act along the vertical symmetry line through M, so the calculation uses first moments of weight with respect to depth below M.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: The magnetic force $NBIL$ on the lowest side acts horizontally to the right. Balancing moments about the pivot gives $Mg(L/2)\sin 30^\circ=NBIL(L\cos 30^\circ)$. Substituting $0.30(0.025)\sin 30^\circ=100B(0.40)(0.050)(0.050)\cos 30^\circ$ gives $B=0.043\ \mathrm T$.

perOption.A: Omits the $\cos 30^\circ$ factor from the magnetic force's moment arm.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Omits the $\sin 30^\circ$ factor from the weight's moment arm.
perOption.D: Uses the full side length in the weight's moment arm.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: By $F_{\mathrm{net}}=ma$, the constant positive force produces constant acceleration, so velocity increases along a straight line. When the net force is zero, acceleration is zero and the velocity–time graph is horizontal.

perOption.A: Copies the force pulse and shows instantaneous changes in velocity.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Shows deceleration after the force has dropped to zero.
perOption.D: Shows increasing acceleration during a constant force.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: The cart has a forward tension $T$ and a backward resistive force of $40\ \mathrm N$. Newton's second law gives $T-40=600(0.15)$, so $T=130\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: A tension of $65\ \mathrm N$ leaves only $25\ \mathrm N$ to accelerate the cart.
perOption.B: A tension of $100\ \mathrm N$ leaves only $60\ \mathrm N$ of net force.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: A tension of $195\ \mathrm N$ gives $155\ \mathrm N$ of net force, exceeding the required $90\ \mathrm N$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: The useful output power is $Fv=1600(11)=17\,600\ \mathrm W$, all of which goes into overcoming resistance at constant speed on level ground. The fuel supplies $1.8\times10^6/60=30\,000\ \mathrm W$. The efficiency is $(17\,600/30\,000)\times100\%\approx59\%$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the ratio of the $17.6\ \mathrm{kW}$ useful power to the $30.0\ \mathrm{kW}$ fuel input.
perOption.B: At the stated fuel input, this percentage accounts for only about $10\ \mathrm{kW}$ of useful power.
perOption.C: This percentage treats the roughly $17.6\ \mathrm{kW}$ useful output as only a little over a third of the $30\ \mathrm{kW}$ input.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: The total energy is the initial kinetic energy $E=\tfrac12mu^2$. At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, but the constant horizontal velocity is $u\cos60^\circ=u/2$, so the kinetic energy is $\tfrac12m(u/2)^2=E/4$. By energy conservation, the gravitational potential energy there is $3E/4$, so the two curves cross.

perOption.A: Shows zero kinetic energy at the top, as for a vertical launch.
perOption.B: Shows equal energies at the top, as for a $45^\circ$ launch.
perOption.C: Keeps kinetic energy above half the total, as for a launch below $45^\circ$.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: Take right as positive and let $V$ be P's final velocity. In an elastic collision, the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation, so $v-0=0.4v-V$. Thus $V=-0.6v$ and P's speed is $0.6v$.

perOption.A: Stopping P would leave a separation speed of only $0.4v$.
perOption.B: Even if P rebounds at $0.4v$, the separation speed would be only $0.8v$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: If P rebounded at $v$, the separation speed would be $1.4v$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: The centripetal acceleration is $a=r\omega^2=r(2\pi/T)^2$. With $r=7.70\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm m$ and $T=2.36\ \mathrm s$, this gives $a=0.546\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the acceleration by using too small a value for the squared angular speed.
perOption.B: The value is $r\omega$, which is the tangential speed in metres per second.
perOption.C: Underestimates the acceleration given by multiplying the radius by the squared angular speed.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The gravitational field is perpendicular to the equipotential through X, leaving A and C as candidates. Since $g=-\mathrm d\phi/\mathrm dx$ along the normal, the field points toward decreasing potential, from $-300$ toward $-400\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Points along the tangent to the equipotential through X.
perOption.C: Points toward increasing gravitational potential.
perOption.D: Points along the tangent to the equipotential through X.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: The potential is $-GM/r$, so doubling P's distance halves the potential magnitude to $\phi/2$. The inverse-distance curve is steeper nearer the mass, so moving P and Q outward by the same distance reduces the potential magnitude at P by more than at Q. The magnitude of the potential difference therefore decreases.

perOption.A: Reduces P's potential magnitude by too much for a doubling of distance.
perOption.B: Reduces P's potential magnitude by too much and assumes P and Q change by equal amounts.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assumes equal outward shifts cause equal potential changes.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: At $t=0$, acceleration is zero, so the particle is at equilibrium and its kinetic energy is maximum. Acceleration is zero three times from $t=0$ to $2\ \mathrm s$ inclusive, so the kinetic energy has three maxima in that interval.

perOption.A: Misses the kinetic-energy peak at the middle equilibrium crossing.
perOption.B: Shows zero kinetic energy at the initial and final equilibrium crossings.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Puts kinetic-energy minima at the equilibrium crossings.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: The pulse takes $0.25/0.50=0.5\ \mathrm s$ to travel $0.25\ \mathrm m$. Its leading edge reaches O at $1.0\ \mathrm s$, where the fixed end reflects and inverts the pulse. By $1.5\ \mathrm s$ that edge has travelled $0.75\ \mathrm m$ and reached P on its return. As the reflected pulse passes P between $1.5$ and $2.0\ \mathrm s$, P moves first through a larger upward displacement and then a smaller downward one.

perOption.A: Shows the smaller upward displacement first, reversing the order of the reflected lobes.
perOption.B: Shows the incoming pulse's displacement sequence, missing the inversion at the fixed end.
perOption.C: Inverts the lobes but puts the trailing lobe first.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: At distance $r$ from the source, the intensity is $I=P_s/(4\pi r^2)$. The surface receives $P=IA$, so for fixed area $P\propto P_s/r^2$. Doubling both $P_s$ and $r$ gives $P_R/P_S=2/2^2=1/2$, so $P_R=0.70\ \mathrm W$.

perOption.A: Applies the inverse-square decrease but misses the doubling of source power.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses an inverse-distance law, making the two doublings cancel.
perOption.D: Doubles the received power without accounting for the greater distance.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: The third-order maxima are symmetric, so each is at $\theta=60^\circ/2=30^\circ$ to the central direction. With line density $N=1/d$, the grating equation $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ gives $N=\sin30^\circ/(3\times500\times10^{-9})=3.33\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$. This is $333$ lines per millimetre.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses an incorrect sine factor for the $30^\circ$ diffraction angle.
perOption.C: Drops the factor $\sin30^\circ=0.5$ from the line-density calculation.
perOption.D: Reports the line count per metre.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: Using Rayleigh's criterion in the form $\theta_{\min}\approx\lambda/b$, take $b=2.4\ \mathrm m$ and a typical visible wavelength $\lambda=500\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm m$. The stars are just resolved, so their separation is $\theta_{\min}\approx(500\times10^{-9})/2.4\approx2\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the diffraction limit by more than an order of magnitude.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the angular separation by about a factor of 50.
perOption.D: Overestimates the angular separation by about a factor of 100.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.issues: The key uses the order-of-magnitude form of Rayleigh's criterion. Including the circular-aperture factor of 1.22 still gives B.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: Internal energy is a state property, so its change depends only on states A and B. Along A–C–B, the first law gives $\Delta U=Q+W_{\mathrm{on}}=16-6=10\ \mathrm J$. Along A–D–B, $10=Q-2$, so $Q=+12\ \mathrm J$ and heat enters the gas.

perOption.A: Reverses the sign of the internal energy change and treats work done by the gas as work done on it.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Assumes that heat transfer is the same along both paths.
perOption.D: Adds the $4\ \mathrm J$ difference in work to the original heat input even though the gas does less work.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: Heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the cold water. With equilibrium temperature $\theta$, density $\rho$ and specific heat capacity $c$, this gives $120\rho c(60-\theta)=30\rho c(\theta-20)$. Cancelling the common factors gives $4(60-\theta)=\theta-20$, so $5\theta=260$ and $\theta=52^\circ\mathrm C$.

perOption.A: Weights the mixture too heavily toward the cold water despite the hot water having four times its mass.
perOption.B: Reverses the hot and cold mass weights, giving the cold water four times the influence.
perOption.C: Underweights the hot water, which has four times the mass of the cold water.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: The field from $+2q$ is $E_{2q}=2q/[4\pi\varepsilon_0(0.30)^2]=24\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$ to the right. The field from $-q$ is also to the right and has magnitude $q/[4\pi\varepsilon_0(0.60)^2]=E_{2q}/8=3\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$. Adding the two gives $27\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the fields and treats the charge magnitudes as equal.
perOption.B: Subtracts the field of the negative charge even though both fields point right.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Treats the charges as equal in magnitude, doubling the negative charge's contribution.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: For each wire, $I=enAv=en(\pi d^2/4)v$. The wires are in series, so $I_X=I_Y$ and $n_Xd_X^2v_X=n_Yd_Y^2v_Y$. Hence $v_Y=(n_X/n_Y)(d_X/d_Y)^2v_X=2(1/2)^2(0.52)=0.26\ \mathrm{mm\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the diameter ratio directly as the area ratio.
perOption.C: Accounts for the density ratio alone and ignores the different areas.
perOption.D: Inverts the area ratio and omits the density ratio.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The voltmeter reads highest when the fixed resistor has the smallest potential difference. By the potential-divider principle, this happens when the combined resistance of the thermistor and LDR is greatest. Low temperature increases the NTC thermistor’s resistance, and low brightness increases the LDR’s resistance.

perOption.A: High temperature and high brightness both lower the measured pair’s resistance.
perOption.B: High temperature lowers the NTC thermistor’s resistance.
perOption.C: High brightness lowers the LDR’s resistance.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.issues: The worked solution swaps the temperature and brightness dependencies and incorrectly says the LDR resistance should be low. The explanation corrects those slips using the same potential-divider method.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The two parallel $2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors give $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$. This combination is in series with the other two $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors, so $C_{\mathrm{eq}}=(1/4+1/4+1/4)^{-1}\ \mu\mathrm{F}=1.3333\ \mu\mathrm{F}$. The battery circulates $Q=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V=(1.3333\ \mu\mathrm{F})(12\ \mathrm{V})=16\ \mu\mathrm{C}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Counts only the two standalone $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitors in series.
perOption.C: Assumes an equivalent capacitance of $3\ \mu\mathrm{F}$, which the parallel-then-series reduction does not give.
perOption.D: Implies an equivalent capacitance of about $9.2\ \mu\mathrm{F}$, even though the series combination must be below $4\ \mu\mathrm{F}$.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: The instantaneous power is $P=I_0^2R\sin^2(\omega t)$, so the graph has smooth minima at zero. The mean power is $\langle P\rangle=I^2R$. The peak is twice the mean, giving $P_0=2I^2R=2I^2(2)=4I^2$.

perOption.A: The sharp minima resemble a rectified sine rather than a squared sine.
perOption.B: The curve has the right shape but peaks at $\sqrt{2}I^2$ instead of $4I^2$.
perOption.C: Uses the mean power as the peak.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: In B, the magnetic force on the upward-moving electron points left, and the electric force points out of the page. Both forces are transverse to the path and point in perpendicular directions, so they cannot cancel. The resulting transverse force deflects the electron from the straight path.

perOption.A: The magnetic field is parallel to the velocity, so only the electric force acts, accelerating the electron along the path.
perOption.B: Correct. The transverse forces cannot cancel.
perOption.C: The key treats C as possible by balancing lateral forces, but the upward electric force changes the speed and breaks that balance.
perOption.D: The electric force into the page can balance the magnetic force out of the page.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.issues: Both B and C are impossible for the full path in uniform fields. In C, the upward electric force changes the electron’s speed, so the speed-dependent rightward magnetic force can balance the constant leftward electric component only instantaneously. B is a valid choice, but the question has no unique correct letter.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: The flux cut is $\Delta\Phi=BA=BL(vt)$. In $30\ \mathrm{s}$, the rod sweeps out $A=0.24(0.50\times30)=3.6\ \mathrm{m^2}$. The flux cut is therefore $0.15\times3.6=0.54\ \mathrm{Wb}$.

perOption.A: Gives the flux cut in one second.
perOption.B: Gives the flux cut in two seconds.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a full minute instead of half a minute.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: Intensity equals the number of photons crossing unit area per unit time multiplied by the energy per photon. The beams have the same frequency, so their photons carry the same energy. The more intense beam therefore has more photons crossing unit area each second.

perOption.A: Equal frequencies give equal photon energies.
perOption.B: All photons travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
perOption.C: Amplitude describes the electric and magnetic field oscillations in the wave picture.
perOption.D: Correct.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The slit confines the electron in the transverse $y$ direction, so $\Delta y$ is defined at the slit. The electrons spread in $y$ as they pass through, giving a transverse momentum uncertainty $\Delta p_y$. The uncertainty principle pairs position and momentum along the same axis.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Places both uncertainties at the screen, although the slit sets the position uncertainty used here.
perOption.C: Pairs a transverse position uncertainty with longitudinal momentum uncertainty.
perOption.D: Uses the screen for the position uncertainty and pairs it with longitudinal momentum uncertainty.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: In $\beta^-$ decay, a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. The proton number rises from $94$ to $95$, and the neutron number falls from $145$ to $144$. This is one square right and one square down from X, at B.

perOption.A: Lowers both counts, whereas beta-minus decay raises the proton count by one and lowers the neutron count by one.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Lowers the proton count and leaves the neutron count unchanged.
perOption.D: Raises the proton count correctly but leaves the neutron count unchanged.

cjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The foil contains small, heavy, positively charged nuclei that repel the positively charged alpha particles. Close encounters can deflect an alpha particle by more than $90^\circ$, including nearly straight back. These large deflections are explained by scattering from individual nuclei in the foil.

perOption.A: Attributes the large-angle scattering to diffraction by the crystal lattice.
perOption.B: Treats the foil surface as a reflector and misses scattering by nuclei within the foil.
perOption.C: Electrons are too light to produce the observed large deflections of alpha particles.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q11.body: The net force is the centripetal force, $F=mr\omega^2$. The forces on the $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $8.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ masses are $(5.0)(2.0)\omega^2=10\omega^2$ and $(8.0)(6.0)\omega^2=48\omega^2$, respectively. Both masses have the same $\omega$, so the ratio is $10:48=5:24$.

perOption.A: Inverts the ratio obtained by assuming both masses have the same linear speed.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the inverse-radius dependence for equal linear speeds, although the platform fixes the angular speed.
perOption.D: Reverses the order of the two forces.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q12.body: For a uniform sphere of density $\rho$, the surface field is $g=GM/r^2=(G/r^2)(\rho\,4\pi r^3/3)=(4\pi G\rho/3)r$. Doubling the radius at the same density doubles the surface field to $2X$.

perOption.A: Applies the inverse-square law while holding the mass fixed.
perOption.B: Treats the surface field as inversely proportional to radius at fixed density.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a quadratic dependence on radius, although the mass scales as the cube of the radius.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q13.body: A geostationary satellite has a period of $24$ hours. Its orbital speed is $v=r\omega=2\pi r/T=2\pi(6.40\times10^6+3.59\times10^7)/(24\times60\times60)=3.08\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Omits the factor of $2\pi$ in the circumference.
perOption.B: Uses the altitude alone as the orbital radius.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the period in minutes and reports the result in kilometres per second.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q14.body: The two curves are half a cycle apart. In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration–time and displacement–time graphs are $\pi$ radians out of phase.

perOption.A: Acceleration and velocity are a quarter of a cycle apart.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Displacement and velocity are a quarter of a cycle apart.
perOption.D: Resultant force is in phase with acceleration and a quarter of a cycle from velocity.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q15.body: The total energy scales as $E\propto\omega^2x_0^2\propto x_0^2/T^2$, where $x_0$ is the amplitude and $T$ is the period. Thus $E_2/E_1=(T_1/3T_1)^2(2x_{0,1}/x_{0,1})^2=4/9$, giving $E_2=(4/9)(18\ \mathrm{mJ})=8.0\ \mathrm{mJ}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Scales the energy by the unsquared ratio $2/3$.
perOption.C: Doubles the energy as if it were proportional to amplitude alone.
perOption.D: Squares the amplitude factor but leaves out the change in period.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q16.body: The period is $T=1/f=1/5000=0.20\ \mathrm{ms}$. One period spans two horizontal squares ($2\ \mathrm{cm}$), so the time base is $0.20/2=0.10\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}=100\ \mathrm{\mu s\,cm^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: This time base gives only $20\ \mathrm{\mu s}$ across the two squares of one cycle.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This setting gives a period of $20\ \mathrm{ms}$, a factor of 100 too large.
perOption.D: This setting gives a period of $200\ \mathrm{ms}$, a factor of 1000 too large.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q17.body: For the position shown, the path difference is $OY-OX=XY$. The waves meet in phase when this is $n\lambda$, with $n$ an integer. With $\lambda=0.75\ \mathrm{m}$, $XY=1.50\ \mathrm{m}$ gives $n=2$.

perOption.A: The path difference is $3.50\ \mathrm{m}$ outside the pair or $1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ between the speakers, neither an integer multiple of the wavelength.
perOption.B: The path difference is $2.75\ \mathrm{m}$ outside the pair or $1.25\ \mathrm{m}$ between the speakers, neither an integer multiple of the wavelength.
perOption.C: The path difference is $2.00\ \mathrm{m}$, which is not an integer multiple of $0.75\ \mathrm{m}$.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q17.issues: The key applies the path-difference formula for the exterior position shown. The stem also permits O between the speakers, but checking those positions gives no additional correct option.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q18.body: The first diffraction minimum satisfies $\sin\theta=\lambda/b$, where $b$ is the slit width. At small angles this makes the central maximum width proportional to $D\lambda/b$, where $D$ is the slit-to-screen distance, so B, C and D are true. Widening the slit lets more light through and increases the area under the intensity graph, making A the incorrect statement.

perOption.A: Correct. A wider slit increases the area under the graph.
perOption.B: A longer wavelength increases the width of the central maximum, so this statement is true.
perOption.C: A larger slit-to-screen distance increases the width of the central maximum, so this statement is true.
perOption.D: A narrower slit increases the width of the central maximum, so this statement is true.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q18.issues: The key writes $x/D=\lambda/b$ as a small-angle relation. The diagram defines $x$ as the full central maximum width, so $x/D\approx2\lambda/b$. The proportionality and answer are unaffected.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q19.body: At constant horizontal speed $u$, travelling a horizontal distance $s_x$ takes $t=s_x/u$. The vertical displacement is $s_y=\tfrac12 at^2=\tfrac12 a(s_x/u)^2$, so for constant $a$ and $u$ it is proportional to $s_x^2$. With $p=kx^2=1.0\ \mathrm{mm}$, $q=4p=4.0\ \mathrm{mm}$, $r=9p=9.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ and $s=16p=16.0\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: Uses a square-root dependence on horizontal distance.
perOption.B: Uses a linear dependence on horizontal distance.
perOption.C: Doubles the deflection at each equal horizontal interval, assuming exponential growth.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q20.body: Redraw the ladder so that the two rightmost resistors in series form a branch parallel to the middle vertical resistor. The series branch carries $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$ and drops $2.0\ \mathrm{V}$, so the parallel resistor carries $2.0\ \mathrm{A}$ and the middle top resistor carries $3.0\ \mathrm{A}$. This makes the first vertical branch’s p.d. $5.0\ \mathrm{V}$, so it draws $5.0\ \mathrm{A}$ and the first top resistor carries $8.0\ \mathrm{A}$. The input p.d. is $V=8.0+3.0+2.0=13.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Counts only the voltage across the two rightmost resistors in series.
perOption.B: Stops at the voltage across the first vertical branch.
perOption.C: Counts only the voltage across the first top resistor.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q21.body: The filament lamp’s $I$-against-$V$ graph starts at the origin and flattens as $V$ rises. Swapping the axes reflects the curve across the line that interchanges the axes, giving a $V$-against-$I$ graph that gets steeper as $I$ rises.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows a constant resistance characteristic.
perOption.C: Shows a nonzero potential difference at zero current and the wrong curvature.
perOption.D: Uses the flattening shape of the $I$-against-$V$ characteristic with the axes swapped.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q22.body: The branches share the same p.d., so $2I_1=3I_2=4I_3$. The supply current is $I=I_1+I_2+I_3=(3/2)I_2+I_2+(3/4)I_2$, giving $I_2=4I/13$. Substitution gives $I_1=6I/13$ and $I_3=3I/13$, so $I_1:I_2:I_3=6:4:3$.

perOption.A: Reverses the branch-current order, putting the smallest current through the smallest resistance.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Makes current increase with resistance despite the common branch voltage.
perOption.D: Splits the current in descending order but gives unequal branch voltages, since $2(18)\ne3(16)$.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q23.body: The cable carries current into the page and the field lies in the plane of the page, so the angle between them is $90^\circ$. The force is $F=BIL\sin\theta=(4.0\times10^{-5})(3.0)(2.0)\sin90^\circ=240\ \mathrm{\mu N}$.

perOption.A: Uses too small an effective field component even though the entire field is perpendicular to the cable.
perOption.B: Uses $\sin65^\circ$ by taking the field’s inclination to the horizontal as the current–field angle.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Exceeds $BIL$, the maximum possible force for the given field, current and length.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q24.body: A neutral point occurs where the two magnetic flux densities are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. By the right-hand grip rule, the fields oppose each other only between the wires, in region 2.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The fields reinforce each other in both outer regions.
perOption.C: Changing the relative current magnitudes cannot reverse either field in an outer region.
perOption.D: The fields oppose each other in region 2 and can have equal magnitudes there.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q25.body: The two oppositely oriented diodes allow current through $R_1$ in both directions. One diode is in series with $R_2$, so the current in that direction has a smaller peak magnitude.

perOption.A: Shows equal peak magnitudes even though one direction adds $R_2$ in series.
perOption.B: Suppresses one half-cycle even though the second diode provides a path for it.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Shows both half-cycles with the same sign, although the current reverses through $R_1$.

dhs-2022-prelim-p1-q25.issues: The supplied question PNG crops the lower parts of graphs C and D. The circuit and worked key establish that C represents alternating current with unequal peak magnitudes.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Let $z=3PQ^4/R^2$. The fractional uncertainty is $\Delta z/z=\Delta P/P+4\Delta Q/Q+2\Delta R/R$. For C the percentage uncertainty is $(3+4(1)+2(2))\%=11\%$.

perOption.A: Gives 9.0% after weighting the uncertainties by the powers.
perOption.B: Gives 13% after weighting the uncertainties by the powers.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives 15% after weighting the uncertainties by the powers.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: Displacement is the area above the time axis minus the area below it. For X both triangles lie above the axis, while the negative area for Y partly cancels its positive area, so Y has the smaller displacement. Distance adds the magnitudes of the areas on both sides of the axis. Y has a lower positive peak ($3v/4$ versus $v$), and even after including its negative portion as a positive area, its total distance is smaller than X’s.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Adding the magnitude of Y’s negative area still leaves Y with less total distance.
perOption.C: Subtracting Y’s negative-area magnitude gives a smaller displacement than X’s.
perOption.D: Both Y’s signed area and its total unsigned area are smaller than X’s.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q2.issues: Page 6 incorrectly invokes cancellation in its distance discussion. The unsigned areas are 5vt₂/16 for Y and vt₂/2 for X, so the keyed comparison still holds.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: The elastic potential energy is the area under the force–extension graph. The triangular area grows from $\tfrac12F_1x_1$ to $\tfrac12F_2x_2$. The increase is therefore $\tfrac12(F_2x_2-F_1x_1)$.

perOption.A: Uses rectangular areas and misses the factor of one-half.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Squares the extensions and omits the triangular-area factor.
perOption.D: Squares the extensions even though the base of each triangle is the extension itself.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: Applying Newton’s second law to the lift gives $T-W_2-D=m_{\mathrm{lift}}a$. If $T=D+W_2$, the resultant is zero, so $a=0$ and the lift has constant velocity, including the possibility of rest.

perOption.A: The cable tension equals the combined weight only when the lift system has zero acceleration.
perOption.B: Equal forces on the man imply zero acceleration, which also allows motion at constant nonzero velocity.
perOption.C: Both forces act on the man, and their magnitudes can differ when he accelerates.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: The downhill component of weight is $F=mg\sin\theta$, so $a=F/m=g\sin\theta$. With double the mass, the downhill force doubles to $F'=2mg\sin\theta$. Dividing by the new mass gives $a'=F'/(2m)=g\sin\theta=a$.

perOption.A: The downhill component of weight doubles when the mass doubles.
perOption.B: Assumes the downhill force stays fixed as the mass doubles.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Doubles the force but overlooks the doubling of the mass.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: For the two blocks together, the net force is $54-6.0=48\ \mathrm{N}$, so their common acceleration is $48/8.0=6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Applying Newton’s second law to the $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ block gives a resultant horizontal force of $2.0(6.0)=12\ \mathrm{N}$. This is also the contact force if the friction shown acts entirely on the larger block, as assumed in the key.

perOption.A: Correct. This is the resultant force on the smaller block.
perOption.B: Uses the mass of the larger block with the common acceleration.
perOption.C: Uses the wrong system or force balance for the smaller block, whose resultant is 12 N.
perOption.D: Uses the resultant force on both blocks combined.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q6.issues: The wording gives only total friction and does not explicitly distinguish resultant force from contact force. A gives the resultant, and it gives the contact force if the 2.0 kg block has no friction, as the key assumes from the diagram.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: At the top, tension and weight both act downwards towards the centre, so $T+W=mv^2/r$. The required resultant is $0.10(6.0)^2/0.50=7.2\ \mathrm{N}$ and the weight is $0.10(9.81)=0.98\ \mathrm{N}$. Hence $T=7.2-0.98=6.22\ \mathrm{N}\approx6.2\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Gives the ball’s weight alone.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the entire centripetal force and ignores the contribution of weight.
perOption.D: Adds the weight even though it already acts towards the centre.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: The key takes $g_X=g_Y=GM/r^2$ and $g_Z=2GM/r^2$. It resolves the fields of X and Y along the line through O and Z, using $30^\circ$ for each angle, so their components perpendicular to that line cancel and their components away from Z sum to $2(GM/r^2)\cos30^\circ=\sqrt{3}GM/r^2$. Subtracting this from Z’s field gives the key’s result, $G(2M-\sqrt{3}M)/r^2$ towards Z.

perOption.A: Treats the three fields as cancelling despite Z having twice the mass of X or Y.
perOption.B: Points the resultant towards X even though the additional mass is at Z.
perOption.C: This is the physical result at the centre, where the three equal-mass contributions cancel and the extra mass at Z supplies the net field.
perOption.D: Correct according to the key’s component calculation.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q8.issues: The key uses 30° instead of 60° between each of the X and Y field vectors and the direction directly away from Z. With O at the centre as drawn, three equal-mass contributions cancel and Z’s extra mass gives GM/r² towards Z, option C.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: Gravitational potential is a scalar, so add the three contributions at O directly. This gives $\phi=-GM/r-GM/r-G(2M)/r=-4GM/r$. The potential has no direction.

perOption.A: Treats the three negative potentials as if they could cancel by symmetry.
perOption.B: Uses a single mass-M contribution and assigns a direction to a scalar.
perOption.C: Uses the wrong sign and assigns a direction to a scalar.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q9.issues: Option D explicitly prints the minus sign, although the key’s closing comment describes it as implied.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: The total energy is $E=\tfrac12mv_0^2=\tfrac12m(\omega x_0)^2$, so $E\propto(x_0/T)^2$. Doubling $x_0$ and tripling $T$ gives $E_{\mathrm{new}}/E_{\mathrm{old}}=(2/3)^2=4/9$. The new energy is $(4/9)(18\ \mathrm{mJ})=8\ \mathrm{mJ}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Applies the factor of $2/3$ without squaring it.
perOption.C: Doubles the energy directly and ignores the change in period.
perOption.D: Squares the amplitude factor but ignores the longer period.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The angles between successive polariser axes are $40^\circ-30^\circ=10^\circ$ and $60^\circ-40^\circ=20^\circ$. W transmits half the incident unpolarised intensity, so $I_W=0.5I_0$. By Malus's law, $I_X=0.5I_0\cos^2 10^\circ=0.4849I_0$, then $I_Y=I_X\cos^2 20^\circ\approx 0.428I_0\approx 0.43I_0$.

perOption.A: Uses the absolute $60^\circ$ angle at Y instead of its $20^\circ$ angle relative to X.
perOption.B: Uses the absolute axis angles instead of the angles between successive axes.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Exceeds the $0.5I_0$ already transmitted by W.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: At the original area, intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so doubling the amplitude gives $k(2A)^2=4I$. Focusing the same power onto one-third of the original area then gives $(4IS)/(S/3)=12I$.

perOption.A: Treats intensity as proportional to amplitude instead of amplitude squared.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the gain from doubling the amplitude, which is a factor of four.
perOption.D: Doubles the result again even though squaring the amplitude ratio already accounts for the doubling.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: Using the key's resolution approximation, $\theta_{\min}\approx\lambda/b$, where $b$ is the dish diameter. This gives $\theta_{\min}=(0.40\times10^{-6})/5.1=7.843\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{rad}$. For a small angle, the minimum separation is $x=\theta_{\min}D=(7.843\times10^{-8})(2.8\times10^{25})\approx2.2\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Halves the separation, as would happen if the stated diameter were doubled.
perOption.B: Correct. This follows from the key's resolution approximation.
perOption.C: Inverts the angular ratio to $b/\lambda$ and halves the resulting separation.
perOption.D: Uses $b/\lambda$ instead of $\lambda/b$, giving a vastly larger separation.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The key uses the syllabus approximation $\lambda/b$. The circular-aperture Rayleigh factor of 1.22 gives about $2.7\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}$, which is unlisted. B is still the closest listed value.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: The mean translational kinetic energy satisfies $\tfrac12mc_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\tfrac32kT$, so $c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2\propto T$. Hence $T/(2T)=c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2/c_{\mathrm{rms,new}}^2$, which gives $c_{\mathrm{rms,new}}=\sqrt{2}\,c_{\mathrm{rms}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the rms speed itself as directly proportional to temperature.
perOption.C: Applies an extra factor of two after taking the square root of the temperature ratio.
perOption.D: Squares the temperature ratio instead of taking its square root.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: The connected containers have the same pressure $p$ at equilibrium. Using $n=pV/(RT)$ gives $n_X=p(2V)/[R(2T)]=pV/(RT)$ and $n_Y=pV/(RT)$. The school's working therefore gives $n_X/n_Y=1.00$, even though its answer label is A.

perOption.A: Inverts the volume ratio while keeping the temperature ratio in the denominator.
perOption.B: Correct. The volume and temperature factors cancel.
perOption.C: Accounts for the doubled volume but ignores the doubled temperature.
perOption.D: Treats the amount of gas as directly proportional to temperature at fixed pressure and volume.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q15.issues: The summary table and worked-solution label show A, matching keyAnswer, but the worked calculation gives 1.00, which is B. A is incorrect.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: The water releases $0.150(4180)(20.0)=12540\ \mathrm{J}$ as it cools to $0^\circ\mathrm C$. Warming the ice to $0^\circ\mathrm C$ takes $0.100(2100)(10.0)=2100\ \mathrm{J}$, leaving $10440\ \mathrm{J}$ for melting. This melts $10440/334000=0.03126\ \mathrm{kg}$, or $31.3\ \mathrm g$. The remaining $68.7\ \mathrm g$ of ice coexists with water at $0^\circ\mathrm C$.

perOption.A: Confuses absolute zero with the melting point and reports the mass melted as the mass remaining.
perOption.B: Finds the correct ice mass but confuses absolute zero with the melting point.
perOption.C: Reports the mass that melts as the mass that remains.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: In $I=nAvq$, the number density is $n=N/V$ and the wire volume is $V=AL$, giving $I=Nvq/L$. Hence $N=IL/(vq)=(12)(0.35)/[(5.0\times10^{-4})(1.60\times10^{-19})]=5.3\times10^{22}$.

perOption.A: Treats the drift speed as a multiplier, effectively using a short transit time for slow electrons.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Omits the wire length when converting the carrier count per unit length to the total count.
perOption.D: Divides by the wire length instead of multiplying by it.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: The ideal diode conducts only during the positive half-cycle, and the peak load voltage is $V_0=12.0\ \mathrm V$. The full-cycle average power is half that for an unrectified sine wave of the same peak voltage, so $\langle P\rangle=\tfrac12(V_0^2/2R)=12.0^2/(4\times50)=0.72\ \mathrm W$.

perOption.A: Assumes the diode blocks both half-cycles.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the average power for an unrectified sine wave.
perOption.D: Uses the peak power as the cycle average.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: Closing all three switches puts the external resistors in parallel, so $1/R_{\mathrm p}=1/4+1/8+1/12=11/24$ in inverse ohms. Adding the internal resistance gives $R_{\mathrm{tot}}=(24/11+1.00)\ \Omega=(35/11)\ \Omega$. The cell current is $I=2.00/(35/11)=0.629\ \mathrm A$.

perOption.A: Adds all four resistances as though they were in series.
perOption.B: Uses only the $4.00\ \Omega$ branch and neglects the internal resistance.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the parallel resistance alone and omits the internal resistance.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: Let $k$ be the fraction of the way the slider has moved from the top of the upper resistor, with $0\le k\le1$. The equal resistors each drop $3.0\ \mathrm V$, so $V_X=6.0-3.0k$ in volts. The potential difference $V_Y-V_X=3.0k$ therefore ranges from $0$ to $3.0\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: Measures from the bottom rail, giving a range of $3.0$ to $6.0\ \mathrm V$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Connects X and Y across the supply, fixing the output at $6.0\ \mathrm V$.
perOption.D: Measures across the fixed lower resistor, so the output ranges from $3.0$ to $6.0\ \mathrm V$ as the effective upper resistance varies.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q20.issues: The key's distractor note says D is fixed at 3.0 V. The diagram shows the slider bypassing part of the upper resistor, so D actually varies from 3.0 V to 6.0 V.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The capacitor on AB is in parallel with the AC–CB series branch, so the branch has $5.0\ \mathrm V$ across it. Its equivalent capacitance is $(1/2+1/3)^{-1}\ \mathrm{\mu F}=1.2\ \mathrm{\mu F}$, giving each series capacitor a charge of $Q=C_{\mathrm{eq}}V=6.0\ \mathrm{\mu C}$. Thus $V_{BC}=Q/C_{BC}=6.0/3=2.0\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the charge required on the series capacitors for a total drop of $5.0\ \mathrm V$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Splits the voltage equally across two unequal capacitances.
perOption.D: Gives the voltage across AC instead of BC.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: By Newton's third law, the forces on the two wires have equal magnitudes. Currents in the same direction attract, while currents in opposite directions repel. In A, both currents flow downwards, so each force points towards the other wire.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows unequal forces and repulsion between currents flowing in the same direction.
perOption.C: Shows attraction even though the currents flow in opposite directions and should repel.
perOption.D: Shows unequal forces even though the two forces are a Newton's third-law pair.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The field points downwards from the $5.00\ \mathrm{kV}$ plate to the $0\ \mathrm V$ plate, so the positive proton experiences a downward force. Its magnitude is $F=qE=(1.60\times10^{-19})(5000/0.100)=8.00\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm N$. This gives $a=F/m=4.790\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, and the transit time is $t=L/v_x=0.150/(2.52\times10^6)=5.952\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm s$. Thus $y=\tfrac12at^2=8.49\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m$, or $8.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m$ downwards.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Reverses the direction of the force on the positive proton.
perOption.C: Overestimates the displacement from the downward acceleration and horizontal transit time.
perOption.D: Overestimates the displacement and reverses the force direction.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: The original force is $F=kQ^2/r^2$. Each charge becomes $Q+3Q=4Q$ and the separation becomes $2r$, so $F_{\mathrm{new}}=k(4Q)(4Q)/(2r)^2=4kQ^2/r^2$. Hence $F_{\mathrm{new}}/F=4$.

perOption.A: Applies the charge increase to only one charge, making it cancel the factor of four from the distance.
perOption.B: Treats each new charge as $3Q$ instead of $4Q$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses an inverse-distance law instead of the inverse-square law.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: The magnetic flux density $B$ stays constant because the external field is unaffected by the rotation. The initial flux is maximal, and the tilt reduces the area projected perpendicular to the field, so the flux decreases.

perOption.A: Confuses the decreasing component normal to the coil with a decrease in the field magnitude.
perOption.B: Assumes rotation strengthens the external field and increases the flux.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assumes the flux increases as the coil tilts away from its maximum-flux orientation.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: By Faraday's law, the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is $|\mathcal E|=N|\Delta\Phi|/\Delta t$. With $1500$ turns and a flux change of $0.85\ \mathrm{Wb}$ in $0.19\ \mathrm s$, this gives $1500(0.85/0.19)\approx6711\ \mathrm V\approx6710\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: Uses the zero final flux in place of the nonzero change in flux.
perOption.B: Calculates the induced e.m.f. for one turn only.
perOption.C: Underestimates the rate of change of flux linkage across all 1500 turns.
perOption.D: Correct.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: Photon energy is $E=hf=hc/\lambda$, so $E$ is directly proportional to $1/\lambda$. The graph of $E$ against $1/\lambda$ is therefore a straight line through the origin.

perOption.A: Shows a nonlinear dependence on reciprocal wavelength.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Makes energy directly proportional to wavelength.
perOption.D: Shows energy increasing with wavelength even though it decreases.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The energy levels are $E_n=h^2n^2/(8mL^2)$, and the ground state has $n=1$, giving $E=h^2/(8mL^2)$. For the second particle, $E'=h^2/[8(2m)(2L)^2]=E/8$.

perOption.A: Accounts only for the doubling of mass.
perOption.B: Accounts only for the width doubling, or treats both effects as linear.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Squares the mass ratio as well as the width ratio.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Starting with $N$ nuclei, $3N/4$ decay in two half-lives. Approximating nuclear masses by their nucleon numbers in atomic mass units, the change is $\Delta m=[-(3N/4)(210)+(3N/4)(206)]\,\mathrm u=-3N\,\mathrm u$. Relative to the initial mass $210N\,\mathrm u$, this is a decrease of $1/70\approx1.43\%$.

perOption.A: Uses the surviving quarter of the parent nuclei to count the emitted alpha particles.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Confuses the fraction of parent nuclei remaining with the fraction of mass lost.
perOption.D: Assumes the full mass of each decayed nucleus leaves the sample.

dhs-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: Beta particles can penetrate several millimetres into tissue and deposit ionising energy in surface and near-surface tumours. Their limited range helps spare deeper healthy tissue.

perOption.A: Alpha particles are stopped by the outer layer of skin before reaching a deep tumour.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gamma rays can reach deep tissues, so their use is not limited to surface conditions.
perOption.D: Alpha particles emitted inside the body have too short a range to reach external detectors.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Using $V=P/I$, one volt is one watt per ampere. Since $\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}}$, the volt has base units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,A^{-1}\,s^{-3}}$.

perOption.A: Leaves the derived unit ohm unexpanded.
perOption.B: Uses the derived units coulomb and ohm.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Leaves the coulomb unexpanded as an ampere-second.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: The maximum speed occurs at a peak or trough of the velocity–time graph, where $a=dv/dt=0$. Direction changes when velocity changes sign, and displacement increases wherever velocity is positive.

perOption.A: At $t=T$ the velocity is zero and the displacement has returned to zero, although the interior zero crossing does coincide with maximum displacement.
perOption.B: Direction changes when $v$ changes sign, while $a=0$ at the velocity extrema.
perOption.C: Displacement increases whenever $v>0$, even if the acceleration is negative.
perOption.D: Correct. The greatest speed occurs at a horizontal tangent.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.issues: The key rejects A using the endpoint at t = T. The interior zero crossing does give the greatest displacement, so A is also defensible if read as identifying when the maximum occurs.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: Let $L$ be the lift. On descent, Newton’s second law gives $Mg-L=2M$, so $L=M(g-2)$. On ascent, for the remaining mass $M_1$, $L-M_1g=4M_1$, so $L=M_1(g+4)$. Equating the lifts gives $M_1=0.57M$, so the mass removed is $0.43M$.

perOption.A: Counts only the initial downward acceleration in the required change of acceleration.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the mass remaining after removal.
perOption.D: Overstates the mass reduction by doubling the required fraction.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: Balancing moments about A gives $F_B(5.0)=200(2.5)+880(0.80)$, so $F_B=240.8\ \mathrm{N}$. Vertical force balance gives $F_A=880+200-240.8=839.2\ \mathrm{N}$. Hence $F_A/F_B=839.2/240.8\approx3.48\approx3.5$.

perOption.A: Inverts the ratio to $F_B/F_A$.
perOption.B: Divides $F_A$ by the total weight of $1080\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Divides the total weight by $F_B$ without first subtracting $F_B$ to find $F_A$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: By Hooke’s law, $15=k(0.090-0.060)$, so $k=500\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. The maximum extension is $0.100\ \mathrm{m}$, giving a maximum load $ke_{\max}=500(0.100)=50\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Treats the loaded length of 90 mm as the extension when finding the spring constant.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Adds the 60 mm unstretched length to the 100 mm extension before applying Hooke’s law.
perOption.D: Adds the initial 15 N load to a force already calculated using the full 160 mm spring length.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: Assuming Hooke’s law, the force–extension graph is a straight line through the origin, so its triangular area gives stored energy $\tfrac12 Fe$. At equilibrium $F=mg$ and $e=y-x$, so the stored energy is $\tfrac12 mg(y-x)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the rectangular area under the final force and omits the factor of one-half.
perOption.C: Squares the extension even though the expression already uses the final force.
perOption.D: Squares the extension and omits the triangular-area factor.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: The work done against friction becomes heat, $30(3.0)=90\ \mathrm{J}$. The pulling force does work $80(3.0)=\Delta E_k+40(3.0\sin30^\circ)+90$. Solving gives $\Delta E_k=90\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Overstates the frictional work and assumes the object gains zero kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the full slope distance as the vertical rise, overstating the gravitational energy gain.
perOption.D: Treats all the pulling work as kinetic energy and overstates the heat from friction.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: All points on the rigid disc complete one revolution in the same time, so Y has period $3.2\ \mathrm{s}$. Since $v=r\omega$ and Y is half as far from the centre as X, $v_Y=0.5v_X=0.50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Scales the speed with the square of the radius and halves the shared period.
perOption.B: Scales the speed with the square of the radius.
perOption.C: Halves the period along with the speed.
perOption.D: Correct.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$ and $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$. The speed therefore increases as the orbital radius decreases. The period $T=2\pi r/v=2\pi\sqrt{r^3/(GM)}$ decreases because the orbit is shorter and the satellite travels faster.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Both orbital speed and gravitational force increase at the smaller radius.
perOption.C: Kinetic energy increases and gravitational potential energy decreases.
perOption.D: Both total mechanical energy and orbital period decrease.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: At Earth’s surface, $W=GMm/R^2$ and $\phi=-GM/R$. At height $3R$, the distance from Earth’s centre is $4R$. Thus $W'=GMm/(4R)^2=W/16$ and $\phi'=-GM/(4R)=\phi/4$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the height above the surface as the distance for the potential.
perOption.C: Scales weight with inverse distance instead of inverse distance squared.
perOption.D: Uses inverse-distance scaling for weight and uses the height above the surface for the potential.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The mean kinetic energy is $\tfrac12 m c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\tfrac32 kT$, so at the same temperature $m\propto1/c_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$. For neon, $m/(5m)=c_{\mathrm{Ne}}^2/1800^2$, giving $c_{\mathrm{Ne}}=804.98\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx800\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Divides the speed by five instead of dividing by the square root of five.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Makes r.m.s. speed increase with the square root of mass.
perOption.D: Makes r.m.s. speed directly proportional to mass.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: The energy removed to cool and freeze the water is $mc\Delta T+mL_f=0.750(4200)(18)+0.750(330000)=304200\ \mathrm{J}$. Dividing by the cooling power gives $t=304200/135=2253.3\ \mathrm{s}$, or about $38\ \mathrm{min}$.

perOption.A: Counts only the energy removed while cooling the liquid to its freezing point.
perOption.B: Counts only the latent heat removed during freezing.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overcounts the energy to be removed, for example by including the latent heat of fusion twice.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: From $pV=nRT$, at fixed cylinder volume $p\propto nT$. Thus $9.5/10=n_1(273.15+7)/[n_2(273.15+27)]$, giving $n_2=0.98249n_1$. Mass is proportional to amount of gas, so $m_2=0.98249(19)=18.667\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $19-18.667\approx0.33\ \mathrm{kg}$ escapes.

perOption.A: Underestimates the loss by leaving too much gas in the cylinder for the final pressure and temperature.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates the loss by leaving too little gas in the cylinder for the final pressure and temperature.
perOption.D: Uses a temperature ratio based on Celsius readings instead of absolute temperatures.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The key says V and n are constant. The cylinder volume is fixed, but n decreases as air escapes.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: In SHM the maximum acceleration has magnitude $\omega^2 A$. Thus $3=(\omega_Y/\omega_X)^2(0.5)$, so $(\omega_Y/\omega_X)^2=6$. Using $E=\tfrac12 m\omega^2 A^2$, the energy ratio is $2(6)(0.5)^2=3.0$.

perOption.A: Omits the doubling of the mass.
perOption.B: Uses only the mass ratio and ignores the changes in angular frequency and amplitude.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the amplitude ratio to the first power in the energy expression.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: Starting at the extreme position gives $x=A\cos(2\pi t/T)$. At the halfway point, $0.5A=A\cos[(2\pi/2.0)t]$. The first solution is $t=0.33\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Uses a sine equation with zero initial displacement, as if the pendulum started at equilibrium.
perOption.B: Assumes the pendulum covers half the distance to equilibrium in half the time.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses half a period, when the pendulum reaches the opposite extreme.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: The first polariser reduces the incident intensity $I$ to $I/2$. The final intensity is $0.125I$, so Malus’s law gives $(I/2)\cos^2\theta=0.125I$. Hence $\theta=60^\circ$.

perOption.A: Using $30^\circ$ as the angle between the axes gives a transmitted fraction of $0.375$.
perOption.B: Using $40^\circ$ gives a transmitted fraction of about $0.293$, which is too high.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Using $75^\circ$ gives a transmitted fraction of about $0.033$, which is too low.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: For the open tube’s fundamental, $\lambda/2=L$, so $f=v/(2L)$. With one end closed, the fundamental satisfies $\lambda_1/4=L$, so $f_1=v/(4L)=0.5f$.

perOption.A: Treats the quarter-wave condition as a fourfold frequency increase relative to the open tube.
perOption.B: Treats frequency as increasing when the fundamental wavelength doubles.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses a quarter of the original frequency, overlooking that the open tube already contains only half a wavelength.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: Using the key’s Rayleigh estimate with visible light at about $500\ \mathrm{nm}$, $\sin\theta=\lambda/b=(500\times10^{-9})/(5\times10^{-3})$, so $\theta\approx0.0001\ \mathrm{rad}$. The minimum separation is approximately $3.0(0.0001)=0.0003\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Overestimates the diffraction angle by a factor of ten.
perOption.C: Overestimates the diffraction angle by a factor of one hundred.
perOption.D: Overestimates the diffraction angle by a factor of one thousand.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.issues: The question omits wavelength. The key assumes 500 nm and omits the 1.22 factor for a circular aperture. Including the factor still leaves A as the closest choice.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: The fixed charge’s potential doubles in magnitude at half the distance, giving $-2.4\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$ at the midpoint. The given potential and distance imply a fixed charge of about $-e$, so the alpha particle’s charge of $+2e$ contributes $+4.8\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$ there. Adding the signed potentials gives $+2.4\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the magnitude of the fixed charge’s potential at X without calculating the net midpoint potential.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Includes only the alpha particle’s contribution.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes of the two contributions despite their opposite signs.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The key calls the fixed charge an electron. The printed question leaves its identity unspecified, but its magnitude and sign follow from the given potential and distance.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: When the variable resistance is $r$, the voltage divider gives $V=Er/(r+r)=0.5E$ and $v=0.5E$. At $3r$, it gives $V=E(3r)/(3r+r)=0.75E$ and $v=0.25E$. Since $v+V=E$, the graph is the descending line segment joining these points.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows both voltages falling together, although their sum must stay at $E$.
perOption.C: Reverses the coordinates of the endpoint at $3r$, making $V$ decrease as the load resistance rises.
perOption.D: Shows both voltages increasing together, although their sum must stay at $E$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: Closing switches can add parallel current paths and reduce the effective resistance. With all three switches open, the left section is a single resistor $R$ in series with the right section, where three resistors remain in parallel. The total resistance is $R+R/3\approx 1.33R$, the largest of the listed combinations.

perOption.A: Closing all three switches gives $R_{XY}=0.85R$.
perOption.B: Closing $S_1$ and $S_3$ gives $R_{XY}=0.92R$.
perOption.C: Closing $S_3$ adds a right-hand parallel path, giving $R_{XY}=1.25R$.
perOption.D: Correct. All three open give the largest resistance.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.issues: The key says the all-open circuit contains only series resistors, but three right-hand resistors remain in parallel. Its resistance values and answer letter are correct.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The capacitor stores $\tfrac12 CV^2$. If a constant fraction $k$ becomes gravitational potential energy, then $mgh=k(\tfrac12 CV^2)$ and $h=\frac{kC}{2mg}V^2$. Thus a graph of $h$ against $V^2$ is a straight line.

perOption.A: Correct. The height is proportional to the squared voltage.
perOption.B: This treats $h$ as linear in $V$, though it is quadratic.
perOption.C: If the horizontal variable is $\sqrt V$, the height varies as its fourth power.
perOption.D: If the horizontal variable is $1/\sqrt V$, the height varies as its inverse fourth power.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.issues: The key drops the factor of one-half when rearranging for h. Its proportionality and answer letter are correct.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The normal reaction falls to half the weight, so the upward magnetic force must supply the other half for equilibrium. Thus $0.5mg=BIL\sin60^\circ$, giving $B=\frac{0.5(50\times10^{-3})(9.81)}{10(0.20)(0.866)}=0.142\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The upward magnetic force balances half the weight.
perOption.B: Using $\cos60^\circ$ in the force expression gives about $0.25\ \mathrm{T}$.
perOption.C: Using the full weight as the magnetic force gives about $0.28\ \mathrm{T}$.
perOption.D: Using the full weight together with $\cos60^\circ$ gives about $0.49\ \mathrm{T}$.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: Acceleration from rest gives $\tfrac12 mv^2=eV$, so $e/m=v^2/(2V)$. In the velocity selector, the electric and magnetic forces balance, giving $Bev=eE$ and $v=E/B$. Substituting this speed gives $\frac{e}{m}=\frac{E^2}{2VB^2}$.

perOption.A: This substitutes $v$ where the energy equation requires $v^2$.
perOption.B: This inverts the speed ratio $E/B$ before squaring it.
perOption.C: This multiplies by $2V$ when isolating $e/m$, which requires division by $2V$.
perOption.D: Correct. It combines the energy equation with the force balance.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: The left vertical arm moves across the field, making P positive relative to the bottom of that arm. The horizontal arm moves along its length, so it develops no e.m.f. along the wire. The right arm develops the same e.m.f. as the left arm, making Q positive by the same amount. P and Q therefore stay at the same potential throughout the motion in the uniform field.

perOption.A: This assigns a nonzero terminal e.m.f. at the ends of the motion even though the arm e.m.f.s cancel.
perOption.B: Changing speed changes both arm e.m.f.s equally, so there are no terminal pulses.
perOption.C: Correct. The terminal e.m.f. stays zero.
perOption.D: This follows the speed as if only one vertical arm contributed to the terminal e.m.f.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: A transformer couples the primary and secondary coils through a shared magnetic field, usually guided by a soft iron core. An alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic flux linkage in the secondary, inducing an e.m.f. by Faraday’s law.

perOption.A: The coils couple magnetically, and steady direct current produces a constant flux after switch-on.
perOption.B: Magnetic coupling is required, but steady direct current cannot sustain a changing flux.
perOption.C: Alternating current supplies the changing flux, but the coupling between the coils is magnetic.
perOption.D: Correct. Alternating current produces the changing flux needed for mutual induction.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: The slit confines each electron’s vertical position to approximately the slit width $\Delta y$. Narrowing the slit raises the lower bound on the vertical momentum uncertainty $\Delta p_y$ under Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle. The larger spread of vertical momenta makes the beam fan out more in the vertical direction after the slit.

perOption.A: Narrowing the slit increases the spread in $p_y$, causing more vertical spreading.
perOption.B: The slit confines the $y$ coordinate, so the relevant uncertainty is in $p_y$.
perOption.C: Correct. The beam spreads out more vertically.
perOption.D: The uncertainty principle applies to electrons as well as photons.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.issues: The key prints $\Delta y\Delta p_y\ge h$. For standard deviations, the bound is $\Delta y\Delta p_y\ge\hbar/2$, and slit width is an estimate of position spread. The qualitative conclusion is correct.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The concentric rings arise from electron diffraction by the carbon film. Decreasing the electron speed reduces its momentum and increases its de Broglie wavelength, $\lambda=h/p$. The longer wavelength gives greater diffraction angles, so the rings grow in diameter.

perOption.A: This attributes the rings to electrostatic repulsion and predicts smaller rings for a longer wavelength.
perOption.B: The predicted increase in diameter is right, but electron diffraction produces the rings.
perOption.C: The longer wavelength at lower speed gives larger diffraction angles and larger rings.
perOption.D: Correct. Diffraction produces larger rings at lower speed.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Subtracting the background of 300 counts per minute gives net counts of 744, 738, 196 and 1 per minute for no absorber, paper, aluminium and lead respectively. Paper makes little difference, so the readings give no evidence of alpha radiation. The aluminium reduces the count by 542 per minute, consistent with beta absorption. With 1 mm of lead the count returns to approximately background, so the residual count through aluminium is consistent with more penetrating beta particles.

perOption.A: Correct. The absorption pattern suggests beta only.
perOption.B: The negligible change with paper gives no evidence of alpha radiation.
perOption.C: The count with lead is approximately background, so the measurements give no evidence of a detectable gamma component.
perOption.D: Paper and lead give no evidence of detectable alpha or gamma components.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.issues: The solution continues on page 9. Page 8 says 0.1 mm of lead in its prose, while the table and question specify 1 mm. The readings suggest beta only, but the near-background count cannot prove that other emissions are absent.

jpjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The present ratio is $N_{\mathrm{Sr}}/N_{\mathrm{Rb}}=0.062$. Since $N_{\mathrm{Sr}}=N_0-N_{\mathrm{Rb}}$, the surviving rubidium fraction is $N_{\mathrm{Rb}}/N_0=1/1.062\approx0.9416$. Using $N_{\mathrm{Rb}}/N_0=e^{-\lambda t}$ and $\lambda=\ln2/t_{1/2}$ gives $t=-\frac{\ln(0.9416)}{\ln2}(4.88\times10^{10})\approx4.24\times10^9$ years.

perOption.A: This age is too short to produce the observed strontium-to-rubidium ratio.
perOption.B: Correct. The surviving fraction gives an age of about 4.24 billion years.
perOption.C: Treating 0.062 as the fraction of the initial rubidium that decayed gives an age close to this value.
perOption.D: This age is almost one half-life, which would give a daughter-to-parent ratio near one.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: The quantity $\tan\alpha$ is unitless, so both $Q$ and $P/\sqrt M$ are unitless. Therefore $P$ has the same units as $\sqrt M$, namely $\mathrm{kg}^{1/2}$.

perOption.A: The inverse square-root unit fails to cancel $\sqrt M$, and $Q$ must be unitless.
perOption.B: The units of $P$ must match the denominator $\sqrt M$.
perOption.C: This gives the units of the angle to $Q$, which is added to a unitless quantity.
perOption.D: Correct. The units of $P$ cancel those of the denominator.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: Taking downward as positive, Newton’s second law gives $ma=W-R$, where $R$ is air resistance. At release the speed and air resistance are zero, so $a=g$. As the speed rises, air resistance increases and acceleration falls. When air resistance balances the weight, the acceleration is zero and the object reaches terminal velocity.

perOption.A: A positive final acceleration would mean the object was still speeding up at terminal velocity.
perOption.B: At release, the absence of drag gives an initial acceleration of $g$.
perOption.C: The graph starts at zero, though gravity gives an acceleration of $g$ immediately on release.
perOption.D: Correct. Acceleration falls from $g$ towards zero.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: An elastic collision has the same total kinetic energy before and after impact. During contact, some kinetic energy can temporarily become elastic potential energy as the spheres deform. The claim that kinetic energy is conserved throughout the collision is therefore the incorrect statement.

perOption.A: This statement is true because the conserved total momentum is $2Mv-Mv=Mv$, so the spheres cannot both be at rest.
perOption.B: Correct. Kinetic energy can temporarily become elastic potential energy.
perOption.C: This statement is true because conservation of momentum requires equal and opposite momentum changes.
perOption.D: This statement is true by Newton’s third law.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: Along the runway at $15^\circ$, Newton’s second law gives $mg\sin15^\circ-f=ma$. At $20^\circ$, it gives $mg\sin20^\circ-f=2ma$. Doubling the first equation and subtracting the second eliminates $a$, giving $f=mg(2\sin15^\circ-\sin20^\circ)=0.86\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: This friction is too small to make the second net force twice the first.
perOption.B: This is the increase in the downhill component of weight, which equals $ma$ for the first incline.
perOption.C: Correct. This friction satisfies both force equations.
perOption.D: This is the trolley’s full weight and would exceed the downhill component on both inclines.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: Removing the quarter reduces the weight and shifts the centre of gravity to the right. The submerged volume is initially unchanged, so the upthrust stays the same and exceeds the new weight. The upthrust acts to the left of the new centre of gravity, producing a clockwise moment about it.

perOption.A: The unchanged upthrust exceeds the new weight and produces a clockwise moment about the new centre of gravity.
perOption.B: Correct. The resultant force is upward and the moment is clockwise.
perOption.C: The clockwise moment is right, but the reduced weight leaves a net upward force.
perOption.D: The upthrust acts to the left of the new centre of gravity, making the moment clockwise.
