mi-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: Constant velocity means the net force along the slope is zero. The engine force and the downhill component of weight together balance the resistive force, so $F=2000-1500(9.81)\sin6.0^\circ=462\ \mathrm N$. The engine power is $P=Fv=462(30)\approx14\ \mathrm{kW}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Gravity supplies part of the downhill force.
perOption.B: This assigns the full resistive force to the engine and omits gravity’s downhill contribution.
perOption.C: This adds the downhill component of weight to the resistance when solving for the engine force.
perOption.D: This power implies a driving force far above the resistance, even before gravity’s downhill contribution is included.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: The useful output power is $P_o=0.25P_i=0.25(10)=2.5\ \mathrm W$. The useful energy required is $E=mgh=20(0.50)=10\ \mathrm J$. Using $P_o=E/t$ gives $t=10/2.5=4.0\ \mathrm s$.

perOption.A: This time would require 250 W of useful power, far above the 2.5 W available.
perOption.B: This is the result of multiplying the ideal lifting time by the efficiency, which understates the time.
perOption.C: Correct. The motor delivers 10 J of useful work in 4.0 s.
perOption.D: This treats the load’s 20 N weight as a 20 kg mass and multiplies by gravitational acceleration again.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: At the top of the circle, both tension and weight point down towards the centre. Their sum is the required centripetal force, so $T+mg=mv^2/r$. Hence $T=mv^2/r-mg$.

perOption.A: This reverses the subtraction needed to isolate the tension.
perOption.B: This attributes the entire centripetal force to tension and omits weight.
perOption.C: Correct. Weight supplies part of the required inward force.
perOption.D: This uses the sign appropriate to the bottom of the circle, where weight points away from the centre.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: At Earth’s surface the satellite’s weight is $W=GMm/R^2$. Its orbit is at a distance $R+5R=6R$ from Earth’s centre. There its weight is $GMm/(6R)^2=W/36$.

perOption.A: Correct. The centre-to-satellite distance is six Earth radii.
perOption.B: This uses the altitude as the distance from Earth’s centre.
perOption.C: This uses the altitude as the orbital radius and assumes an inverse-linear dependence.
perOption.D: Orbital free fall gives zero apparent weight, while gravity still supplies the centripetal force.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: In a uniform gravitational field, the potential energy lost over displacement $x$ along the field is $E=mgx$, giving $g=E/(mx)$. The field points towards lower gravitational potential, so the acceleration is from P to Q, to the right.

perOption.A: The quantity $E/x$ gives the gravitational force and must be divided by the mass.
perOption.B: The expression $E/x$ gives a force, and the leftward arrow points towards higher potential.
perOption.C: Correct. The acceleration points from P to Q.
perOption.D: The magnitude is right, but gravity points towards lower potential at Q.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The average translational kinetic energy of one helium atom is $\frac32 kT$, with $T$ in kelvin. Substituting gives $\frac32(1.38\times10^{-23})(27+273.15)=6.2\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Substitutes $27$ directly instead of converting the temperature to kelvin.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The calculation must use the Boltzmann constant to obtain the energy per atom.
perOption.D: Uses the energy of the full $2.0\ \mathrm{mol}$ of helium.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: At steady state the pressures in the two flasks are equal. The ideal gas law gives $\frac{n_PRT_P}{V_P}=\frac{n_QRT_Q}{V_Q}$. Since both flasks contain the same gas, $\frac{M_P}{M_Q}=\frac{n_P}{n_Q}=\frac{T_Q}{T_P}\frac{V_P}{V_Q}=3\times3=9$.

perOption.A: Reverses the requested mass ratio.
perOption.B: Uses only the inverse volume ratio and misses the temperature difference.
perOption.C: Accounts for only one of the two factors of three.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: Internal energy is the sum of the microscopic kinetic and potential energies of the molecules in a system. Work done on the system can increase that sum even when no energy is transferred by heating.

perOption.A: During a change of state, internal energy can rise while the temperature stays constant.
perOption.B: Correct. Work can increase internal energy by itself.
perOption.C: Samples with different amounts of gas can have the same total internal energy at different temperatures.
perOption.D: Heat transferred into the system plus work done on it gives the change in internal energy.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: For resonance, the frequency of hitting the bumps equals the suspension’s natural frequency. The time between bumps is $T=1/2.0=0.50\ \mathrm{s}$. Using $d=vT$ gives $5.0=v(0.50)$, so $v=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: This speed gives one bump every $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$, so the driving frequency is too low.
perOption.B: Multiplies by the period instead of dividing the spacing by it.
perOption.C: This speed gives one bump per second, only half the natural frequency.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: Increasing the damping decreases the oscillation frequency and therefore increases the period. With the damping held fixed, the amplitude decreases over time while the period stays constant.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Increasing the damping increases the period because the frequency falls.
perOption.C: Damping dissipates energy, so the amplitude decreases over time.
perOption.D: At fixed damping the period stays constant as the amplitude decays.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q15.issues: The key says damping does not change the period or frequency when discussing C and D. This applies to the passage of time at fixed damping. Changing the damping changes the period and frequency.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: By Malus’ law, the intensity after rotating Q through $\theta$ is $I\cos^2\theta$. A 30% reduction gives $0.70I=I\cos^2\theta$, with an acute solution of $33^\circ$. Since $\cos^2\theta$ repeats every $180^\circ$, $180^\circ+33^\circ=213^\circ$ is a possible rotation.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Its equivalent angle of $46^\circ$ transmits about 48% of $I$.
perOption.C: Its equivalent angle of $57^\circ$ transmits about 30% of $I$, a reduction of about 70%.
perOption.D: Its equivalent angle of $73^\circ$ transmits only about 9% of $I$.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: Sound intensity $I$ is proportional to the square of the amplitude $A$. With $y$ as one vertical grid unit, the original amplitude is $4y$, so $\frac{I_{\mathrm{new}}}{I_{\mathrm{old}}}=0.50=\left(\frac{A_{\mathrm{new}}}{4y}\right)^2$. This gives $A_{\mathrm{new}}=2.8y$, with the original period unchanged.

perOption.A: Keeps the original amplitude and halves the period.
perOption.B: Keeps the original amplitude and shortens the period.
perOption.C: Halves the amplitude, which would reduce the intensity to one-quarter.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: Using the limiting angle $\theta \approx \lambda/b$, the minimum angular separation is $\frac{500\times10^{-9}}{25\times10^{-3}}=2.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{rad}$. At $9.0\ \mathrm{m}$, the small-angle relation gives a minimum separation of $(9.0)(2.0\times10^{-5})=0.18\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: Halves the calculated separation, which already represents the full gap between the points.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses a separation much larger than the diffraction limit at the given distance.
perOption.D: Overestimates the limiting angle for a $25\ \mathrm{mm}$ aperture.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q18.issues: The key uses the syllabus approximation θ ≈ λ/b. The circular-aperture Rayleigh factor 1.22 would give about 0.22 mm, which is absent from the options.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: Each corner contributes the same field magnitude at the centre. The vectors cancel completely in A and B, while D leaves two aligned contributions. In C the vertical components cancel and all four horizontal components add, giving $4\cos45^\circ=2\sqrt2$ times the field from one corner, the largest resultant.

perOption.A: The fields from diagonally opposite charges cancel in pairs.
perOption.B: The equal-sign charges on each diagonal produce opposing fields that cancel.
perOption.C: Correct. All four horizontal components reinforce each other.
perOption.D: One diagonal pair cancels, leaving only two aligned fields.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: For proton number density $n$ and beam cross-sectional area $A$, the current is $I=evAn$. A beam segment of length $\ell$ containing $N$ protons has $An=A\frac{N}{A\ell}=\frac{N}{\ell}$. Thus the number per unit length is $An=\frac{I}{ev}$.

perOption.A: Gives the number of protons passing per unit time.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Multiplies the proton rate by $v$ instead of dividing by it.
perOption.D: Gives charge per unit length and omits division by the charge $e$ per proton.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The diodes in A and B are reverse-biased. When the thermistor is cold, its resistance is high and the potential difference across it is high. The heater branch should therefore be connected across the thermistor with the diode forward-biased.

perOption.A: Its reverse-biased diode blocks current through the heater.
perOption.B: Its reverse-biased diode blocks current through the heater.
perOption.C: The heater branch is across the fixed resistor, whose potential difference falls as the thermistor cools.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The current is $I=Q/t=6.0/(2.0\times60)=0.050\ \mathrm A$. The power dissipated in $R$ satisfies $P=VI$, so $48/(2.0\times60)=V(0.050)$ and $V=8.0\ \mathrm V$. Using $\mathcal E=IR+Ir$ gives $9.0=8.0+0.050r$, so $r=20\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Divides the $1.0\ \mathrm V$ lost voltage by the charge $6.0\ \mathrm C$ instead of by the current.
perOption.B: Treats the current in coulombs per minute as amperes when dividing the lost voltage by current.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the voltage across the external resistor and finds its resistance.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q22.issues: The question expands e.m.f. as electromagnetic force. The term is electromotive force.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force, so $B|q|v=mv^2/r$. Cancelling $v$ and using $v=2\pi r/T$ gives $B|q|=2\pi m/T$. Therefore $T=2\pi m/(B|q|)$, independent of the particle’s velocity.

perOption.A: The period is directly proportional to the mass.
perOption.B: The period is inversely proportional to the magnitude of the charge.
perOption.C: The period is inversely proportional to the magnetic flux density.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: The electric force gives a vertical acceleration of $a=F_E/m=|q|E/m=(1.6\times10^{-19})(20000)/(9.11\times10^{-31})=3.51\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The initial vertical velocity is zero, so $s=ut+\frac12 at^2=\frac12(3.51\times10^{15})(4.0\times10^{-9})^2=0.0281\ \mathrm m$.

perOption.A: The vertical displacement must be calculated using the electron’s acceleration $|q|E/m$ and the squared transit time.
perOption.B: The field acting for $4.0\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm s$ produces a much larger displacement when the electron’s mass is included in the acceleration.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Adds the horizontal travel $vt$ to the vertical displacement.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: Over one period $T$, the current spends half the time at $I_0$ and half at $-I_0$, so $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{[I_0^2(T/2)+I_0^2(T/2)]/T}=I_0$. The original average power is $P=I_0^2R$. Doubling the peak doubles the rms current, giving a new average power of $(2I_0)^2R=4P$.

perOption.A: Assumes the rms current is unchanged when the peak doubles.
perOption.B: Uses a square-root factor instead of squaring the doubled current.
perOption.C: Treats average power as proportional to current instead of current squared.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: The de Broglie relation $\lambda=h/(mv)$ gives $v=h/(m\lambda)$. At a fixed wavelength, speed is inversely proportional to mass. The helium-4 nucleus has the largest mass, so it has the smallest speed.

perOption.A: A proton is lighter than the helium-4 nucleus and must move faster.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The electron has the smallest mass and requires the greatest speed.
perOption.D: A neutron is lighter than the helium-4 nucleus and must move faster.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: Each photon has momentum of magnitude $p=h/\lambda$. Total reflection reverses that momentum, so the change in momentum has magnitude $p-(-p)=2h/\lambda$. At $n$ photons per second, the force on the mirror is the rate of momentum transfer, $2nh/\lambda$.

perOption.A: Multiplies by $\lambda$ instead of dividing and omits the factor of two from reflection.
perOption.B: Counts only the incident momentum, as for absorption.
perOption.C: Accounts for the reversal but multiplies by wavelength instead of dividing.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: The total linear momentum is zero before the stationary nucleus emits the $\gamma$ photon. By conservation of linear momentum, the recoiling nucleus must have momentum equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the photon’s momentum.

perOption.A: Nuclear stability is compared using binding energy per nucleon rather than total binding energy.
perOption.B: A reaction with greater product rest mass can occur if enough energy is supplied to the reactants.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: In the usual nuclear-decay model, chemical reactions leave the half-life of the radionuclide unchanged.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The energy released is the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactant. Multiplying each binding energy per nucleon by its nucleon number gives $(8.2\times146)+(8.6\times87)-(7.6\times235)=159.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Combines the tabulated per-nucleon values without weighting by nucleon number.
perOption.B: Undercounts the net binding-energy gain of the two fragments combined.
perOption.C: Undercounts the net binding-energy gain of the two fragments combined.
perOption.D: Correct.

mi-2026-prelim-p1-q30.issues: The two named fragments account for 233 of the 235 nucleons. Two free neutrons are implicit and contribute zero binding energy.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Rearranging gives $g=2h/t^2$. The maximum fractional uncertainties add as $\frac{\Delta g}{g}=\frac{\Delta h}{h}+2\frac{\Delta t}{t}$. The maximum percentage uncertainty in $h$ is therefore $2.0\%-2(0.0008/0.4000)\times100\%=1.6\%$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Subtracts the time uncertainty only once, forgetting the squared time in the denominator.
perOption.C: Adds the time uncertainty once instead of subtracting it twice.
perOption.D: Adds the doubled percentage uncertainty in time to the 2% budget.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: Estimate the football’s diameter as $20\ \mathrm{cm}=0.20\ \mathrm{m}$, giving a radius of $0.10\ \mathrm{m}$. The volume scales as $r^3$, and $\frac{4}{3}\pi(0.10)^3\approx 4\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}$, closest to $10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^3}$.

perOption.A: Implies a sphere only about a centimetre across.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the surface area $4\pi r^2$, which is measured in $\mathrm{m^2}$.
perOption.D: Implies a sphere over ten metres across.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: At the threshold of slipping, the maximum friction $0.25mg$ balances the downslope component $mg\sin\theta$. Thus $\sin\theta=0.25$ and $\theta\approx14^\circ$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses an angle at which the downslope component is already half the weight.
perOption.C: Uses the $60^\circ$ angle at which the downslope component is about $0.87mg$.
perOption.D: Uses the perpendicular component $mg\cos\theta$ in the friction balance.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.issues: The key and option A give 14°, while arcsin(0.25) is about 14.48°.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: In the regular hexagon, $\angle OBA=60^\circ$. Balancing moments about $O$ gives $P(OD)=200(OB)\sin60^\circ$, so with $OD=OB$, $P\approx170\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\cos60^\circ$ for the moment factor.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Treats the $200\ \mathrm{N}$ force as perpendicular to $OB$.
perOption.D: Divides by $\sin60^\circ$, applying the moment factor to the wrong force.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: Let $a=g\sin30^\circ$ be the common downslope acceleration. At collision, A is $4t-\frac12at^2$ up from the bottom and B is $\frac12at^2$ down from the top. These displacements sum to $5.00\ \mathrm{m}$, so the acceleration terms cancel and $t=5.00/4.00=1.25\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Double-counts the effect of gravity on the closing motion by treating A as speeding up the slope.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses a time at which $4.00t=6.00\ \mathrm{m}$, greater than the initial separation.
perOption.D: Uses a time long enough for B to have already reached the bottom.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.issues: The opening sentence reverses the positions of A and B relative to the diagram and launch description. The question’s speed unit is malformed. The key’s first method calls A’s net displacement a distance even though A turns before collision, and one line of its second method prints 1.25 m instead of 1.25 s.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: For a constant interval $T$, bead $n$ must fall for $nT$, so its starting height is $s=\frac12g(nT)^2$. The heights above the floor are therefore proportional to $0,1,4,9,16,\ldots$, as in D.

perOption.A: Spaces the beads more closely toward the ceiling, where the gaps need to be larger.
perOption.B: Uses equal height gaps, which give shorter time gaps at greater heights.
perOption.C: Increases the gaps but misses the square-number heights, starting with heights in the ratio $1:3$ instead of $1:4$.
perOption.D: Correct.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.issues: The worked solution begins on page 1 and continues on page 2.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: Using $P=Fv$ for the useful output power gives $0.40(800)=13F$, so the driving force is $24.6\ \mathrm{N}$. At constant velocity the driving and resistive forces balance, giving a resistive force of about $25\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the $60\%$ of power lost by the engine.
perOption.C: Uses all $800\ \mathrm{W}$ as useful output power.
perOption.D: Divides the input power by the efficiency before using $P=Fv$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: Friction supplies the centripetal force $mr\omega^2$. Before slipping, Q needs more friction because both objects share the same angular velocity and Q is farther from the axis. Q reaches the maximum available static friction first.

perOption.A: Q needs more friction than P before slipping.
perOption.B: P needs less friction because it is closer to the axis.
perOption.C: Q and P have the same angular velocity while they rotate with the turntable.
perOption.D: Correct. Q reaches the friction limit first.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.issues: The stem describes increasing angular velocity and also calls the initial motion uniform. During spin-up friction has a tangential component as well, but the larger-radius object still reaches the friction limit first.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: If $F_T$ is the tension and $T$ is the period, the horizontal component satisfies $F_T\sin\theta=mr(2\pi/T)^2$. Vertically, $F_T\cos\theta=mg$. Dividing gives $\tan\theta=4\pi^2r/(gT^2)$, so $T=\sqrt{4\pi^2r/(g\tan\theta)}$.

perOption.A: Drops the $\tan\theta$ factor from the force ratio.
perOption.B: Uses only the horizontal projection factor and misses the vertical component in the ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Puts $r$ in the denominator, giving the wrong dimensions for a period.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.issues: The question options and key duplicate some trigonometric function names. C is correct with the intended single tangent. The key also uses T for both period and tension.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: The orbital radii measured from Earth's centre are $2R$ for P and $4R$ for Q. Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so $mv^2/r=GMm/r^2$ and orbital speed is proportional to $1/\sqrt r$. Hence $v_P/v_Q=\sqrt{4R/(2R)}=\sqrt2$ and $v_P=\sqrt2\,v$.

perOption.A: Uses the surface altitudes as radii and makes the inner satellite slower.
perOption.B: Inverts the orbital-radius ratio for the two speeds.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the surface altitudes $R$ and $3R$ as orbital radii.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: Gravitational potential at the surface is $\phi=-GM/r$. The Moon’s radius is $0.25$ times Earth’s radius, the same ratio as for the diameters. Thus $\phi_M=(0.012/0.25)(-63)\approx-3.0\ \mathrm{MJ\,kg^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies by the radius ratio although potential varies inversely with radius.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses an inverse-square dependence appropriate to gravitational field strength.
perOption.D: Inverts the ratio of the Moon’s potential to Earth’s potential.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: For simple harmonic motion, the acceleration and displacement amplitudes obey $a_0=\omega^2x_0$. The graph gives $0.30\times10^{-2}=\omega^2(6.0\times10^{-2})$, so $\omega=0.22\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\omega^2$ directly as the angular frequency.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Takes the square root of the reciprocal ratio $x_0/a_0$.
perOption.D: Uses $x_0/a_0$ and also omits the square root.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.issues: The graph omits minus signs at the negative ticks and malforms the acceleration unit. The slope and axis positions establish the intended signs and unit.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: P starts at its positive maximum, so its displacement is $y_P=A\cos(\omega t)$. S is $0.75\lambda$ to the right of P, so it lags by $2\pi(0.75)=3\pi/2$.

perOption.A: Uses the correct initial motion for S but gives half the phase lag.
perOption.B: Makes P start at zero displacement and gives half the phase lag.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Makes S start at $-A$ although it starts at zero.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The angular-frequency symbol is missing from the stem and the option formulas. C uses the intended cosine argument and gives the lag of S relative to P.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: The cross-sectional area grows by a factor of $(16/2.0)^2=64$. The same wave power crosses both areas, so the intensity falls to $I/64$. Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, the amplitude falls to $A/\sqrt{64}=A/8$.

perOption.A: Scales intensity by the width ratio and gives an amplitude inconsistent with that intensity.
perOption.B: Gets the intensity right but takes the wrong square root for the amplitude ratio.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses $16$ as the width ratio instead of dividing by the initial width of $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: The pipe closed at one end has fundamental wavelength $4L$, so the sound speed is $v=4fL$. At frequency $f/2$ the wavelength is $v/(f/2)=8L$. The fundamental of an open pipe fits half a wavelength, so its length is $4L$.

perOption.A: Uses an open pipe whose fundamental is $2f$, already above $f/2$.
perOption.B: Uses a quarter wavelength, which fits the fundamental of a pipe closed at one end.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Fits one and a half half-wavelengths, whereas an open pipe requires a whole number of half-wavelengths.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.issues: The worked solution starts on page 2 and continues on page 3.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: Use the longest wavelength, $600\ \mathrm{nm}$, because it diffracts through the largest angle in each order. With grating spacing $d=0.001/500\ \mathrm{m}$, $d\sin\theta=n\lambda$ gives $\sin\theta=0.30n\leq1$. Orders 1 through 3 are complete on each side, giving six spectra.

perOption.A: Counts the complete spectra on only one side.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Includes the excluded central maximum.
perOption.D: Includes fourth orders, which lack the longest wavelengths.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: Initially, the ideal gas law gives a total of $9pV/(283R)$ moles at common pressure $p$. At steady state, conservation of moles gives $p'V/(353R)+8p'V/(283R)=9pV/(283R)$, so $p'=1.022530p$. The fraction remaining in A is $1.022530(283/353)=0.819762$, so about $0.18n$ moles leave A.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Overestimates the transfer by leaving less gas in A than the final common pressure requires.
perOption.C: Reports the amount remaining in A as the amount transferred.
perOption.D: Overestimates the transfer by leaving only $0.14n$ in A.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.issues: The last line of the key calls 0.18n a fraction. It is the transferred amount in moles.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: For specific latent heat $L$, the two power balances are $P_1=m_1L+h$ and $P_2=m_2L+h$. Subtracting cancels the common heat loss, leaving $P_1-P_2=(m_1-m_2)L$. Thus $L=(P_1-P_2)/(m_1-m_2)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats all of the first heater input as power used for boiling.
perOption.C: Averages two estimates that each include a contribution from heat loss.
perOption.D: Adds the balances, retaining a heat-loss term of $2h$.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: The two charges each contribute $kq/r$ to the potential at R, so $V_R=2k(-30\times10^{-6})/0.20\approx-2.7\times10^6\ \mathrm{V}$. The work required from infinity is $\Delta U=(-e)V_R\approx4.3\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$, where $e$ is the magnitude of the electron charge.

perOption.A: Has the wrong sign and power of ten for the work required to bring in the electron.
perOption.B: Uses the negative electric potential directly as the work.
perOption.C: Uses the magnitude of the electric potential as work without multiplying by the electron charge magnitude.
perOption.D: Correct.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The question PNG corrupts or omits the micro prefix on the two source charges. The key’s intermediate potential confirms the intended microcoulombs, but the key labels the potential in C and omits the electron’s negative sign in the work expression. The literal diagram labels in coulombs would give no listed answer.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: For square side $r$, the fields at Z from W and X initially have magnitudes $kQ/r^2$ and $kQ/(2r^2)$, with $45^\circ$ between them. The cosine rule gives an initial resultant of about $1.399kQ/r^2$. At Y, the moved charge produces a field at Z of magnitude $kQ/r^2$ perpendicular to W’s field, so the resultant rises to about $1.414kQ/r^2$.

perOption.A: The moved charge is closer to Z, so the potential there increases.
perOption.B: The charges are farther apart, so their potential energy decreases.
perOption.C: The charges are farther apart, so their repulsive force decreases.
perOption.D: Correct. The resultant field at Z increases.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.issues: The key’s proof spans pages 3–4 and describes the field from Y at Z as rightward. It points left. The perpendicular geometry and numerical result are unaffected.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The turns ratio gives the secondary r.m.s. voltage $V_S=(1600/200)(25)=200\ \mathrm{V}$. Ohm’s law gives the secondary r.m.s. current $200/150=1.333\ \mathrm{A}$. The mean resistor power is $V_S^2/R=200^2/150=266.7\ \mathrm{W}$, which rounds to $270\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Inverts the turns ratio and predicts a step-down.
perOption.B: Uses the primary voltage directly across the secondary resistor.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the peak voltage to calculate mean power, doubling the result.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: The charge added is $Q=It=(2.5\times10^{-6})(200)=5.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{C}$. Dividing by the voltage increase gives $C=Q/\Delta V=(5.0\times10^{-4})/5.0=100\ \mathrm{\mu F}$.

perOption.A: Gives too little capacitance to store the calculated charge at the stated voltage increase.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses millifarads and also gives the wrong numerical value in microfarads.
perOption.D: Uses millifarads for a value calculated in microfarads.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: Each parallel group has capacitance $C+C+C=3C$. The two groups are in series, giving $C_{\mathrm{total}}=(1/(3C)+1/(3C))^{-1}=3C/2$.

perOption.A: Treats all six capacitors as being in series.
perOption.B: Reverses the series and parallel connections by treating the circuit as two parallel branches of three series capacitors.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Treats all six capacitors as being in parallel.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: Both ions pass through the velocity selector undeflected, so they have the same speed. In the uniform magnetic field, $Bqv=mv^2/r$, giving $r=mv/(Bq)$. Since $B$ and $v$ are the same for both ions, $r_Q=(3.7)(1.5/2)=2.8\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Divides by both the mass factor and the charge factor.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Inverts the mass-to-charge ratio when scaling the radius.
perOption.D: Multiplies by the charge factor even though radius is inversely proportional to charge.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: From the force on the current-carrying wire, $B=F/(IL)$. The induced e.m.f. peaks at the maximum wire speed, $v_{\max}=\omega x_0=2\pi f x_0$. Thus $E_0=BLv_{\max}=(10\times10^{-3})(2\pi\times90)(1.8\times10^{-3})/5.0=0.00204\ \mathrm{V}$, or $2.0\ \mathrm{mV}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Uses frequency in place of angular frequency and misses the factor of $2\pi$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Misses the factor of $2\pi$ and reads the result in volts instead of millivolts.
perOption.D: Reads the numerical result in volts instead of millivolts.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: The flux linkage is $NBA\cos(\omega t)$. Taking its negative time derivative gives $E=2\pi NBAf\sin(2\pi ft)$. Doubling $f$ doubles the peak e.m.f. to $2(2\pi NBAf)$ and halves the period.

perOption.A: Doubles the peak e.m.f. but keeps the original period.
perOption.B: Halves the period but incorrectly reduces the peak e.m.f.
perOption.C: Halves the period but keeps the original peak e.m.f.
perOption.D: Correct.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: The threshold frequency depends on the minimum energy required to release an electron from europium, which is independent of light intensity. At the same frequency, higher intensity means more photons reach the metal per unit time, so more electrons are emitted per unit time.

perOption.A: Incorrectly lowers the threshold and overlooks the increase in photon arrival rate.
perOption.B: Incorrectly lowers the threshold frequency when only intensity changes.
perOption.C: Overlooks the increase in electron emission rate as more photons arrive each second.
perOption.D: Correct.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: When electrons escape, the electroscope becomes positively charged and the gold leaf rises. Using $E=hc/\lambda$, a red photon has energy $1.9125\ \mathrm{eV}$, below both work functions. A blue photon has energy $2.7625\ \mathrm{eV}$, above potassium’s work function but below aluminium’s, so the leaf rises only for potassium under blue light.

perOption.A: Assumes blue photons can also overcome aluminium’s $4.3\ \mathrm{eV}$ work function.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reverses the predictions for potassium and assumes both photon energies exceed aluminium’s work function.
perOption.D: Reverses the predictions for potassium and incorrectly treats red photons as energetic enough for aluminium.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: The positively charged gold nucleus repels both alpha particles. Of the two particles with equal energies, the one passing closer to the nucleus is deflected through the larger angle.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Shows the farther particle continuing straight even though the nucleus also repels it.
perOption.C: Shows the same deflection for both particles despite their different distances from the nucleus.
perOption.D: Shows both particles bending towards the positively charged nucleus.

njc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The number of parent nuclei halves from its initial value in about 3 years. To estimate the half-life of $D_1$, use the part of the curve where very little P remains, so production of new $D_1$ is negligible. The number of $D_1$ nuclei at year 29 is about halved by year 44, giving 15 years.

perOption.A: Uses a 20-year interval for the daughter, whose late-time count halves in about 15 years.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Overestimates both half-lives by reading intervals longer than the respective halving times.
perOption.D: Uses about 6 years for P, by which time its count has roughly quartered.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Rearrange the expression to $k=2E/\omega^2$. Since radians are dimensionless, the unit of $k$ is $(\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}})(\mathrm{s^{-1}})^{-2}=\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Gives the units of linear momentum instead of dividing the energy units by angular speed squared.
perOption.C: Gives the units of force and loses a power of length from the energy units.
perOption.D: Multiplies the energy units by angular speed squared instead of dividing.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: The density is $\rho=m/(\pi D^2t/4)$. The percentage uncertainty contributions are $0.19\%$ from mass, $2(0.97\%)=1.94\%$ from diameter, and $1.5\%$ from thickness. The diameter contributes the most.

perOption.A: Mass contributes only $0.19\%$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Thickness appears to contribute the most if the diameter’s percentage uncertainty is counted only once.
perOption.D: Resistance does not enter the density calculation.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: The spring’s extension increases from $5\ \mathrm{mm}$ to $15\ \mathrm{mm}$. The increase in elastic potential energy is $\tfrac12 k(x_f^2-x_i^2)=\tfrac12(380)(0.015^2-0.005^2)=0.038\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\tfrac12 k(\Delta x)^2$ instead of subtracting the initial energy from the final energy.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Omits the factor of $\tfrac12$.
perOption.D: Uses the spring’s total lengths in place of its extensions.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: A couple consists of two equal and opposite forces and produces a pure turning effect. When their moments are added, the terms that depend on the pivot cancel, leaving a torque that is independent of the pivot.

perOption.A: Zero resultant force still allows a nonzero resultant torque.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The forces have zero total moment about their intersection, but their resultant force can be nonzero.
perOption.D: If the forces share a line of action, their net torque is zero.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: PQ describes the initial fall, so positive velocity on this graph is directed downwards. Q is the greatest downward velocity, while the greatest upward speed occurs at R immediately after the first bounce.

perOption.A: The area under PQ gives the downward displacement from release at P to first impact at Q.
perOption.B: The reduced speed after each impact shows a loss of kinetic energy in the collision.
perOption.C: The positive gradient of RS gives the downward acceleration of free fall.
perOption.D: Correct. Q is the point of maximum downward speed.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.issues: The key’s comment on option A misidentifies P as the point of impact. P is release and Q is first impact.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: The rotor sweeps out area $A=\pi(D/2)^2=\pi D^2/4$, so the mass flow rate is $\Delta m/\Delta t=\rho Av$. The air starts at rest, so the rate of increase of its kinetic energy is $P=\tfrac12(\Delta m/\Delta t)v^2=\tfrac18\pi\rho D^2v^3$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the diameter as the radius when calculating the swept area.
perOption.C: Applies $P=Fv$ with the outgoing air speed and misses the factor of $\tfrac12$ in the kinetic energy.
perOption.D: Gives the force from the change in momentum per unit time instead of the power.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: Thermal energy dissipated equals the work done against air resistance. This is the area under the force–displacement graph for $R$, which is region $Q$.

perOption.A: Uses the work done by the resultant force, which is the increase in kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Subtracts the resistance work from the net work, which already accounts for resistance.
perOption.D: Uses the total work done by the applied force, including the increase in kinetic energy.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: The initial vertical speed is zero, so the first fall obeys $y=\tfrac12gt_1^2$ and takes $t_1=\sqrt{2y/g}$. The second fall takes $t_2=\sqrt{2(4y)/g}=2t_1$. The horizontal speed stays constant and is the same for both objects, so the second travels $2x$.

perOption.A: Assumes the same launch speed gives the same time of flight.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Treats the time of flight as directly proportional to the drop height.
perOption.D: Treats horizontal distance as proportional to the square of the drop height.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: Taking X’s initial direction as positive, X changes momentum by $\Delta p_X=(2.5)(2.0-6.0)=-10.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. Newton’s third law gives Y the opposite impulse, $+10.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. The average force on Y has magnitude $F_{\mathrm{avg}}=10.0/(20\times10^{-3})=500\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Uses the impulse without dividing by the contact time.
perOption.B: Uses Y’s mass with X’s change in velocity.
perOption.C: Uses X’s final momentum of $5.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ in place of the $10.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ momentum change.
perOption.D: Correct.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.issues: The key’s comment attributes 250 N to using Y’s final momentum. Y’s final momentum is 6 N s, which would give 300 N. Using X’s final momentum would give 250 N.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: At mid-height the limiting speed is zero, so energy conservation gives $\tfrac12mv^2=mgr$ and a minimum entry speed of $\sqrt{2gr}$. At the top, gravity alone supplies the centripetal force at the contact threshold, so the minimum speed there is $\sqrt{gr}$. For an entry speed just sufficient to maintain contact at the top, $\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac12mgr=mg(2r)$, giving $v=\sqrt{5gr}$. The body leaves the track between mid-height and the top, so $\sqrt{2gr}<v<\sqrt{5gr}$.

perOption.A: Gives too little entry energy to reach mid-height.
perOption.B: Only reaches mid-height with zero speed.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Exceeds the minimum entry speed needed to maintain contact throughout the loop.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.issues: The key prints a strict inequality for the centripetal force condition at the top. Equality holds at the minimum speed, where the normal force is zero.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so $GMm/r^2=mr(2\pi/T)^2$ and $T^2=4\pi^2r^3/(GM)$. For the original and new periods, $T^2/T_2^2=r^3/(0.25r)^3=64$. Thus $T=8T_2$, and the planet completes eight revolutions in time $T$.

perOption.A: Gives the new period as a fraction of the original period instead of the number of revolutions.
perOption.B: Uses the radius ratio as the number of revolutions.
perOption.C: Assumes the period is directly proportional to radius.
perOption.D: Correct.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: Gravity provides the centripetal force, so $\frac{GMm}{r^2}=mr(2\pi/T)^2$. This gives $T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$, which is independent of the satellite’s mass. The claim that all such satellites must have the same mass is false.

perOption.A: A geostationary orbit lies in the equatorial plane so the satellite stays above one point on the equator.
perOption.B: Correct. The satellite’s mass cancels.
perOption.C: The orbital period must match Earth’s rotation period, about 24 hours.
perOption.D: The required period fixes a unique radius because $T^2\propto r^3$.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.issues: The 24-hour period is rounded. The exact requirement is one sidereal day.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: At $t=0$, the body is at equilibrium ($x=0$), where its speed and kinetic energy are greatest. It passes through equilibrium twice per oscillation, so the kinetic energy completes two cycles in one displacement period.

perOption.A: Copies the displacement graph and gives negative kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Uses a signed velocity-like curve, which gives negative kinetic energy.
perOption.C: Starts at zero even though the body has maximum speed at equilibrium.
perOption.D: Correct. It starts at a maximum and repeats every half-period.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: Sketch particle displacement against equilibrium position. For a wave travelling to the right, the particle velocity has the opposite sign to the local slope of that graph. Particle D is moving away from equilibrium, while its acceleration points back towards equilibrium.

perOption.A: A is at an extreme displacement, where its instantaneous velocity is zero.
perOption.B: B is moving towards equilibrium, so its velocity and acceleration point in the same direction.
perOption.C: C is at equilibrium, where its speed is greatest and its acceleration is zero.
perOption.D: Correct. D moves away from equilibrium while accelerating towards it.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: Complete destructive interference occurs where a crest from one slit meets a trough from the other. At C, a curved wavefront from one slit is halfway between successive wavefronts from the other slit.

perOption.A: A is at the upper slit, before the two outgoing waves overlap there.
perOption.B: B lies on the central line, where both waves travel equal distances and arrive in phase.
perOption.C: Correct. A crest meets a trough.
perOption.D: D is where two drawn wavefronts meet, so the waves arrive in phase.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: Using $s=r\theta$, the yellow stars subtend $\theta=1.7\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad}$. With $\theta_{\min}\approx\lambda/b$, the aperture diameter is $b\approx0.35\ \mathrm{m}$, or about $0.4\ \mathrm{m}$. Red light has a longer wavelength, so its minimum resolvable angle exceeds the unchanged angular separation of the stars.

perOption.A: The yellow-light limit gives an aperture diameter of about $0.4\ \mathrm{m}$.
perOption.B: The resolution criterion depends on both $\lambda$ and the aperture diameter.
perOption.C: Correct. The red stars are too close in angle to resolve.
perOption.D: The new separation of $3\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad}$ exceeds the yellow-light resolution limit.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: In the kinetic theory of an ideal gas, molecules move randomly with a range of speeds. The temperature fixes their mean translational kinetic energy, so equal molecular speeds are unnecessary.

perOption.A: Correct. Molecules can have different speeds.
perOption.B: Random molecular motion is an assumption of the model.
perOption.C: The model treats the molecules’ own volume as negligible compared with the gas volume.
perOption.D: The model neglects intermolecular forces between collisions.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: The gas returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U=0$. The loop is clockwise, so the net work done on the gas is minus the enclosed area, $W=-[(3-2)\times10^5][(3-1)\times10^{-3}]=-200\ \mathrm{J}$. Using $\Delta U=Q+W$ gives $Q=200\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the signs of work and heat for the clockwise cycle.
perOption.B: Correct. The gas absorbs 200 J of heat over the cycle.
perOption.C: Assigns a nonzero internal-energy change to a complete cycle and reverses the work sign.
perOption.D: Uses the internal-energy change from only W to Y and consequently gives the wrong heat transfer.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: Electric potential is a scalar, so at X it is $V=6\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}+2\frac{-Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}=\frac{Q}{\pi\varepsilon_0r}$. The external work to bring in $+2Q$ equals the increase in potential energy, $(2Q)V=\frac{2Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0r}$. The field does the negative of this work, $-\frac{2Q^2}{\pi\varepsilon_0r}$.

perOption.A: Uses $+Q$ for the incoming charge instead of $+2Q$.
perOption.B: Correct. The field does negative work as potential energy increases.
perOption.C: Gives the work done by the external force.
perOption.D: Treats the two negative charges as positive when summing the potentials.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: The alpha particle has charge $+2e$ and the separation is $0.10\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$. Coulomb’s law gives $F=\frac{(1.4\times10^{-17})(2\times1.6\times10^{-19})}{4\pi(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.10\times10^{-12})^2}=4.0\ \mathrm N$.

perOption.A: Uses the numerical distance in picometres without converting to metres.
perOption.B: Divides by the separation only once instead of squaring it.
perOption.C: Correct. The force is repulsive.
perOption.D: Uses $+4e$ for the alpha particle instead of $+2e$.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.issues: The key includes a stray sentence about scalar potential. Its force calculation is correct.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: Using $R=\rho\ell/A$, the radial path length $\ell$ is fixed by the spacing between the rod and the case. The area for radial conduction in the key’s model is $A=2\pi r_{\mathrm{avg}}x$, so $R=\rho\ell/(2\pi r_{\mathrm{avg}}x)\propto 1/x$.

perOption.A: Treats the depth as setting an area proportional to its square and makes resistance increase with area.
perOption.B: Treats the liquid depth as the current path length, which is radial.
perOption.C: Correct. The area for radial conduction grows in proportion to the depth.
perOption.D: Assumes the conduction area grows with the square of the liquid depth.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.issues: The key uses an average-radius approximation for the resistance. The inverse-depth scaling is exact in the ideal radial model.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: If the third lamp’s filament alone is broken, the open circuit carries no current and the intact lamps have no potential drop. The full supply potential difference appears across the third lamp, so the voltmeter would give a nonzero reading.

perOption.A: A break in another lamp stops current through the intact third lamp, giving zero potential difference.
perOption.B: Correct. The full supply voltage would appear across the break.
perOption.C: A blown fuse interrupts the supply, so the intact third lamp has zero potential difference.
perOption.D: A broken supply wire stops current through the intact third lamp, giving zero potential difference.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: Let $C$ be the capacitance of one capacitor. In P, the three capacitors are in parallel, giving $3C$. In Q, they are in series, so $1/C_Q=3/C$ and $C_Q=C/3$. In R, the series pair is in parallel with the single capacitor, giving $C_R=C+1/(2/C)=3C/2$. The increasing order is Q, R, P.

perOption.A: Lists the capacitances in decreasing order.
perOption.B: Correct. The order is Q, R, P.
perOption.C: Places the all-parallel arrangement first even though it has the greatest capacitance.
perOption.D: Places the mixed arrangement below the all-series arrangement.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: Using $B=\mu_0 I/(2\pi d)$, wire X gives $3.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T}$ towards the bottom of the page at $d=2.0\ \mathrm{m}$. Wire Y gives $4.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T}$ out of the page at $d=3.0\ \mathrm{m}$. The fields are perpendicular, so $B_{\mathrm{resultant}}=\sqrt{(3.0\times10^{-7})^2+(4.0\times10^{-7})^2}=5.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\varepsilon_0$ in place of $\mu_0$.
perOption.B: Correct. The fields add at right angles.
perOption.C: Swaps the distances from P to wires X and Y.
perOption.D: Adds the field magnitudes directly as if the fields were parallel.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: By Lenz’s law, the eddy currents induced in the rotating disc oppose the change in magnetic flux through the disc. Their torque on the suspended magnet reduces the relative rotation, so the magnet turns in the same direction as the disc.

perOption.A: Opposite rotation would increase the relative motion driving the induction.
perOption.B: Correct. The induced torque drags the magnet in the disc’s direction.
perOption.C: Ignores the torque exerted by the induced currents.
perOption.D: Assumes a reversing torque even though the rotating disc initially drags the magnet in one direction.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: The mean input power is $120(60.0)=7200\ \mathrm{W}$. The ideal transformer supplies the same power at $4500/\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{V}$ r.m.s., so the cable current is $I_{\rm rms}=7200\sqrt{2}/4500\ \mathrm{A}$. After the cable loss, the power delivered is $P'=7200-I_{\rm rms}^2(40.0)$. The percentage delivered is $(P'/7200)\times100\%\approx97.2\%$.

perOption.A: Uses the peak cable current in the mean power-loss formula and doubles the loss.
perOption.B: Correct. About 97.2% of the power reaches the consumers.
perOption.C: Treats 4500 V as the r.m.s. voltage, halving the calculated cable loss.
perOption.D: Converts peak voltage to r.m.s. in the wrong direction by multiplying by √2, leaving only a quarter of the correct cable loss.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: Each photon has momentum $h/\lambda$ and energy $hc/\lambda$, so a beam of power $P$ delivers $P/(hc/\lambda)$ photons per second. Assuming complete reflection, each photon’s momentum reverses, giving a force of $2P/c$ on the photons and an equal force magnitude on the screen. Dividing by the spot area $\pi D^2/4$ gives $8P/(c\pi D^2)$. The two beams have equal power and spot diameter, so the red beam also exerts pressure $p$.

perOption.A: Uses the momentum ratio of individual photons and overlooks the higher photon rate for red light.
perOption.B: Correct. The wavelength factors cancel.
perOption.C: Uses the photon-rate ratio and overlooks the lower momentum per red photon.
perOption.D: Squares the per-photon momentum ratio even though the force is the photon rate times the momentum change.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.issues: The key assumes complete reflection. Equal pressure also requires equivalent momentum-transfer conditions for both beams, which the question does not specify.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The electron’s state is represented by a wavefunction $\psi$. Its squared magnitude $|\psi|^2$ is the probability density, and the electron cloud visualises where the electron is likely to be found.

perOption.A: Confines the electron to a single radius even though its probability density extends over a region.
perOption.B: Assumes a uniform charge distribution even though the probability density varies with position.
perOption.C: Treats the electron cloud as a classical trajectory.
perOption.D: Correct. The cloud shows where the electron is likely to be found.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Activity is proportional to the number of radioactive nuclei, so $1.0\ \mathrm{g}$ of live wood would have an activity of $120/10=12.0\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Using $A=A_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and $\lambda=\ln 2/5730\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ gives $8.05=12.0e^{-(\ln 2)t/5730}$, with $t$ in years. Solving gives $t\approx3300$ years.

perOption.A: This age allows too little decay, leaving more than $8.05\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ from a $12.0\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ starting activity.
perOption.B: Correct. The mass-adjusted activity ratio gives about 3300 years.
perOption.C: Uses an age beyond one half-life even though more than half the initial activity remains.
perOption.D: Compares the activities directly without adjusting for the tenfold difference in sample mass.

nyjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The energy released equals the products’ total binding energy minus the reactants’ total binding energy. Free neutrons contribute zero binding energy, so $195=143X+90X-235(7.6)$, with energies in MeV. Solving gives $X=8.50\ \mathrm{MeV}$ per nucleon.

perOption.A: Reverses the energy difference and also uses too many bound product nucleons.
perOption.B: Subtracts the released energy from the initial binding energy instead of adding it.
perOption.C: Averages over too many nucleons by counting free neutrons in the product binding-energy calculation.
perOption.D: Correct. The 195 MeV increase is shared across 233 bound product nucleons.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Systematic error is indicated by how far the mean measured value lies from the true value $x_0$. Random error is indicated by the spread of measurements about the mean. Graph B is narrow and centred well away from $x_0$, showing small random error and large systematic error.

perOption.A: The narrow distribution is centred at $x_0$, showing little systematic error.
perOption.B: Correct. The narrow distribution is offset from the true value.
perOption.C: The distribution is broad and centred at $x_0$, showing large random error and little systematic error.
perOption.D: The offset shows systematic error, but the broad spread indicates large random error.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body:
For $\rho = \dfrac{\pi d^2 V}{4IL}$, the percentage uncertainties add, with $d$ counted twice because it is squared:

$\%\rho = 2(\%d) + \%V + \%I + \%L = 2(3\%) + 1\% + 0.5\% + 2\% = 9.5\%$

perOption.A: Subtracts the uncertainties of the denominator quantities $I$ and $L$ instead of adding them.
perOption.B: Forgets to double the uncertainty in $d$ even though $d$ is squared.
perOption.C: Leaves out the uncertainty in $L$.
perOption.D: Correct. Percentage uncertainties add, with $d$'s counted twice.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body:
When the beam is in equilibrium under three forces ($W$, $X$ and $Y$), their lines of action must meet at a common point, so that there is no resultant moment about any point on the beam.

$W$ acts vertically down through the middle of the beam. $X$ (from the ground) and $Y$ (from the wall) each combine a normal force with friction, so both slope upward, and their lines pass through the point where $W$'s line of action crosses them. Only diagram D shows this.

perOption.A: $Y$ points down along the beam and $X$ is horizontal, so there is no upward force to balance $W$ and the forces cannot be in equilibrium.
perOption.B: $X$ points away from the wall, so nothing balances the horizontal push of $Y$, and the three lines of action do not meet at one point.
perOption.C: $Y$ is drawn horizontal, which ignores friction at the rough wall, and the three lines of action do not meet at a common point.
perOption.D: Correct. The lines of action of $X$, $Y$ and $W$ meet at one point.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body:
Since the drone hovers steadily and stays level, each propeller provides an equal share of the weight:

thrust per propeller $= \dfrac{1.20 \times 9.81}{4} = 2.943\ \mathrm{N}$

By Newton's second law, $F = \dfrac{dp}{dt} = \dfrac{m}{t}(v - 0)$, where $\dfrac{m}{t} = 0.50\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ for each propeller:

$2.943 = 0.50\,v \Rightarrow v = 5.886 \approx 5.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Gives the drone's mass value (1.2) rather than calculating a speed.
perOption.B: Takes the thrust per propeller (2.94 N) as the answer without dividing by the mass flow rate.
perOption.C: Correct. Thrust per propeller = (mass flow rate) $\times$ $v$.
perOption.D: Uses the drone's whole weight for one propeller instead of sharing it among four.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body:
Since the resultant force on the ball is zero, it falls at constant velocity, so its kinetic energy stays constant with time.

Its height decreases at a constant rate, so its gravitational potential energy decreases linearly with time: $\dfrac{\Delta E_p}{t} = \dfrac{mgh}{t} = mgv$, so $\Delta E_p = (mgv)t$.

perOption.A: Correct. $E_k$ is constant and $E_p$ falls linearly.
perOption.B: $E_p$ is drawn falling at an increasing rate, which would need the ball to be speeding up.
perOption.C: $E_k$ is drawn increasing, which suggests the ball is accelerating even though the forces are balanced.
perOption.D: Treats the fall as if $E_p$ were converted into $E_k$, ignoring that the forces are balanced and the speed is constant.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body:
Take downwards as positive. When the ball is thrown, it shares the balloon's upward velocity, so $u_y = -2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$:

$s_y = u_y t + \tfrac{1}{2}a_y t^2 \Rightarrow 10 = -2.0t + \tfrac{1}{2}(9.81)t^2$

$t = -1.239\ \mathrm{s}$ (reject) or $t = 1.646\ \mathrm{s}$

Range $= u_x t = 5.0 \times 1.646 = 8.23 \approx 8.2\ \mathrm{m}$

perOption.A: Takes the initial vertical velocity of 2.0 m s$^{-1}$ as downward instead of upward.
perOption.B: Ignores the balloon's upward velocity and treats the ball as starting from vertical rest.
perOption.C: Uses only the time to fall from the highest point and leaves out the time spent rising.
perOption.D: Correct. The ball starts with the balloon's upward velocity of 2.0 m s$^{-1}$.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body:
At maximum compression the blocks move with a common velocity $v$. By conservation of momentum (taking right as positive):

$mu - 2m(0.5u) = 3mv \Rightarrow v = 0$

So all the initial kinetic energy is stored in the spring:

$\tfrac{1}{2}mu^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(2m)(0.5u)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, with $v = 0$

$\tfrac{3}{4}mu^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 \Rightarrow x = \sqrt{\dfrac{3mu^2}{2k}}$

perOption.A: Treats both velocities as being in the same direction, which gives a non-zero common velocity and too little energy stored.
perOption.B: Does not equate all of the initial kinetic energy, $\tfrac{3}{4}mu^2$, to the elastic potential energy $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.
perOption.C: Correct. The common velocity is zero, so all the KE is stored as elastic PE.
perOption.D: Drops the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in the kinetic energy terms, which doubles the energy stored.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body:
Let $\theta$ be the angle the string makes with the vertical, so $r = L\sin\theta$:

$T\cos\theta = mg$ and $T\sin\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{L\sin\theta} \Rightarrow \sin^2\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{LT}$

Using $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$: $\dfrac{mv^2}{LT} + \left(\dfrac{mg}{T}\right)^2 = 1$

$\dfrac{(2.0)v^2}{(1.5)(30)} = 1 - \left[\dfrac{(2.0)(9.81)}{30}\right]^2 \Rightarrow v = 3.59 \approx 3.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Correct. Resolve $T$ vertically and horizontally with $T = 30\ \mathrm{N}$ and $r = L\sin\theta$.
perOption.B: Mixes up the vertical and horizontal components of the tension.
perOption.C: Uses the string length $L$ as the radius of the circle instead of $L\sin\theta$.
perOption.D: Ignores the weight and takes the whole tension as the centripetal force with $r = L$.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body:
Friction on the tyres provides the centripetal force: $f_{\max} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.

When the road is wet, $f'_{\max} = \dfrac{f_{\max}}{2} = \dfrac{mv_{wet}^2}{r}$, so $\dfrac{mv^2}{2r} = \dfrac{mv_{wet}^2}{r}$.

$v_{wet} = \dfrac{v}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{30}{\sqrt{2}} = 21.2 \approx 21\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Divides the speed by 4, as if $v^2$ were halved twice.
perOption.B: Divides the speed by $2\sqrt{2}$, which does not follow from $f \propto v^2$.
perOption.C: Halves the speed, treating $f$ as proportional to $v$ rather than $v^2$.
perOption.D: Correct. $v \propto \sqrt{f}$, so $v$ falls by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body:
The resultant field is zero where the two field strengths are equal. Let $x$ be the distance from the star of mass $M$:

$\dfrac{GM}{x^2} = \dfrac{G(4M)}{(d - x)^2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{(d - x)^2}{x^2} = 4 \Rightarrow \dfrac{d - x}{x} = 2$

$x = \dfrac{d}{3}$

perOption.A: Uses the mass ratio 4 directly for the distance ratio, forgetting the square in the inverse square law.
perOption.B: Correct. The distance ratio is $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
perOption.C: Takes the midpoint, which would only be correct for equal masses.
perOption.D: Gives the distance from the larger star, $4M$, instead of from $M$.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body:
Work done by the external force $= m\,\Delta\phi$:

$W = m\left[\left(-\dfrac{GM}{3R}\right) - \left(-\dfrac{GM}{R}\right)\right] = \dfrac{2GMm}{3R}$

perOption.A: Has the right magnitude but the wrong sign: work must be done on the object to raise its potential.
perOption.B: Adds the magnitudes of the two potentials instead of taking their difference, and has the wrong sign.
perOption.C: Correct. $W = m(\phi_f - \phi_i)$.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes of the two potentials instead of taking their difference.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body:
Amplitude $x_0 = \dfrac{2.00}{2} = 1.00\ \mathrm{m}$, with the equilibrium position at the 1.00 m mark. So the 0.75 m mark is at $x = -0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ and the 1.50 m mark is at $x = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$.

Taking the swing to be at the 0 m mark at $t = 0$: $x = -1.00\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{2.4}t\right)$

At $x = -0.25\ \mathrm{m}$: $t_1 = 0.5035\ \mathrm{s}$. At $x = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$: $t_2 = 0.8000\ \mathrm{s}$.

Time taken $= t_2 - t_1 = 0.8000 - 0.5035 = 0.2965 \approx 0.30\ \mathrm{s}$

perOption.A: Correct. $t_2 - t_1$ from $x = -x_0\cos\omega t$.
perOption.B: Does not come from applying $x = -x_0\cos\omega t$ to the correct displacements, $-0.25$ m and $+0.50$ m.
perOption.C: Gives roughly $t_1$, the time from the 0 m mark to the 0.75 m mark, instead of the time between the two marks.
perOption.D: Does not come from the sinusoidal relation. The whole journey from 0 m to 1.50 m takes only 0.80 s.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body:
From the graph, $x_0 = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ and $v_0 = 2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so $\omega = \dfrac{v_0}{x_0} = \dfrac{2.0}{0.50} = 4.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

Total energy $E_T = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x_0^2$. Since $E_T$ and $m$ are constant, $\omega x_0$ stays constant:

$\omega' x_0' = \omega x_0 \Rightarrow \omega' = \dfrac{4.0 \times 0.50}{0.25} = 8.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$

$|a_0| = (\omega')^2 x_0' = 8.0^2 \times 0.25 = 16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

perOption.A: Keeps $\omega = 4.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ unchanged and uses the new amplitude: $4.0^2 \times 0.25$.
perOption.B: Gives the original maximum acceleration, $4.0^2 \times 0.50$.
perOption.C: Correct. Constant energy keeps $\omega x_0$ fixed, so $\omega$ doubles.
perOption.D: Uses the new $\omega' = 8.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ with the old amplitude of 0.50 m.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body:
From the diagram, the wavelength is the distance from one compression to the next (or one rarefaction to the next): $\lambda = 16\ \mathrm{m}$.

$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{16}{16} = 1.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$

perOption.A: 8.0 m is the distance from a compression to the next rarefaction, which is half a wavelength.
perOption.B: Particles at different positions along a progressive wave have different phases.
perOption.C: Only transverse waves can be polarised, and this wave is longitudinal.
perOption.D: Correct. $\lambda = 16\ \mathrm{m}$, so $f = v/\lambda = 1.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body:
The second-order lines are $56°$ apart, so each is at $\theta = 28°$: $d\sin 28° = 2\lambda \Rightarrow \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2}{\sin 28°}$.

From $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$ and $\sin\theta \le 1$: $n \le \dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2}{\sin 28°} = 4.26$, so $n_{\max} = 4$.

Number of diffraction lines $= (4 \times 2) + 1 = 9$

perOption.A: Gives only the highest order, $n_{\max}$, instead of counting lines on both sides and the central maximum.
perOption.B: Counts only one side of the central maximum, plus the zeroth order.
perOption.C: Counts both sides but leaves out the zeroth-order (central) line.
perOption.D: Correct. $n_{\max} = 4$ on each side, plus the central maximum.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body:
Distance $r = 20 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m}$. By the Rayleigh criterion, $\theta \approx \lambda/D$, so the minimum separation is $s = r\theta = r\dfrac{\lambda}{D}$.

Violet (400 nm): $s = \dfrac{(20 \times 10^{16})(400 \times 10^{-9})}{3.0} = 2.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$

Red (700 nm): $s = \dfrac{(20 \times 10^{16})(700 \times 10^{-9})}{3.0} = 4.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$

Across the visible range, the order of magnitude is $10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Too small by a factor of about 100, likely from a powers-of-ten slip in $r$ or $\lambda$.
perOption.B: Correct. $s = r\lambda/D \approx 10^{10}\ \mathrm{m}$ for visible light.
perOption.C: Too large by a factor of about 100, likely from a powers-of-ten slip in $\lambda$ (for example, using micrometres as nanometres).
perOption.D: Far too large. It does not follow from $s = r\lambda/D$ with visible wavelengths.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body:
The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is $\tfrac{1}{2}M\langle c^2\rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}kT$, so

$\dfrac{\tfrac{1}{2}M_P c_P^2}{\tfrac{1}{2}M_Q c_Q^2} = \dfrac{\tfrac{3}{2}kT_P}{\tfrac{3}{2}kT_Q}$

$\dfrac{M_P}{M_Q} = \dfrac{T_P}{T_Q} \times \dfrac{c_Q^2}{c_P^2} = 2 \times \dfrac{1}{3^2} = \dfrac{2}{9}$

perOption.A: Inverts the temperature ratio and forgets to square the speed ratio: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{3}$.
perOption.B: Correct. $M \propto T/c^2$.
perOption.C: Forgets to square the r.m.s. speed ratio.
perOption.D: Inverts the whole ratio, giving $M_Q/M_P$.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body:
By the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta U = Q + W$, where $W$ is the work done on the gas.

Heat supplied to the gas: $Q = \Delta U - W$

So the heat transferred from the gas to the surroundings is $W - \Delta U$.

perOption.A: Adds $\Delta U$ to $W$, as if the rise in internal energy also leaves the gas as heat.
perOption.B: Correct. Heat lost $= -Q = W - \Delta U$.
perOption.C: This is the heat supplied to the gas, $Q = \Delta U - W$, not the heat it loses.
perOption.D: Gets the signs of both terms wrong in the first law.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body:
$V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)^3 \Rightarrow V \propto d^3$, so $V_f = \left(\dfrac{2d}{d}\right)^3 V = 8V$.

$\Delta V = 8V - V = 7V$

$W = p\Delta V = 7pV$

perOption.A: Uses $(2^2 - 1)$, treating volume as if it scaled with $d^2$.
perOption.B: Uses a factor of 4, the change in surface area, instead of in volume.
perOption.C: Correct. The volume rises by a factor of 8, so $\Delta V = 7V$.
perOption.D: Uses the final volume $8V$ instead of the change in volume.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body:
Let $r$ be the side of one grid square. The 32.0 N C$^{-1}$ point is $r$ from Q:

$E = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2} = 32.0$

S is $3r$ from Q: $E_S = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 (3r)^2} = \tfrac{1}{9}(32.0) = 3.6\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$

Check: the 16.0 N C$^{-1}$ point is $\sqrt{2}r$ away, giving $\tfrac{1}{2}E = 16.0\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$.

R is $\sqrt{(2r)^2 + r^2} = \sqrt{5}r$ away: $E_R = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(\sqrt{5}r)^2} = \tfrac{1}{5}E = 6.4\ \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Takes R as $\sqrt{8}r$ away (two squares across and two up), giving $\tfrac{1}{8} \times 32 = 4.0$ for R.
perOption.B: Gets R right, but gives half the correct value at S.
perOption.C: Correct. $E \propto 1/r^2$, with R at $\sqrt{5}r$ and S at $3r$.
perOption.D: Uses $E \propto 1/r$ or miscounts the distances, rather than $E \propto 1/r^2$ with the correct geometry.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body:
The sphere is a conductor, so its charge sits only on the outer surface and there is no charge inside. The electric field inside is therefore zero, and the potential inside is constant at $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r}$, the same as the potential at the surface.

Outside the sphere, the potential decreases inversely with the distance $x$ from the centre: $V \propto \dfrac{1}{x}$.

perOption.A: Takes the potential inside to be zero, confusing it with the electric field strength, which is zero inside.
perOption.B: Shows the potential rising from zero inside, but $E = 0$ inside means $V$ cannot change there.
perOption.C: Shows $V$ rising linearly inside, as if the field inside were non-zero.
perOption.D: Correct. $V$ is constant inside and equal to the surface value, then falls as $1/x$ outside.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: Using $V=IR$, substitute $I=nAve$ and $R=\rho L/A$ to get $E=(nAve)(\rho L/A)=nve\rho L$. Therefore $v=E/(ne\rho L)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Retains a spurious area factor and assigns the wrong power to length.
perOption.C: Introduces an inverse-square area dependence and puts length in the numerator.
perOption.D: Retains an extra area factor in the denominator.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body:
Once fully charged, the capacitor has the same p.d. as the battery terminals and the $4.0\ \Omega$ resistor. No current flows through the capacitor, so $\mathrm{A}_2$ reads $0\ \mathrm{A}$.

Current flows only in the upper loop, so $\mathrm{A}_1$ reads $\frac{4.0}{4.0+1.0}=0.80\ \mathrm{A}$. The terminal p.d. is $4.0-(0.80)(1.0)=3.2\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Assigns current to the fully charged capacitor branch.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Assigns current to the capacitor branch and overestimates the battery current.
perOption.D: Treats the capacitor as opening the resistor loop as well.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body:
Taking upward as positive, $BIL\sin\theta-mg=ma$. Initially, $0.040I(0.30\sin90^\circ)-0.0024(9.81)=0.0024(1.2)$, giving $I=2.202\ \mathrm{A}$.

At half the current, $0.040(1.101)(0.30\sin90^\circ)-0.0024(9.81)=0.0024a$. Thus $a=-4.305\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, or $4.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ downward.

perOption.A: Halves the original acceleration even though weight stays the same.
perOption.B: Reverses the direction of the net force, which points downward once weight exceeds magnetic force.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the magnetic force per unit mass as the magnitude of the net acceleration.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: After Y is rotated, its field at P points upward and has magnitude $B_Y=\mu_0 I/(2\pi d)=B$. The field from X points out of the page and has magnitude $B_X=\mu_0 I/(2\pi d)=B$. The fields are perpendicular, so the resultant magnitude is $\sqrt{B^2+B^2}=\sqrt{2}\,B$.

perOption.A: Treats the fields as opposite and cancelling.
perOption.B: Counts only one conductor's field.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Adds magnitudes as if the fields pointed in the same direction.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: For an ideal transformer, $V_s/V_p=N_s/N_p$. With $V_p$ and $N_s$ fixed, decreasing $N_p$ increases $V_s$.

perOption.A: Under the key's flux model, reducing the coil area reduces the induced e.m.f. $E=NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)$.
perOption.B: With $V_p$ and $I_s$ fixed, decreasing $I_p$ would decrease $V_s$ by $V_s/V_p=I_p/I_s$.
perOption.C: A smaller load resistance changes the secondary current while the ideal secondary voltage stays fixed.
perOption.D: Correct.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q26.issues: The key’s option B argument implicitly holds the secondary current fixed. If the primary current decreases because the load changes, both currents can change while the ideal secondary voltage stays fixed.

perOption.A: Inverts the requested ratio.
perOption.B: Uses $(2/3)^2$ where the width ratio needs $2/3$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Omits the quantum-number ratio of $2/3$.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The diameter of an atom is about $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$, so take $\Delta x\approx10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$. Using $\Delta x\,\Delta p\gtrsim h$, the minimum momentum uncertainty is of order $h/\Delta x\sim10^{-34}/10^{-10}=10^{-24}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

perOption.A: Implies a position uncertainty vastly larger than the atom.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Assumes confinement to a much smaller distance than an atomic diameter.
perOption.D: Uses a momentum scale that would require far tighter confinement than even a nuclear diameter.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body:
Paper stops alpha particles, so the initial alpha count rate is $352-256=96\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ and the initial beta count rate is $256-16=240\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Six days is $144\ \mathrm{h}$, or three alpha half-lives and four beta half-lives.

The final alpha and beta count rates are $96/2^3=12\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ and $240/2^4=15\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Adding the background gives $12+15+16=43\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Leaves out the background count at the detector.
perOption.B: Undercounts the source contribution, for example by applying too many half-lives.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overcounts the source contribution by allowing too little decay.

ri-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The energy released is the increase in total binding energy, $(5.607\times7+7.120\times4-6.494\times10)\ \mathrm{MeV}=2.789\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Subtracting the products' total kinetic energy gives a $\gamma$-ray energy of $2.789-2.31=0.479\ \mathrm{MeV}\approx0.48\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the total released energy without deducting the products' kinetic energy.
perOption.C: Adds the products' kinetic energy to the released energy.
perOption.D: Overstates the energy available from the change in binding energy.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Taking downward as positive gives $mg-U=ma$, so $m=U/(g-a)=2.40/(9.81-4.50)=0.451977\ \mathrm{kg}$. The fractional uncertainty is $\Delta m/m=0.06/2.40+0.05/(9.81-4.50)=0.034416$. Multiplying by the mass gives $\Delta m=0.015555\ \mathrm{kg}$, which rounds to $0.02\ \mathrm{kg}$, so the result is $(0.45\pm0.02)\ \mathrm{kg}$.

perOption.A: Uses $g+a$ in the denominator, as if the object accelerated upward.
perOption.B: Uses $g+a$ and overstates the absolute uncertainty for that mass.
perOption.C: Undercounts the uncertainty, for example by including only the upthrust contribution.
perOption.D: Correct.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q1.issues: The key prints incorrect factors (0.032564 and 0.363068) on the absolute-uncertainty line. The previous lines give the correct factors 0.034416 and 0.451977, which reproduce the key's result.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: By Hooke's law, $x=F/k$. If each mass has weight $W$, the upper spring supports both masses and has extension $x_\mathrm{upper}=2W/30$, while the lower supports one mass and has extension $x_\mathrm{lower}=W/10$. Their extension ratio is $x_\mathrm{upper}/x_\mathrm{lower}=2/3$, so $2.0/x_\mathrm{lower}=2/3$ and the lower spring extends $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Halves the extension for half the load and ignores the smaller spring constant.
perOption.B: Inverts the extension ratio and multiplies by $2/3$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives both springs the same tension and accounts only for the difference in spring constants.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: The collected rain gains horizontal momentum at the rate $F=\frac{d(mv)}{dt}=v\frac{dm}{dt}=(20)(0.50)=10\ \mathrm{N}$. The container therefore exerts a $10\ \mathrm{N}$ backward force on the car as the rain pushes back on it.

perOption.A: Ignores the horizontal momentum gained by the rain.
perOption.B: Underestimates the force by using less than the full horizontal velocity gain at the given mass flow rate.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Omits the factor of $0.50$ from the mass flow rate.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: Take the rebound direction as positive. Using $mv_f-mv_i=F\Delta t$ gives $(0.060)[18-(-12)]=F(0.015)$, so the average force is $120\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the two speeds as if the ball kept moving in the same direction.
perOption.B: Assumes the ball starts from rest and counts only the final momentum.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overestimates the force by using too large a momentum change or too short a contact time.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: At constant speed the driving force balances drag, so $F=kv^2$. Since $F_\mathrm{final}/F_\mathrm{initial}=1/2$, the speed ratio is $v_\mathrm{final}/v_\mathrm{initial}=1/\sqrt{2}$. Using $P=Fv=kv^3$, the power ratio is $(1/\sqrt{2})^3=0.354$.

perOption.A: Cubes $1/2$ as if the speed itself were halved.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses only the driving-force ratio and ignores the change in speed.
perOption.D: Uses the speed ratio alone and ignores the change in driving force.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: Let $t$ be the time to the highest point. The average vertical velocity gives $H=\tfrac12(v\sin\alpha+0)t$. In the same time the horizontal displacement is $R/2=v\cos\alpha\,t$. Dividing these equations gives $(R/2)/H=2\cos\alpha/\sin\alpha$, so $R=4H\cos\alpha/\sin\alpha$.

perOption.A: Gives the horizontal displacement to the apex only.
perOption.B: Swaps the sine and cosine and gives only half the corresponding range.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Swaps the horizontal and vertical trigonometric factors.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: The object's speed increases at a decreasing rate and eventually levels off at terminal speed, as in Z. X shows the magnitude of the resultant force, which starts at the weight and tends to zero as drag builds. Y shows the height, whose downward slope starts at zero and approaches a constant magnitude as the speed levels off.

perOption.A: Assigns speed to a graph that starts above zero even though the object is dropped from rest.
perOption.B: Swaps height and resultant force, which tends to zero as terminal speed is reached.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Assigns height to an increasing graph although the object is falling.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q7.issues: The graphs are schematic. Once Z levels off at terminal speed, Y should continue with a constant negative slope. The key’s reference to an increasing gradient of Y means its magnitude increases.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: The ball's weight acts throughout the collision, while the floor's much greater contact force reverses the ball's momentum. Over the short contact time, the impulse due to weight is much smaller than the impulse due to the floor, so weight can be neglected when finding the momentum change.

perOption.A: The ball's weight continues to act throughout the collision.
perOption.B: Weight is a force and momentum is $mv$, so their magnitudes cannot be compared directly.
perOption.C: The floor's contact force exceeds the weight and produces the upward momentum change.
perOption.D: Correct.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: Taking right as positive, momentum conservation gives $2m(5.0)+m(-4.0)=2mv_P+mv_Q$. Since the collision is elastic, relative speed of approach equals relative speed of separation, so $5.0-(-4.0)=v_Q-v_P$. Solving gives $v_P=-1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $v_Q=8.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so P moves left at $1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Interprets P's negative velocity as motion to the right.
perOption.C: Uses Q's speed and gives it the wrong direction.
perOption.D: Reports Q's velocity instead of P's.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: Once released, the gas expands until it reaches atmospheric pressure, the same as its initial pressure. At that pressure the original amount of gas would occupy $V'$ at $80^\circ\mathrm{C}$, with $V/(273+27)=V'/(273+80)$ and hence $V'=(353/300)V$. The container still has volume $V$, so it retains $V/V'=300/353\approx85\%$ of the original gas.

perOption.A: Gives the percentage that escapes.
perOption.B: Uses the Celsius temperatures directly and treats $27/80$ as the remaining fraction.
perOption.C: Uses the complement of the incorrect Celsius ratio.
perOption.D: Correct.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The piston does work on the air as it compresses it. The compression happens so quickly that little thermal energy escapes to the surroundings, making it approximately adiabatic. The air's internal energy and temperature rise enough to ignite the paper.

perOption.A: Attributes the energy input to heat from the surroundings, though rapid compression transfers energy by work.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Assumes compression adds molecules to the sealed cylinder.
perOption.D: Attributes ignition to direct heating by the piston instead of the compressed air.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: In uniform circular motion, the speed $v$ and radius $r$ stay constant. The resultant force is the centripetal force, so its magnitude $F_c=mv^2/r$ is constant throughout the circle.

perOption.A: Constant speed means constant kinetic energy.
perOption.B: At the top, weight contributes its full magnitude inward, so the rod supplies its smallest signed inward radial force.
perOption.C: Correct.
