perOption.D: The acceleration always points towards the centre.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q12.issues: Option B uses “tension” for the rod force. At sufficiently low speed the rod is in compression at the top. B holds if interpreted as the signed inward radial force.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: For orbits around Earth, $T^2\propto R^3$. With the satellite period $T$ in days, $(27.3/T)^2=[R/(R/30)]^3$, so $T=0.166\ \mathrm{day}\approx4.0\ \mathrm{hours}$.

perOption.A: This is approximately the period in days, reported as hours.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This corresponds to reducing the period by only about a factor of 10, whereas the orbital radius change requires a factor of $30^{3/2}$.
perOption.D: This gives too long a period for a radius reduced by a factor of 30, since the period scales as radius to the power $3/2$.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The key labels the solved period as R in its last line. The rewrite uses T.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: Conservation of energy gives $E_\mathrm{final}=E_\mathrm{initial}$. The object starts at rest at radius $3R$ and hits the Moon at radius $R$, so $\tfrac12 mv^2-GMm/R=0-GMm/(3R)$. Solving gives $v=\sqrt{4GM/(3R)}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This loses the factor of two from the kinetic energy term when solving for $v^2$.
perOption.C: This treats the surface gravitational field strength as constant over the entire fall.
perOption.D: This corresponds to starting from rest infinitely far away.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: The mass is at one extreme at $t=0$, passes through equilibrium at $t=T/4$, and reaches the other extreme at $t=T/2$. Its speed is greatest at equilibrium, so it is a maximum at $t=T/4$.

perOption.A: The $70\ \mathrm{cm}$ is the peak-to-peak distance, giving an amplitude of $35\ \mathrm{cm}$.
perOption.B: At $t=T/2$ the mass is at a turning point, so its speed and kinetic energy are zero.
perOption.C: The magnitude of the restoring force falls to zero as the mass approaches equilibrium.
perOption.D: Correct.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q15.issues: Option C implicitly refers to restoring-force magnitude. With downward taken as positive, the signed force increases from a negative value to zero.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: The total energy is $E=\tfrac12m\omega^2A^2$, and the kinetic energy is $E_k=\tfrac12m\omega^2(A^2-x^2)$. Substituting $E_k=\tfrac34 E$ gives $\tfrac34A^2=A^2-x^2$. Thus the displacement has magnitude $|x|=A/2$.

perOption.A: This treats the potential energy fraction $1/4$ as a displacement fraction.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This treats the kinetic energy fraction $3/4$ as a displacement fraction.
perOption.D: This assigns the fraction $3/4$ to potential energy.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q16.issues: The question and key give a positive displacement. The energy condition fixes the magnitude, with signed displacements ±A/2 both possible.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: Particles between successive nodes oscillate in phase. A node has zero displacement at all times, and adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength. At an antinode, the amplitude is twice that of either component wave.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: A node is the point with zero displacement at all times.
perOption.C: Adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength.
perOption.D: At an antinode, the amplitude is twice that of either component wave.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q17.issues: The key’s amplitude statement for D applies at antinodes. The amplitude varies with position.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: A pipe open at both ends supports standing waves when $L=n\lambda/2$ for a positive integer $n$. With $\lambda=20\ \mathrm{cm}$, pipe R fits three half wavelengths. A pipe closed at one end requires $L=(2n-1)\lambda/4$, so pipe P fits five quarter wavelengths.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Pipe S cannot fit a whole number of half wavelengths between its open ends.
perOption.C: Pipe Q fits six quarter wavelengths, but a pipe closed at one end needs an odd number.
perOption.D: Pipe Q fails the odd-quarter-wavelength condition and pipe S fails the whole-half-wavelength condition.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: At M the particle has electric potential energy $U=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{2Qq}{d}-\frac{Qq}{d}\right)=\frac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0d}$. By conservation of energy, the kinetic energy lost equals this gain, so $\tfrac12mu^2-\tfrac12mv^2=U$. Hence $v=\sqrt{u^2-\frac{Qq}{2\pi\varepsilon_0md}}$.

perOption.A: This reverses the order of subtraction under the square root.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This reverses the subtraction and misses the factor of two when converting the energy gain into a change in squared speed.
perOption.D: This misses the factor of two when converting the energy gain into a change in squared speed.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: Each metal plate is an equipotential surface, so the electric field lines meet it at right angles. The plates are farther apart at the top, where the field is weaker and the lines are more widely spaced.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The straight, evenly spaced lines meet the plates obliquely and imply a uniform field.
perOption.C: The even spacing misses the stronger field at the narrow end.
perOption.D: The spacing changes appropriately, but the straight lines meet the plates obliquely.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: For the half-wave rectified sine, the mean of the squared current during the conducting half-cycle is $I_0^2/2$, so over the full cycle it is $I_0^2/4$. Taking the square root gives an RMS current of $I_0/2$. The square wave has constant current magnitude, so its RMS current equals its peak current. Equal mean powers in the same resistor give equal RMS currents, hence the requested peak-current ratio is $1/2$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This uses the RMS factor for a full sinusoidal wave and overlooks the zero-current half-cycle.
perOption.C: This equates peak currents even though equal mean power fixes the RMS currents.
perOption.D: This inverts the requested peak-current ratio.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q21.issues: The worked solution starts on page 5 and continues on page 6.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: Potential is constant along each connecting wire, so label A as $V_1$, B as $V_3$, and the common intermediate node as $V_2$. Redrawing the circuit gives a single resistor $R$ in parallel with two parallel pairs in series. Each pair is $R/2$, so the two branches each have resistance $R$ and combine to give $R/2=0.50\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This counts only one of the two equivalent $1.0\ \Omega$ branches.
perOption.C: This adds a parallel pair’s resistance to the centre resistor as though they were in series.
perOption.D: This adds all five resistances as though the connecting wires were absent.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The currents run in opposite directions, so the fields point the same way between the wires and can only cancel outside. The cancellation point must be nearer the smaller current, so it lies to the right of Q. If its distance from P is $y$, its distance from Q is $y-d$. Equating the two field magnitudes gives $4.0/y=3.0/(y-d)$, so $y=4d$.

perOption.A: Between the wires the fields point the same way, so they add at this position.
perOption.B: This balances field magnitudes between the wires, where the fields reinforce each other.
perOption.C: To the left of P, P has both the larger current and the shorter distance, so its field is stronger.
perOption.D: Correct.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q23.issues: The key’s first field equation shows d in both denominators. Its next line correctly uses y and y − d.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: For perpendicular motion, the magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, giving $r=mv/(|q|B)$. With the same $v$ and $B$ for all four particles, the electron has the smallest mass-to-charge-magnitude ratio and therefore the smallest radius and greatest deflection.

perOption.A: A proton has the same charge magnitude as an electron but a much larger mass.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: A copper ion has a much greater mass per unit charge magnitude than an electron.
perOption.D: A helium nucleus carries twice the electron’s charge magnitude but has a much greater mass per unit charge magnitude.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: The primary current is greatest just before the switch opens, when the variable resistance is at its minimum. Opening the switch quickly then causes the greatest rate of change of magnetic flux through the soft iron. This gives the largest induced e.m.f. and hence the largest current through the ammeter.

perOption.A: The switch closes with the resistance at its maximum, so the change in primary current is smaller.
perOption.B: The gradual resistance change changes the flux more slowly.
perOption.C: Minimum resistance gives the largest steady primary current, but the secondary current depends on how fast the flux is changing.
perOption.D: Correct.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: Faraday’s law gives $\mathcal E=-\mathrm d(NBA)/\mathrm dt$. Using $\mathcal E=RI$ and $I=\mathrm dQ/\mathrm dt$ gives $R\,\mathrm dQ/\mathrm dt=-\mathrm d(NBA)/\mathrm dt$. The flux drops to zero, so the charge magnitude is $\Delta Q=NBA/R=\frac{50}{10+10}(0.0500)(300\times10^{-4})=3.75\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm C$.

perOption.A: This omits the circuit’s additional resistance and makes the converted area 100 times too small.
perOption.B: This makes the converted area 100 times too small.
perOption.C: This includes only one of the two $10.0\ \Omega$ resistances.
perOption.D: Correct.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: At the minimum momentum uncertainty, both electrons have the same position–momentum uncertainty product, so $\Delta x_A\Delta p_A=\Delta x_B\Delta p_B$. Thus $\Delta p_A/\Delta p_B=\Delta x_B/\Delta x_A=0.50/0.20=2.5$.

perOption.A: This takes the ratio of position uncertainties in the same order as the requested momentum ratio.
perOption.B: This puts the momentum ratio below one even though A has the tighter position constraint.
perOption.C: This is close to taking the square root of the inverse position ratio, but the relation is directly inverse.
perOption.D: Correct.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q27.issues: The key writes the syllabus order-of-magnitude form as an exact bound with h. For standard deviations the exact lower bound is ℏ/2. The common constant cancels.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: The kinetic energy is $E=\tfrac12mv^2=(mv)^2/(2m)=p^2/(2m)$, so $p=\sqrt{2mE}$. The de Broglie relation then gives $\lambda=h/p=h/\sqrt{2mE}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: This gives the inverse wavelength $p/h$.
perOption.C: This drops the factor of two when rearranging $E=p^2/(2m)$.
perOption.D: This multiplies Planck’s constant by the momentum instead of dividing by it.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: The scattering experiment reveals a small, massive, charged nucleus. The scattering observations do not reveal whether the nucleus contains neutrons, so they cannot establish that it contains both protons and neutrons.

perOption.A: Most alpha particles pass straight through or are only slightly deflected, which supports this inference.
perOption.B: The rare rebounds show that mass is concentrated in a small nucleus capable of deflecting an alpha particle through a large angle.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The deflections of the charged alpha particles show that they interact electrically with the nucleus.

rvhs-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: Each $\beta^-$ decay increases the proton number by one and leaves the mass number unchanged. The $\alpha$ decay decreases the proton number by two and the mass number by four. Thus S has the same proton number as P and four fewer nucleons, making them isotopes of the same element.

perOption.A: The alpha decay leaves S with four fewer nucleons than P.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This overlooks the two beta decays that cancel the alpha decay’s effect on proton number.
perOption.D: The mass number falls, but the unchanged proton number means S belongs to the same element.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: In SI base units, $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}=(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}})^p(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-1}})^q$. Matching the powers of seconds gives $-1=-2p$, and matching the powers of kilograms gives $0=p+q$. Hence $p=\tfrac12$ and $q=-\tfrac12$.

perOption.A: These exponents give $mathrm{s}$ instead of $mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and leave an extra inverse kilogram.
perOption.B: A negative $p$ gives $mathrm{s}$ instead of $mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: With both exponents positive, the mass factors multiply to give a kilogram instead of cancelling.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: From $F=BIL$ and $I=Q/t$, $B=F/(IL)=Ft/(QL)$, with units $\mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{N\,s\,C^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$. From $\Phi=BA$, $B=\Phi/A$, so its units can also be written $\mathrm{Wb\,m^{-2}}$. Since $\mathrm{Wb}=\mathrm{J\,A^{-1}}$, this gives $\mathrm{J\,A^{-1}\,m^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Has an extra inverse metre compared with $\mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Omits the second in $\mathrm{N\,s\,C^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: A tesla is already a unit of flux density, so dividing it by current and length changes the dimensions.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: For the two blocks together, $F_{\mathrm{net}}=ma$ gives $12=(4+2)a$, so $a=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. For X, the tension is the net horizontal force, so $T=2(2)=4\ \mathrm{N}$. Using Y gives the same result from $12-T=4(2)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The acceleration is right, but the tension is the force needed to accelerate the $2\ \mathrm{kg}$ block, giving $4\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.C: The tension is right, but dividing $12\ \mathrm{N}$ by Y’s mass alone ignores X.
perOption.D: Dividing by Y’s mass alone ignores X, and the tension must equal X’s mass times the common acceleration.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: The area under the force–distance graph up to $s_1$ is the net work, $\tfrac12 F_1s_1$. The object starts at rest, so this work equals its final kinetic energy, $\tfrac12 mv^2$. Equating the two gives $v=\sqrt{F_1s_1/m}$.

perOption.A: Omits the factor of $\tfrac12$ in the kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the full rectangle $F_1s_1$ for work instead of the triangular area.
perOption.D: Overestimates the work by a factor of four compared with the triangular area.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.issues: The stem says ‘at the distance s’ without a subscript. The key evaluates the speed at the marked endpoint s₁.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: Set the potential energy at Q to zero, so the potential energy at P is $50\ \mathrm{kJ}$. The total energy at P is $50+5=55\ \mathrm{kJ}$. At Q, the energy balance is $55=0+K_Q+10$ in kilojoules, so $K_Q=45\ \mathrm{kJ}$.

perOption.A: Undercounts the final kinetic energy, for example by subtracting the friction loss twice.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Ignores the $10\ \mathrm{kJ}$ lost to friction.
perOption.D: Adds the work done against friction to the mechanical energy.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: The component of weight down the slope is $mg\sin 2^\circ=1400(9.81)\sin 2^\circ\approx479.3\ \mathrm{N}$. The extra power against gravity is $P_g=Fv=479.3(25)\approx12\ \mathrm{kW}$. Adding this to the original $30\ \mathrm{kW}$ gives $42\ \mathrm{kW}$.

perOption.A: Counts only the additional power needed against gravity.
perOption.B: Adds too little power for the downslope component of weight, which requires about $12\ \mathrm{kW}$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overestimates the additional power needed against gravity at this slope.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.issues: The key assumes the power needed to overcome resistive forces stays at 30 kW on the slope.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: For cars starting from rest, $s=\tfrac12at^2$ and $s'=\tfrac12a't^2$. At $3\ \mathrm{s}$, $12=\tfrac12(9)(a'-a)$, giving $a'-a=\tfrac83\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. At $6\ \mathrm{s}$, the separation is $\tfrac12(36)(\tfrac83)=48\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the separation by treating the added time as a fixed increment instead of applying the square-time relation.
perOption.B: Doubles the separation as if it were proportional to time.
perOption.C: Triples the separation, though doubling the time multiplies it by four.
perOption.D: Correct.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.issues: The key writes 2.6 for the acceleration difference and then uses it as if exact. The rewrite retains 8/3 to obtain 48 m.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: From release to P, the positive velocity gradient falls from $g$ to zero. From P to Q, air resistance balances weight at the first terminal velocity, so acceleration is zero. When the parachute opens at Q, the steep negative gradient gives a negative acceleration with a magnitude much greater than $g$. The gradient returns to zero at R and stays there through S at the second terminal velocity.

perOption.A: Shows too small a negative acceleration at Q for the steep velocity gradient.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Reverses the signs of the velocity gradients before P and after Q.
perOption.D: Reverses the signs of both changing-velocity intervals, even though it shows a large spike at Q.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.issues: The larger deceleration magnitude follows from the steeper graph at Q. Air resistance exceeding weight establishes the sign, but does not by itself establish that magnitude.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q10.body: The tension is smallest at the top, where $T_{\mathrm{top}}+mg=mr\omega^2$. It is largest at the bottom, where $T_{\mathrm{bottom}}-mg=mr\omega^2$. The difference is $(mr\omega^2+mg)-(mr\omega^2-mg)=2mg$.

perOption.A: Treats constant centripetal force magnitude as constant tension.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives the net inward force magnitude instead of the difference in tension.
perOption.D: Doubles the net inward force magnitude, although that term cancels in the subtraction.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The gravitational force supplies the centripetal force on star $b$, so $Gm^2/(d_a+d_b)^2=md_b\omega^2$. Hence $\omega^2=Gm/[d_b(d_a+d_b)^2]$. Taking the positive square root gives $\omega=\frac{1}{d_a+d_b}\sqrt{\frac{Gm}{d_b}}$.

perOption.A: Uses the full separation as star $b$’s orbital radius.
perOption.B: Uses star $a$’s orbital radius, which equals star $b$’s radius under the equal-mass assumption.
perOption.C: Uses $d_b$ as the separation in the gravitational force.
perOption.D: Correct.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.issues: The equal masses imply d_a = d_b, which makes B algebraically equivalent to D for this system. D is the direct expression from the force equation for star b. The schematic appears asymmetric.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: The straight force–displacement line through the origin has negative gradient, so the motion is simple harmonic. Its kinetic energy is $K=\tfrac12mv^2=\tfrac12m\omega^2(x_0^2-x^2)$, an inverted parabola with a maximum at $x=0$. Total energy $K+U$ is constant, so potential energy rises quadratically as kinetic energy falls.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Swaps kinetic and potential energy, placing minimum kinetic energy at equilibrium.
perOption.C: Places maximum kinetic energy at equilibrium but gives it the wrong, non-parabolic shape.
perOption.D: Places minimum kinetic energy at equilibrium and gives it a non-parabolic shape.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: In simple harmonic motion, speed is greatest at equilibrium, so the candidates are A and C. Immediately after A the displacement is negative, so the particle is moving downwards there. Immediately after C it is positive, so the particle is moving upwards there.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: B is a turning point with zero instantaneous speed.
perOption.C: The particle crosses equilibrium at maximum speed but is moving upwards.
perOption.D: D is a turning point with zero instantaneous speed.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: In the standing wave, B and D are in the same loop, so they oscillate in phase. This makes the Graph 2 statement in option D incorrect. The other seven statements are correct.

perOption.A: Both statements are true because P and S are half a wavelength apart and A and C are in adjacent loops.
perOption.B: Both statements are true because P and Q are one wavelength apart and A and E are separated by two loops.
perOption.C: Both statements are true because Q and S are half a wavelength apart and B and E are in adjacent loops.
perOption.D: Correct. B and D oscillate in phase.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: Using $pV=NkT$, the initial state gives $pV=Nk(250)$ and the final state gives $2pV=N'k(1250)$. The fraction that escapes is $(N-N')/N=\left(\frac{pV}{250k}-\frac{2pV}{1250k}\right)\frac{250k}{pV}=0.6$.

perOption.A: Gives the fraction of molecules remaining in the container.
perOption.B: Results from using $1000\ \mathrm{K}$ as the final temperature instead of the temperature rise.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Would leave only one tenth of the molecules, which at five times the temperature would halve the original pressure.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: Gas pressure comes from momentum transferred to the walls in elastic collisions. Averaging over many freely moving molecules, with isotropic velocities, gives $p=\tfrac13(N/V)m\langle c^2\rangle$. This derivation uses molecular speeds without a temperature relation. Comparing it with $pV=NkT$ then gives the proportionality between mean kinetic energy and temperature.

perOption.A: A large molecular population in a representative volume supports the statistical average used to describe steady pressure.
perOption.B: Elastic wall collisions give the momentum change used to calculate pressure.
perOption.C: Neglecting intermolecular attraction allows the model to treat molecules as moving freely between collisions.
perOption.D: Correct.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.issues: The key gives D and a prompt about A, with no worked explanation. A is understood as a statistical averaging assumption, rather than a strict lower bound on number density.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: The change in internal energy depends only on states P and Q. Along PRQ, $\Delta U=Q+W=8-3=5\ \mathrm{J}$, with $W$ denoting work done on the gas. Along PSQ, $\Delta U=Q'-1=5\ \mathrm{J}$, so $Q'=+6\ \mathrm{J}$ and heat enters the gas.

perOption.A: Reverses the direction of the $6\ \mathrm{J}$ heat transfer.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Results from treating the work done by the gas as positive work on it on both paths.
perOption.D: Gives a heat loss that, together with work done by the gas, would decrease internal energy.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.issues: The key drops the prime on Q in one intermediate expression for the second path.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: The drop’s weight is $mg=(2.6\times10^{-15})(9.81)=2.55\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{N}$. The field has magnitude $E=V/d=1200/0.02=60\,000\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, giving the negative drop an upward electric force of $2.88\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{N}$. The net force is upward, so $a=(2.88-2.55)\times10^{-14}/(2.6\times10^{-15})\approx1.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: Assumes the electric force and weight balance exactly.
perOption.B: Treats the drop as nearly in free fall even though the upward electric force exceeds its weight.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the electric force alone and neglects weight.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: The electron is negatively charged, so the electric force acts opposite to the field and moves it towards higher electric potential. The field does positive work as the electron accelerates, increasing its kinetic energy. By energy conservation, its electric potential energy decreases.

perOption.A: Assumes increasing electric potential also increases the potential energy of a negative charge.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Treats the electron as moving along the field and gaining potential energy as it accelerates.
perOption.D: Assumes the electron follows the field towards lower potential, even though the force on it is opposite to the field.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: In one period, one elementary charge passes a given point on the orbit. With $\omega=4.1\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, the period is $T=2\pi/\omega$. The average current is $I=e/T=(1.60\times10^{-19})/(2\pi/\omega)\approx1.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies charge by the period instead of dividing by it.
perOption.B: Gives the elementary charge without accounting for how often it passes the point.
perOption.C: Multiplies charge by orbital speed instead of revolutions per second.
perOption.D: Correct.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The resistance at each point is the ratio $R=V/I$. The larger resistance at X is $V_X/I_X$, and the smaller resistance at Y is $V_Y/I_Y$. The decrease is therefore $V_X/I_X-V_Y/I_Y$.

perOption.A: Assumes the straight line implies constant $V/I$ even though it misses the origin.
perOption.B: Finds the reciprocal gradient between X and Y instead of the decrease in $V/I$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Subtracts the voltage intercept before calculating the ratios, effectively comparing reciprocal gradients.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: Take the bottom wire to be at $0\ \mathrm{V}$. By potential division, each $800\ \Omega$ resistor has a drop of $\frac{800}{800+800}(12)=6\ \mathrm{V}$, so Y is at $+6\ \mathrm{V}$. X is also at $+6\ \mathrm{V}$. The potential difference across the connecting wire is zero, so $V=IR$ gives zero current through it.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats a $6\ \mathrm{V}$ source as driving current through a $900\ \Omega$ series path involving the wire, overlooking equal midpoint potentials.
perOption.C: Gives the current through the $800\ \Omega$ resistors instead of through the connecting wire.
perOption.D: Uses $6\ \mathrm{V}$ as the voltage across the wire, although both ends are at $6\ \mathrm{V}$.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: At $300\ \mathrm{V}$, the stored charge is $Q=CV=(20\times10^{-6})(300)\ \mathrm{C}$. The current is constant, so $Q=It$ gives $t=(20\times10^{-6})(300)/(10\times10^{-3})=0.60\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Treats $10 mathrm{mA}$ as $10 mathrm{A}$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Does not use the charge required at $300 mathrm{V}$ divided by the given charging current.
perOption.D: Does not satisfy $It=CV$ for the specified voltage.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: For a long straight wire, $B=\mu_0 I/(2\pi r)$, so for the adjacent wires X and Y the force per unit length $F$ is proportional to $2I^2/r$. On Z, X gives an attractive force per unit length proportional to $4I^2/(2r)$, equal to $F$, and Y gives a repulsive one proportional to $8I^2/r$, equal to $4F$. These act in opposite directions, so the resultant is $4F-F=3F$.

perOption.A: Assumes the opposing forces have equal magnitudes.
perOption.B: Counts only the attraction towards X.
perOption.C: Treats X and Z as adjacent, giving an attraction of $2F$ instead of $F$.
perOption.D: Correct.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: Fleming’s left-hand rule gives a magnetic field directed out of the plane of the paper. After the rotation, the current remains in the plane of the paper and perpendicular to the field, so the force still has magnitude $F$.

perOption.A: An inward field would give an upward force in the initial diagram.
perOption.B: Reverses the field and uses the rotation angle as the angle between current and field.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the rotation angle as the angle between current and field.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: The same magnetic flux $\Phi$ passes through the soft-iron ring at all four coils. Since $\Phi=BA$, the variation in $B$ is greatest where the core area is smallest, at C. The number of turns affects the induced emf through flux linkage.

perOption.A: The wider core at A gives a smaller variation in flux density.
perOption.B: Being connected to the supply does not give B the smallest core area.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The extra turn affects flux linkage, while D has a larger core area than C.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: The ideal transformer has no power loss, so the primary transfers $20\ \mathrm{W}$. With the assumed unity power factor, $P_{\mathrm p}=V_{\mathrm p}I_{\mathrm p}$ gives $20=V_{\mathrm p}(2.0)$ and $V_{\mathrm p}=10\ \mathrm{V}$. The turns ratio is $N_{\mathrm p}/N_{\mathrm s}=V_{\mathrm p}/V_{\mathrm s}=10/50=1/5$.

perOption.A: Scales the power by the turns ratio, despite power conservation.
perOption.B: Inverts the turns ratio obtained under the unity-power-factor assumption.
perOption.C: Correct under the unity-power-factor assumption.
perOption.D: Uses the secondary voltage with the primary current and overstates the transmitted power.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.issues: The key assumes unity power factor (for example, a resistive load). The question does not specify the load or power factor. With a power factor of 0.04, B is also possible.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: An incident electron can raise the atom’s energy from $-13.6\ \mathrm{eV}$ to at most $-13.6+12.9=-0.7\ \mathrm{eV}$. The highest accessible level is $-0.85\ \mathrm{eV}$. The four accessible levels give six possible downward transitions, so at most six emission lines can be observed.

perOption.B: Counts only three transitions, for example those ending at the ground state.

sajc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Set the surviving populations equal using $N=N_0(1/2)^{t/t_{1/2}}$. Cancelling the common factor of $10^{12}$ gives $64(1/2)^{t/2}=8(1/2)^{t/3}$, with $t$ in days. Thus $(1/2)^{t/2-t/3}=2^{3-6}$, so $t/6=3$ and $t=18$ days.

perOption.A: Allows for a difference of only one half-life, leaving P with four times as many nuclei as Q.
perOption.B: Allows for a difference of only 1.5 half-lives, leaving more P nuclei than Q nuclei.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Thermal energy $Q$ has SI base units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$. From $k=(Q/t)L/[A(T_1-T_2)]$, the units of $k$ are $(\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}})(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})/(\mathrm{m^2\,K})=\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-3}\,K^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses degrees Celsius for the temperature difference in a base-unit expression.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses degrees Celsius and fails to carry the inverse-square seconds from the energy unit through the calculation.

perOption.A: Underestimates how many atoms fit by using an atomic volume much too large.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: For P the resultant force is zero, but the forces have a non-zero torque about the centre. For Q the torque about the centre vanishes, but there is a net upward force. For R the torque also vanishes, but the two upward components total only $2(50)\cos30^\circ$, leaving a net downward force.

perOption.B: Misses P’s net torque and assumes the inclined forces on R balance the downward force.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: Let $N$ be the reaction of the sloping plane and $F$ that of the vertical plane. Vertical equilibrium gives $N\sin60^\circ=mg$, and horizontal equilibrium gives $N\cos60^\circ=F$. Dividing gives $F=mg\cot60^\circ=1.5(9.81)\cot60^\circ=8.5\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Omits the wall reaction needed to balance the horizontal component of the sloping plane’s reaction.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the sphere’s weight as the wall reaction.
perOption.D: Calculates the full reaction of the sloping plane.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: The magnitude of the momentum–time gradient is $(2.7-1.5)/0.40=3.0\ \mathrm{N}$, giving the magnitude of the resultant force. Momentum decreases, so the resultant acts opposite to the motion. Thus $5.0-F=3.0$ and $F=2.0\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Takes the magnitude of the resultant as the applied force.

perOption.D: Adds the resultant magnitude to the resistive force, giving a resultant in the direction of motion.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: Let $h$ be the total rise and $v$ the speed at the start of the final second. Over that second, $0=v^2-2g(0.25h)$ and $0=\sqrt{0.50gh}-g(1)$, giving $h=19.62\ \mathrm{m}$. For the whole ascent, $0=u^2-2(9.81)(19.62)$ gives the launch speed $u=19.62\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The ascent time $T$ then follows from $0=19.62-9.81T$, so $T=2.00\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Adds 25% of a second to the final second, confusing a distance fraction with a time increment.
perOption.B: This time makes the final second cover about 44% of the rise, from the constant-acceleration distance relation.
perOption.C: This time makes the final second cover about 36% of the rise, from the constant-acceleration distance relation.
perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: The balls start with equal total mechanical energy and there are no resistive forces, so their final total mechanical energies are equal. They undergo the same net energy conversion between X and Y, and ball 2 takes less time, so it has the higher average rate of conversion.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Assigns extra energy to ball 2 and credits the slower ball with the higher average rate.
perOption.C: Confuses ball 2’s higher rate of energy conversion with a higher final total energy.
perOption.D: Assigns the higher rate to the ball that takes longer to undergo the same net energy conversion.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: Let $T$ be the tension in the string. The blocks move at constant speed, so force balance gives $T=Mg\sin\theta=mg$. The rate at which the tension transfers energy to P is $Tv=Mgv\sin\theta=mgv$, so expressions 1 and 2 both apply.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Misses that the tension also equals the component of P’s weight along the slope.
perOption.C: Includes the sum of the weights and misses that Q’s weight equals the tension.
perOption.D: Misses that the tension equals the weight of Q.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: The horizontal velocity is constant, with $u_x=18/1.5=12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. At the highest point the vertical component is zero, so $E_{\mathrm k}=\tfrac12 m u_x^2=\tfrac12(0.40)(12)^2=28.8\ \mathrm{J}$, or $29\ \mathrm{J}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Treats zero vertical velocity at the apex as zero total velocity.
perOption.B: Uses the horizontal speed without squaring it in the kinetic energy formula.
perOption.C: Uses the launch vertical speed of about $7.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in place of the horizontal speed at the apex.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.issues: The letter and horizontal-speed calculation are on page 2, with the kinetic-energy calculation on page 3.

The horizontal acceleration is therefore non-zero. The downward component of drag adds to the weight, making the vertical acceleration greater than $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ in magnitude.

perOption.A: Ignores the horizontal component of drag.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the acceleration components for a projectile with negligible air resistance.
perOption.D: Includes the horizontal drag but omits the downward component of drag.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: The momentum component parallel to the side of the table is unchanged, so the average force is perpendicular to the side. Taking away from the side as positive, the average force is $\Delta p/\Delta t=[m(v\cos30^\circ)-m(-v\cos30^\circ)]/\Delta t=2mv\cos30^\circ/\Delta t$.

perOption.A: Uses the initial momentum magnitude in place of the change in normal momentum.
perOption.B: Uses just one normal component and misses the reversal.

perOption.D: Doubles the component along the side, which is the component that stays constant.

For an actual collision the proton takes the incoming velocity, $w=u$, and the neutron stops, $v=0$. Opposite outgoing velocities of equal magnitude would give zero total momentum, so statement C is wrong.

perOption.A: This statement correctly applies momentum conservation after cancelling the equal masses.
perOption.B: This statement correctly applies kinetic-energy conservation for an elastic collision.

perOption.D: This statement correctly describes the transfer of velocity to the initially stationary proton.

perOption.B: This is tangent to the circle opposite the velocity, so it would slow the mass.
perOption.C: This is tangent to the circle along the velocity, so it would speed the mass up.
perOption.D: This points radially outward, opposite the centripetal acceleration.

perOption.D: Gives the net inward force on the block and omits the weight term.

perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The worked solution starts on page 4 and continues on page 5.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: The heater heats both the water and the tank, so $Q=(mc+C)\Delta T=[10(4200)+5000](45-25)=9.4\times10^5\ \mathrm{J}$. Using $P=Q/t$, the time is $t=(9.4\times10^5)/(3.0\times10^3)=313\ \mathrm{s}$, which rounds to $310\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Uses too small an energy input for the combined heat capacities and the $20\ \mathrm{K}$ rise.
perOption.B: Accounts for heating the water alone and omits the tank.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses too large an energy input for the stated temperature rise and combined heat capacities.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: For a fixed amount of ideal gas, $pV\propto T$, so $T_f/T_i=(p_fV_f)/(p_iV_i)=2\times2=4$. Since $\frac12mv_{\mathrm{rms}}^2=\frac32kT$, the squared speed ratio is also 4. Hence $v_f=2v_i=2u$.

perOption.A: Assumes the temperature stays constant even though $pV$ quadruples.
perOption.B: Counts only one of the two factors of two in $pV$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Scales speed directly with temperature instead of scaling its square.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: Both gases have the same temperature, so their molecules have the same mean translational kinetic energy, $\frac32 kT$. Since this energy is also $\frac12m\langle v^2\rangle$, the lighter nitrogen molecules have a greater mean square speed and rms speed.

perOption.A: Internal energy is a system quantity and can depend on the amount of each gas.
perOption.B: The lighter nitrogen molecules have greater mean square speed at the same temperature.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Taking the square root of the mean square speed preserves the difference between the gases.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: The drift current is $I=nqvA=(8.2\times10^{28})(1.6\times10^{-19})(2.3\times10^{-5})(8.0\times10^{-6})=2.41\ \mathrm{A}$. The resistance is $R=V/I=3.0/2.41=1.2\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Would require a current of about $38\ \mathrm{A}$, much larger than the drift current.
perOption.B: Would require a current of about $19\ \mathrm{A}$, much larger than the drift current.
perOption.C: Implies a current of $3.75\ \mathrm{A}$, overestimating the drift current.
perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.issues: The school prints no letter, but its worked value of 1.2 Ω corresponds to D. The batch keyAnswer is A and keyStatus is answer-missing.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: Reducing the light intensity increases the LDR’s resistance. The total circuit resistance therefore increases and the current decreases. The potential difference across the fixed resistor decreases as well.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Applies the voltage change across the LDR to the voltmeter, which is across the fixed resistor.
perOption.C: Reverses the current change and overlooks that the fixed resistor’s voltage follows the current.
perOption.D: Overlooks that the increased total resistance reduces the current.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: For the original stationary droplet, $qE=mg$. The oil density stays the same, so $m\propto r^3$ and doubling the radius gives $m_2=8m$. The second droplet has charge $q/2$, so $(q/2)E_2=8mg=8qE$. Cancelling $q$ gives $E_2=16E$.

perOption.A: Accounts for halving the charge but keeps the original weight.
perOption.B: Treats the mass as proportional to radius, giving only a factor of two in weight.
perOption.C: Accounts for the eightfold weight increase but keeps the original charge.
perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: Electric field lines are perpendicular to equipotentials at every crossing. They point from higher to lower potential, here from $7\ \mathrm{V}$ through $5\ \mathrm{V}$ to $3\ \mathrm{V}$. Only C satisfies both rules.

perOption.A: The arrows point towards lower potential but cross the outer equipotentials obliquely.
perOption.B: The arrows point towards higher potential and cross the outer equipotentials obliquely.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: The lines cross perpendicularly but the arrows point towards higher potential.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: Each segment experiences a force of magnitude $BIL$. Fleming’s left-hand rule gives upward components for both forces and horizontal components that cancel. Each upward component is $BIL\sin30^\circ$, so the resultant is $2BIL\sin30^\circ=BIL$ towards the top of the page.

perOption.A: Reverses the force direction given by the current and inward field.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Adds the full force magnitudes and reverses the resultant direction.
perOption.D: Adds the full magnitudes instead of their upward components.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.issues: The printed letter B agrees with the batch and the question. The key’s worked text describes a different straight-wire question, so it provides no usable working for this diagram.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: At the rim, $v=r\omega=2\pi fr$, so $f=v/(2\pi r)$. A radius sweeps an area $\pi r^2$ per revolution, giving $E=B\pi r^2f$. Substituting gives $E=Brv/2=Bdv/4$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Treats the entire radius as moving at the rim speed, giving $B(d/2)v$.
perOption.C: Uses the full diameter with the rim speed in the straight-conductor expression.
perOption.D: Omits a length factor, so the expression does not have units of voltage.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.issues: The letter is on page 6 and the working is on page 7.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: Using $K=p^2/(2m)$ with $K=(1.00\times10^6)(1.6\times10^{-19})\ \mathrm{J}$ and $m=1.67\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$ gives $p=2.312\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. The momentum uncertainty is $\Delta p=0.01p=2.312\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. Using the syllabus estimate $\Delta p\,\Delta x\approx h$, the minimum position uncertainty is approximately $2.87\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Requires a much smaller momentum uncertainty than the stated 1.0% of the calculated momentum.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Is about $\sqrt{10}$ too large, consistent with a factor-of-ten underestimate of the energy in the momentum calculation.
perOption.D: Implies a momentum uncertainty larger than the full proton momentum under the syllabus estimate.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.issues: The key and syllabus use the order-of-magnitude convention ΔxΔp ≳ h. The exact standard-deviation bound ħ/2 would yield about 2.28 × 10⁻¹³ m, which is absent from the options.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The energy released is the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactants. Multiply each binding energy per nucleon by the corresponding nucleon number, with zero binding energy for free neutrons. This gives $121(8.26)+113(8.52)-235(7.59)=178.57\ \mathrm{MeV}\approx179\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Uses a much smaller binding-energy gain than the difference between the nuclear totals.
perOption.B: Underestimates the gain by failing to account for the full change in nuclear binding energy.
perOption.C: Undercounts the binding-energy gain of the two daughter nuclei.
perOption.D: Correct.

tjc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.issues: The printed key shows D, but the batch keyAnswer is A and keyStatus is answer-missing. The key prints 112 for silver-113, which gives 170.05 MeV. Using the printed question’s 113 gives the key’s stated 179 MeV.

tmjc-2023-other-p1-q25.body:
For an ideal transformer, $V_s = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}V_p$.

Power in the secondary $= \dfrac{V_s^2}{R} = \dfrac{(N_s V_p/N_p)^2}{R} = \dfrac{N_s^2 V_p^2}{N_p^2 R}$, and since the transformer is ideal this equals the power in the primary coil.

perOption.A: Inverts the turns ratio and does not square $V_p$.
perOption.B: Does not square the turns ratio when squaring $V_s$.
perOption.C: Correct. $P = V_s^2/R$ with $V_s = (N_s/N_p)V_p$.
perOption.D: Squares the turns ratio but forgets to square $V_p$.

tmjc-2023-other-p1-q26.body:
Consider one period ($1.0\ \mathrm{ms}$), in which $V = 46\ \mathrm{V}$ for $0.25\ \mathrm{ms}$ and zero otherwise.

1. Square the graph: $V^2 = 46^2 = 2116\ \mathrm{V^2}$.

2. Mean over one period: $\langle V^2 \rangle = \dfrac{\text{area}}{\text{period}} = \dfrac{(2116)(0.25\times10^{-3})}{1.0\times10^{-3}} = 529\ \mathrm{V^2}$.

3. Take the square root: $V_{rms} = \sqrt{529} = 23\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: This is roughly the mean voltage ($46 \times 0.25 \approx 12\ \mathrm{V}$), not the r.m.s. value.
perOption.B: Correct. $\sqrt{\langle V^2\rangle} = \sqrt{529} = 23\ \mathrm{V}$.
perOption.C: Uses $V_0/\sqrt{2}$, which applies only to sinusoidal voltages.
perOption.D: Gives the mean of $V^2$ but forgets to take the square root.

tmjc-2023-other-p1-q27.body:
From $hf = \phi + E_{max}$, $E_{max} = hf - hf_0$.

The $x$-intercept is the threshold frequency $f_0 = \phi/h$, so a larger work function gives a larger threshold frequency: Y's line starts further right. The gradient of the graph is Planck's constant, so it does not change and the lines are parallel.

perOption.A: Shows a smaller threshold frequency, which corresponds to a smaller work function.
perOption.B: Correct. Larger $f_0$, same gradient $h$.
perOption.C: Shows a smaller threshold frequency and a steeper gradient; the gradient must stay $h$.
perOption.D: Has the larger threshold frequency but a smaller gradient; the gradient must stay $h$.

tmjc-2023-other-p1-q28.body:
Uncertainty in momentum: $\Delta p = m\Delta v = (9.11\times10^{-31})(5.8\times10^{6})\left(\dfrac{0.2}{100}\right) = 1.0568\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

Using $\Delta p\,\Delta x \geq h$: $\Delta x_{min} = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{1.0568\times10^{-26}} = 6.3\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Divides $h$ by $\Delta v$ only, omitting the electron mass.
perOption.B: This is $\Delta p$, not $\Delta x$.
perOption.C: Uses the full momentum $mv$ (giving the de Broglie wavelength) instead of the uncertainty $\Delta p$.
perOption.D: Correct. $\Delta x = h/\Delta p$ with $\Delta p = 0.2\%$ of $mv$.

tmjc-2023-other-p1-q30.body:
The count rate drops sharply when paper is inserted, so the radiation is stopped by paper: it must be $\alpha$ radiation, which has low penetrating power.

The remaining $24\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ is the background count rate, so the initial count rate due to the source is $532 - 24 = 508\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

After two half-lives the source count rate is $\tfrac{1}{4}(508) = 127\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$, so the reading is $127 + 24 = 151\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct radiation, but forgets to add the background count back to the reading.
perOption.B: $\beta$ radiation would not be stopped by paper, and the background is not added back.
perOption.C: Correct. $\alpha$; $\tfrac{1}{4}(532-24) + 24 = 151\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: $\beta$ radiation would pass through paper.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q1.body:
Estimate a pen as a cylinder of length $14.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and diameter $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

Volume $= \pi\left(\dfrac{1.0}{2}\right)^2(14.0) \approx 11\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, closest to $10\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.

perOption.A: Far too small; about the volume of a small bead.
perOption.B: Too small by a factor of ten; a pen is much longer than 1 cm.
perOption.C: Correct. $\pi(0.5)^2(14) \approx 11\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.
perOption.D: Too large; that is about the volume of a small cup of water.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q2.body:
Change in velocity = total area under the $a$–$t$ graph.

Total area $= \tfrac{1}{2}(4.0)(2.4) + \left(-\tfrac{1}{2}(6.0)(3.6)\right) = 4.8 - 10.8 = -6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Assumes the positive and negative areas cancel; they do not.
perOption.B: Averages the two extreme accelerations instead of finding the area.
perOption.C: Correct. Net area $= 4.8 - 10.8 = -6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.D: Treats both areas as negative ($-(4.8 + 10.8)$) instead of taking the area above the axis as positive.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q3.body:
Newton's 2nd law: the forces must act on the same body to produce a resultant force. Only $F_3$ and $F_4$ (both on the concrete) satisfy this.

Newton's 3rd law: the forces must act on different bodies. Only $F_2$ (on the Earth) and $F_4$ (on the concrete) satisfy this.

perOption.A: Correct. $F_3, F_4$ both act on the concrete; $F_2, F_4$ act on different bodies.
perOption.B: $F_1$ and $F_2$ both act on the Earth, so they cannot be a 3rd-law pair.
perOption.C: $F_1$ acts on the Earth and $F_3$ on the concrete, so they cannot combine into one body's resultant force.
perOption.D: $F_1, F_3$ act on different bodies (not a 2nd-law pair) and $F_1, F_2$ act on the same body (not a 3rd-law pair).

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q4.body:
Two pairs of the forces are antiparallel and separated by a perpendicular distance $d$, forming two couples, each of torque $Fd$.

Total torque $= Fd + Fd = 2Fd$.

The other forces act along lines through the centre, so they produce no torque.

perOption.A: Counts only one of the two couples.
perOption.B: Correct. Two couples of $Fd$ each.
perOption.C: Counts an extra couple; forces whose lines of action pass through the centre give no torque.
perOption.D: Treats all eight forces as producing torque, but four act through the centre.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q5.body:
Atmospheric pressure acts on both the top and bottom of the drum, so its effect cancels.

At equilibrium, weight of drum and content = weight of water displaced $= V\rho g = 0.80\times0.19\times1.1\times10^{3}\times9.81 = 1640\ \mathrm{N}$.

Mass of drum and content $= \dfrac{1640}{9.81} = 167\ \mathrm{kg}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $m = \rho V = 1.1\times10^3 \times 0.80 \times 0.19 = 167\ \mathrm{kg}$.
perOption.B: Does not follow from the displaced volume and the seawater density.
perOption.C: This is the weight in newtons, not the mass in kilograms.
perOption.D: Does not follow from the displaced volume; the upthrust equals the weight, so the mass is $\rho V$.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q6.body:
The net force from the rope on the wheel is $100 - 20 = 80\ \mathrm{N}$, and the rim moves at $0.30 \times 50\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Output power of the motor $= (100-20)(0.30)(50) = 1200\ \mathrm{W}$.

Electrical power supplied $= \dfrac{1200}{0.2} = 6000\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies the output power by the efficiency instead of dividing.
perOption.B: Adds the two tensions and multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing.
perOption.D: Adds the tensions ($120\ \mathrm{N}$) instead of taking their difference.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q7.body:
Angular velocity $\omega = \dfrac{v}{r} = \dfrac{6.0}{0.40} = 15\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

From A to B the body turns through a right angle, so the angular displacement is $\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 1.6\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Multiplies $v$ by $r$ for $\omega$ and gives the arc length ($0.63\ \mathrm{m}$) instead of the angle.
perOption.B: Multiplies $v$ by $r$ instead of dividing.
perOption.C: Gives the arc length $r\theta = 0.63\ \mathrm{m}$ instead of the angle in radians.
perOption.D: Correct. $\omega = v/r$ and $\theta = \pi/2$.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q8.body:
Gravitational force $F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$.

On the ground, $r = R$: $W = \dfrac{GMm}{R^2}$ (1). At a height $2R$ above the ground, $r = 3R$: $F = \dfrac{GMm}{(3R)^2}$ (2).

Dividing (2) by (1) gives $F = \dfrac{W}{9}$.

perOption.A: Treats the force as inversely proportional to height, not to the square of distance from the centre.
perOption.B: Uses $r = 3R$ but forgets to square it.
perOption.C: Uses the height $2R$ as the distance from the Earth's centre.
perOption.D: Correct. $r = 3R$, so $F = W/3^2$.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q9.body:
For an orbiting satellite, gravitational force provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{GMm}{r^2} = mr\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2$, so $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$.

The orbit radius is independent of the satellite's mass $m$, so with the same period the radius is the same: ratio $= 1$.

perOption.A: Wrongly assumes the radius is inversely proportional to the satellite's mass.
perOption.B: Correct. $m$ cancels, so $r$ depends only on $T$.
perOption.C: Wrongly assumes the radius depends on the square root of the satellite's mass.
perOption.D: Wrongly assumes the radius is proportional to the satellite's mass.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q10.body:
From the graph, amplitude $x_0 = 4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and maximum speed $v_0 = 20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

$v_0 = \omega x_0 \Rightarrow 20 = \omega \times 4.0$, so $\omega = 5.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ and $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{5.0} = 1.257\ \mathrm{s}$.

Speed goes from maximum (at equilibrium) to zero (at the extreme) in $\tfrac{1}{4}T = 0.31\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Gives $1/\omega$ instead of a quarter period.
perOption.B: Correct. $\tfrac{1}{4}T = \tfrac{1}{4}(2\pi/5.0) = 0.31\ \mathrm{s}$.
perOption.C: This is the full period; maximum to zero speed takes only a quarter period.
perOption.D: Reads the amplitude in metres as a time.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q11.body:
Taking displacement to the right as positive: molecules with positive displacement have moved right, those with negative displacement have moved left.

Just to the left of C (around B) the displacement is negative, so molecules move to the left; just to the right of C the displacement is positive, so molecules move to the right. Molecules move away from C on both sides, so C is the centre of a rarefaction.

Hence C has the minimum pressure.

perOption.A: At A, molecules on the left are displaced right and those on the right are displaced left, so A is a compression (maximum pressure).
perOption.B: B has maximum displacement but zero displacement gradient, so the pressure there is at its normal (undisturbed) value.
perOption.C: Correct. Molecules on both sides are displaced away from C, giving a rarefaction.
perOption.D: D has maximum displacement but the pressure there is at its undisturbed value, not a minimum.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q12.body:
Since $I \propto A^2$: $\dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = \dfrac{A_1^2}{A_2^2} \Rightarrow \sqrt{\dfrac{0.36}{0.25}} = \dfrac{A_1}{A_2} \Rightarrow A_1 = 1.2A_2$.

At P (a minimum) the waves arrive in antiphase, so the resultant amplitude is $A_P = 1.2A_2 - A_2 = 0.2A_2$.

$\dfrac{I_P}{0.25I} = \dfrac{(0.2A_2)^2}{A_2^2} = 0.040 \Rightarrow I_P = 0.010I$.

Equivalently, $A_P = 0.6A - 0.5A = 0.1A$, so $I_P = 0.010I$.

perOption.A: Zero only if the two waves had equal amplitudes; here the amplitudes differ.
perOption.B: Correct. Amplitudes subtract: $(0.6-0.5)^2 I = 0.010I$.
perOption.C: Subtracts the intensities ($0.36I - 0.25I$) instead of the amplitudes.
perOption.D: Does not come from subtracting amplitudes and squaring; intensities cannot be combined linearly.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q13.body:
Points in alternate segments (loops) of a standing wave are in antiphase, with a phase difference of $\pi$, while points in the same segment, or in segments two apart, are in phase.

X is in the first segment, so the point in the adjacent (second) segment, B, has a phase difference of $\pi$ with X.

perOption.A: A is in the same segment as X, so it oscillates in phase with X.
perOption.B: Correct. B is in the adjacent segment, so it is in antiphase with X.
perOption.C: C is two segments away from X, so it is in phase with X.
perOption.D: D is two segments away from X, so it is in phase with X.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q14.body:
Since the container is sealed and rigid, the volume and the number of molecules stay constant. Hence the average distance between the gas molecules does not change.

Heating raises the temperature, so the molecules move faster and hit the walls harder and more often.

perOption.A: Heating raises the temperature, so the mean kinetic energy and hence the average speed increase.
perOption.B: Correct. Fixed volume and fixed number of molecules means fixed average separation.
perOption.C: Faster molecules undergo larger momentum changes at the wall, so the average force increases (the pressure rises).
perOption.D: Faster molecules reach the walls more often, so the collision rate increases.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q15.body:
From the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta U = Q + W$.

When $Q$ is zero, the internal energy of the system can still increase if work is done on the system ($W$ positive). So internal energy can be increased without any transfer of heat.

perOption.A: Internal energy also depends on the amount of substance and its potential energy; temperature depends only on mean kinetic energy per molecule.
perOption.B: During a change of state, internal energy rises (potential energy increases) while temperature stays constant.
perOption.C: Internal energy is the sum of the random kinetic and potential energies of the molecules, not just the kinetic energies.
perOption.D: Correct. Work done on the system raises $U$ with $Q = 0$.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q16.body:
The liquid loses heat at the same rate while cooling and while freezing: $P_\text{cooling} = P_\text{freezing}$.

$\dfrac{mc\Delta\theta}{t} = \dfrac{m l_f}{t_f}$

With $\Delta\theta / t = 1.5\ \mathrm{K\ min^{-1}}$ and $t_f = 30\ \mathrm{min}$: $\dfrac{c}{l_f} = \dfrac{1}{1.5 \times 30} = \dfrac{1}{45}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $c/l_f = 1/(1.5 	imes 30)$.
perOption.B: Divides 30 by 1.5 instead of multiplying them.
perOption.C: Gives $30/1.5$, inverting the ratio and dividing instead of multiplying.
perOption.D: Gives $l_f/c$, the inverse of the required ratio.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q17.body:
Y is the same distance from both charges, so the field strengths due to $+q$ and $-q$ have equal magnitude.

The field $E_A$ due to $+q$ at P points away from P (down and to the right), and the field $E_B$ due to $-q$ at Q points towards Q (down and to the left).

Their horizontal components cancel and their vertical components add, so the resultant field at Y is downwards.

perOption.A: Correct. Horizontal components cancel; both vertical components point down.
perOption.B: Reverses the field directions: field points away from $+q$ and towards $-q$, which gives downward components.
perOption.C: The horizontal components are equal and opposite and cancel, so there is no leftward resultant.
perOption.D: Fields from opposite charges only cancel in magnitude horizontally; the vertical components add.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q18.body:
The middle (vertical) resistor is redundant: by symmetry the potential is the same at both of its ends, so no current flows through it.

Hence $R_E = \left(\dfrac{1}{R+R} + \dfrac{1}{R+R}\right)^{-1} = R$.

perOption.A: Treats all the resistors as if they were in parallel paths incorrectly, or includes the middle resistor as carrying current.
perOption.B: Correct. Two parallel paths of $2R$ each give $R$.
perOption.C: Takes only one path of $2R$, ignoring the second parallel branch.
perOption.D: Adds resistors in series that are actually in parallel.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q19.body:
Between P and Q, the 20 Ω resistor is in parallel with the 8.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω in series:

$R_{PQ} = \left(\dfrac{1}{20} + \dfrac{1}{8 + 3}\right)^{-1} = 7.10\ \Omega$

This combination is in series with the 10 Ω resistor across the 6.0 V battery, so by the potential divider:

$V_{PQ} = \dfrac{7.10}{7.10 + 10} \times 6.0 = 2.5\ \mathrm{V}$

perOption.A: Gives the p.d. across only part of the parallel network, e.g. across the 8.0 Ω or 3.0 Ω resistor alone.
perOption.B: Results from an incorrect combination of the resistances in the parallel network.
perOption.C: Correct. Potential divider with $R_{PQ} = 7.10\ \Omega$ and 10 Ω.
perOption.D: Uses the 20 Ω branch alone with the 10 Ω resistor ($ rac{20}{30} 	imes 6.0$), ignoring the parallel 11 Ω branch.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q20.body:
With bulb 3 in parallel with bulb 2, the p.d. across bulb 2 is a smaller fraction of the cell's e.m.f. than the p.d. across bulbs 1 and 4.

With bulb 3 removed, the resistance of that section increases, so the p.d. across bulb 2 increases while the p.d.s across bulbs 1 and 4 decrease correspondingly.

With fixed resistance, power dissipated increases as p.d. increases, so bulbs 1 and 4 become dimmer and bulb 2 becomes brighter.

perOption.A: Correct. Bulb 2 gets a larger share of the e.m.f.; bulbs 1 and 4 get less.
perOption.B: Bulbs 1 and 4 are in series and carry the same current, so they must change in the same way.
perOption.C: Reverses the effect: removing bulb 3 raises the resistance of the parallel section, increasing its share of the p.d.
perOption.D: Bulbs 1 and 4 carry the same current and cannot change differently; bulb 2 actually gets brighter.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q21.body:
Apply $F = BIL\sin\theta$ to each section:

$F_{AB} = (0.50)(1.0)(0.20)\sin 30^\circ = 0.050\ \mathrm{N}$ into the paper

$F_{BC} = (0.50)(1.0)(0.20)\sin 0^\circ = 0$

$F_{CD} = (0.50)(1.0)(0.20)\sin 90^\circ = 0.10\ \mathrm{N}$ out of the paper

Net force $= 0.10 - 0.050 = 0.050\ \mathrm{N}$ out of the paper.

perOption.A: Correct. $0.10\ \mathrm{N}$ out minus $0.050\ \mathrm{N}$ in.
perOption.B: Gets the directions of the forces on AB and CD reversed.
perOption.C: Adds the magnitudes of the forces on AB and CD instead of taking their opposite directions into account.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes and also takes the wrong net direction.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q22.body:
Each wire produces a field at the centre perpendicular to the line joining it to the centre, with directions given by the right-hand grip rule.

$B_Q$ (into the page) points down-left, $B_R$ (into the page) points up-left, and $B_S$ (out of the page) points to the left.

The vertical components of $B_Q$ and $B_R$ cancel, and all three have components to the left, so $B_\text{resultant}$ points towards C.

perOption.A: Reverses the right-hand grip rule for all three wires.
perOption.B: The vertical components of $B_Q$ and $B_R$ cancel by symmetry, so there is no upward resultant.
perOption.C: Correct. Vertical components cancel; all horizontal components point left.
perOption.D: The vertical components of $B_Q$ and $B_R$ cancel by symmetry, so there is no downward resultant.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q23.body:
As the coil moves parallel to the conductor, its distance from the wire does not change, so the magnetic flux linking it stays constant.

The rate of change of magnetic flux linkage is zero, so the induced e.m.f. is zero and there is no induced current.

perOption.A: Correct. The flux linkage does not change, so no e.m.f. is induced.
perOption.B: There is no induced current at all, so it has no direction.
perOption.C: There is no induced current, so its magnitude cannot depend on anything.
perOption.D: Moving faster parallel to the wire still gives no change in flux, so the current stays zero.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q24.body:
Electrons accumulate either at the centre or at the rim. In either case, two points equidistant from O have the same potential, and the potential difference between O and a point gets larger with distance from O. Y and X are on the same line from O, and Z is at the same radius as X, so $E_{XY} = E_{YZ}$.

Points further from O travel faster, so the segment XY cuts flux faster than YO. Therefore $E_{XY} > E_{YO}$.

perOption.A: Section XY moves faster than YO and cuts flux faster, so $E_{XY} > E_{YO}$.
perOption.B: Points further from O move faster, so equal lengths XY and YO do not give equal e.m.f.s.
perOption.C: X and Z are at the same radius and hence the same potential, so $E_{YZ} = E_{XY}$.
perOption.D: Correct. X and Z are equidistant from O, so they have the same potential.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q25.body:
Using $I_\text{rms} = \dfrac{P}{V}$, $I_\text{rms}$ ranges from $9.55\ \mathrm{A}$ to $10.4\ \mathrm{A}$, so the peak current $I_0 = \sqrt{2}\,I_\text{rms}$ ranges from $13.5\ \mathrm{A}$ to $14.7\ \mathrm{A}$.

For $f = 50$ to $60\ \mathrm{Hz}$, $\omega = 2\pi f$ lies between $314$ and $377\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

Hence the most probable expression for the current is $I = 14.1 \sin(375t)$.

perOption.A: Uses the r.m.s. value as the peak, and $\omega = 300\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ corresponds to $f pprox 48\ \mathrm{Hz}$, outside the rated range.
perOption.B: The peak is reasonable, but $\omega = 300\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ gives $f pprox 48\ \mathrm{Hz}$, below 50 Hz.
perOption.C: Uses the r.m.s. current as the amplitude of the sinusoid instead of $\sqrt{2}\,I_	ext{rms}$.
perOption.D: Correct. Peak 14.1 A and $\omega = 375\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ ($f pprox 60\ \mathrm{Hz}$) both fit the label.

tmjc-2024-other-p1-q25.issues: School's I_rms range (9.55–10.4 A) pairs 2100 W with 220 V and 2500 W with 240 V; the full possible range is 8.75–11.4 A. Answer D is unaffected.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q11.body:
A frequency of $2\ \mathrm{kHz}$ has a period of $T = 1/f = 0.5\ \mathrm{ms}$.

A typical C.R.O. screen has 10 horizontal divisions of $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ each. With a time-base of $0.1\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}$, one period spans $0.5/0.1 = 5$ divisions, so two full cycles fill the screen.

perOption.A: At $10\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}$ one period is only $0.05\ \mathrm{cm}$ wide, so about 200 cycles are crammed onto the screen.
perOption.B: Correct. One period spans 5 cm, so two clear cycles fit on the 10 cm screen.
perOption.C: At $1\ \mathrm{\mu s\,cm^{-1}}$ one period would be $500\ \mathrm{cm}$ wide, so the screen shows only a tiny fraction of a cycle.
perOption.D: At $10\ \mathrm{ns\,cm^{-1}}$ the screen spans only $100\ \mathrm{ns}$, a minute fraction of the $0.5\ \mathrm{ms}$ period.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q12.body:
The two supports must be nodes. Taking the distance between the supports as $L$, the wave shown (one loop) has wavelength $2L$, and the next possible stationary wave (two loops) has wavelength $L$.

Using $v = f\lambda$ with the same wave speed: $f = \dfrac{v}{2L}$ and $f' = \dfrac{v}{L} = 2f$.

perOption.A: Correct. The next mode has two loops, halving the wavelength and doubling the frequency.
perOption.B: $3f$ is the third harmonic; it skips the two-loop mode, as if only odd harmonics were allowed (as in a pipe closed at one end).
perOption.C: $\tfrac{1}{2}f$ would need wavelength $4L$, which cannot have nodes at both supports; the mode shown is already the lowest.
perOption.D: $\tfrac{3}{2}f$ would need 1.5 loops, leaving an antinode at a fixed support.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q13.body:
For a diffraction grating, $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$. Coinciding maxima are at the same angle $\theta$ for the same grating spacing $d$, so

$3\lambda_X = 5\lambda_Y$

$\dfrac{\lambda_X}{\lambda_Y} = \dfrac{5}{3}$

perOption.A: Has no basis in the orders given; the ratio follows from $3\lambda_X = 5\lambda_Y$.
perOption.B: Inverts the ratio: $3/5$ is $\lambda_Y/\lambda_X$.
perOption.C: Correct. $3\lambda_X = 5\lambda_Y$ gives $\lambda_X/\lambda_Y = 5/3$.
perOption.D: $d$ and $\sin\theta$ are the same for both, so they cancel and the ratio can be found.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q14.body:
Use the first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta U = Q + W$.

The container is insulated, so $Q = 0$, and $W$ (work done on the gas) is positive for a compression. Hence $\Delta U$ is positive, so the internal energy and the temperature of the ideal gas increase.

perOption.A: $\Delta U = 0 + W > 0$, so the internal energy increases.
perOption.B: Correct. Positive work on the gas with no heat loss raises its internal energy and hence its temperature.
perOption.C: The container is insulated, so $Q = 0$.
perOption.D: In a compression, positive work is done on the gas (negative work is done by the gas).

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q15.body:
The blocks are identical, so the final temperature at thermal equilibrium is the midpoint, $50\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The hot block falls by $30\ \mathrm{K}$.

$Q = mc\Delta\theta = 0.200 \times 390 \times 30 = 2340 \approx 2300\ \mathrm{J}$

perOption.A: Correct. The hot block cools by 30 K to the 50 °C equilibrium temperature.
perOption.B: Uses the full $60\ \mathrm{K}$ initial temperature difference instead of the $30\ \mathrm{K}$ drop of the hot block.
perOption.C: Does not match the 30 K drop of the hot block; the change in temperature has been taken wrongly.
perOption.D: Far too large; it uses a temperature change much greater than the 30 K drop of the hot block.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q16.body:
Mean kinetic energy is $\tfrac{3}{2}kT$, so $(c_{rms})^2 \propto T$.

$\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = \dfrac{(1.2\,c_{rms})^2}{c_{rms}^2} = 1.44$

$T_2 = 1.44 \times 350 = 504 \approx 500\ \mathrm{K}$

perOption.A: Treats a 20% increase as adding 20 K to the temperature.
perOption.B: Does not follow from $T \propto c_{rms}^2$; the temperature must rise by a factor of 1.44.
perOption.C: Assumes $T \propto c_{rms}$, giving $1.2 \times 350 = 420\ \mathrm{K}$.
perOption.D: Correct. $T \propto c_{rms}^2$, so $T_2 = 1.2^2 \times 350 \approx 500\ \mathrm{K}$.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q17.body:
The force on a charge in the field is $F = qE$. The field is uniform, so $E$ is constant, and the proton and electron have the same magnitude of charge. So the proton experiences the same magnitude of force as the electron, making C the incorrect statement.

The other statements are correct. A: the electric force does positive work on both particles, and $W_{\text{by field}} = -\Delta U$, so both lose electric potential energy. B: the proton feels the same force but has a larger mass, so it has a smaller acceleration and a smaller deflection; the work done on it is smaller, giving a smaller $|\Delta U|$. D: the proton loses less electric potential energy, so by conservation of energy it gains less kinetic energy.

perOption.A: True statement: the field does positive work on both particles, so both lose electric potential energy.
perOption.B: True statement: equal force but larger mass gives a smaller deflection, so less work is done and $|\Delta U|$ is smaller.
perOption.C: Correct (this is the incorrect statement). $F = qE$ is the same in magnitude for both, since $|q|$ and $E$ are equal.
perOption.D: True statement: the proton loses less potential energy, so by conservation of energy it gains less kinetic energy.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q18.body:
Both resistors are connected directly across the supply, so they are in parallel.

$R_{\text{eff}} = \left(\dfrac{1}{1300} + \dfrac{1}{1900}\right)^{-1} = 772\ \Omega$

$I = \dfrac{240}{772} = 0.31\ \mathrm{A}$

$P_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{240^2}{1300} + \dfrac{240^2}{1900} = 75\ \mathrm{W}$

perOption.A: Treats the resistors as being in series: $240/3200 = 0.075\ \mathrm{A}$ and $240^2/3200 = 18\ \mathrm{W}$.
perOption.B: Series current $240/3200 = 0.075\ \mathrm{A}$ is wrong; the resistors are in parallel.
perOption.C: Series power $240^2/3200 = 18\ \mathrm{W}$ is wrong; each parallel resistor has the full 240 V across it.
perOption.D: Correct. In parallel, $I = 240/772 = 0.31\ \mathrm{A}$ and $P = 75\ \mathrm{W}$.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q19.body:
At about $2.4\ \mathrm{V}$ the graphs of the diode and the lamp intersect, so they have the same $V$ and $I$ there.

Since $R = V/I$, the diode and the lamp have the same resistance at that voltage.

perOption.A: Above 1.8 V the diode's graph is roughly straight but does not pass through the origin, so $V/I$ still changes.
perOption.B: At 2.0 V the lamp has $2.0/0.4 = 5\ \Omega$ and the resistor $2.0/0.2 = 10\ \Omega$, so the lamp's resistance is half, not twice.
perOption.C: Correct. The lamp and diode curves cross near 2.4 V, so $V/I$ is equal there.
perOption.D: At 2.0 V the diode and resistor share a point (10 Ω), but the lamp is at 0.4 A (5 Ω); no voltage has all three equal.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q20.body:
The voltmeter measures the p.d. across the fixed resistor, which is in series with the LDR and thermistor (in parallel). For the voltmeter reading to be highest, the combined resistance of the thermistor and LDR must be lowest (potential divider principle).

High brightness (high light intensity) gives the LDR its lowest resistance, and high temperature gives the NTC thermistor its lowest resistance.

perOption.A: Low temperature gives the thermistor a high resistance, so the fixed resistor gets a smaller share of the e.m.f.
perOption.B: Correct. Both the LDR and the thermistor have their lowest resistance, so the fixed resistor takes the largest p.d.
perOption.C: Low brightness and low temperature both raise the resistances, giving the lowest voltmeter reading.
perOption.D: Low brightness gives the LDR a high resistance, so the fixed resistor gets a smaller share of the e.m.f.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q21.body:
The electron moves to the left, so the equivalent conventional current (middle finger) is to the right.

Using the right-hand grip rule for the upward current in the wire, the magnetic field at the electron (left of the wire) is out of the paper.

Applying Fleming's left-hand rule with field out of the paper and conventional current to the right, the force on the electron is vertically downwards.

perOption.A: The force must be perpendicular to the field, which is into/out of the paper here, so it cannot be into the paper.
perOption.B: Out of the paper is the direction of the magnetic field at the electron, not of the force.
perOption.C: Correct. Field out of paper, conventional current to the right, so the force is downwards.
perOption.D: This is the force on a positive charge moving left; the electron's negative charge reverses it.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q21.issues: The school's working is cut off mid-sentence ('force on electron'); the final step (force vertically downwards) was completed to match the key letter C. The key also says 'Flemming's left hand grip rule', rewritten as Fleming's left-hand rule.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q22.body:
For the wire to start to lift off, the magnetic force must equal the weight of the wire.

$mg = BIL\sin\theta$

$0.004(9.81) = 0.040(0.30)(\sin 30^\circ)\,I$

$I = 6.54 \approx 6.5\ \mathrm{A}$

perOption.A: Ignores the angle (takes $\sin\theta = 1$), giving 3.3 A.
perOption.B: Correct. $I = mg/(BL\sin 30^\circ) = 6.5\ \mathrm{A}$.
perOption.C: Uses 0.04 kg instead of 0.004 kg for 4.0 g and also ignores the $\sin 30^\circ$ factor.
perOption.D: Uses 0.04 kg instead of 0.004 kg for the 4.0 g mass.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q23.body:
The induced e.m.f. is $\varepsilon = BLv\cos\theta$, where $v$ is the rod's speed at the bottom of the slope (only the component of velocity perpendicular to the vertical field counts).

To find $v$: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as = 0 + 2(g\sin\theta)y$, so $v = \sqrt{2yg\sin\theta}$.

Hence $\varepsilon = BL\sqrt{2yg}\,\left(\sqrt{\sin\theta}\right)\cos\theta$.

Evaluating $\sqrt{\sin\theta}\cos\theta$: $35^\circ$ gives $0.620$, $40^\circ$ gives $0.614$, $45^\circ$ gives $0.595$, $50^\circ$ gives $0.563$. So $35^\circ$ gives the largest e.m.f.

perOption.A: Correct. $\sqrt{\sin\theta}\cos\theta = 0.620$ is the largest of the four.
perOption.B: $\sqrt{\sin 40^\circ}\cos 40^\circ = 0.614$, slightly smaller than at $35^\circ$.
perOption.C: $\sqrt{\sin 45^\circ}\cos 45^\circ = 0.595$; maximising $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ (forgetting the square root on speed) would wrongly favour $45^\circ$.
perOption.D: $\sqrt{\sin 50^\circ}\cos 50^\circ = 0.563$; a steeper slope gives more speed but a smaller perpendicular velocity component.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q24.body: Inserting an iron core concentrates the magnetic field lines and gives better flux linkage between coils P and Q. The flux linkage through both coils is larger, so the amplitude of the voltage induced in coil Q increases, while the frequency stays at 50 Hz.

perOption.A: Increasing the frequency raises the amplitude in Q (faster rate of change of flux linkage), but the number of cycles per unit time also increases.
perOption.B: According to the school, decreasing the cross-sectional area of coil P does not change the flux density it produces, so the flux linkage does not increase.
perOption.C: Fewer turns in Q gives a lower amplitude, since $V_Q/V_P = N_Q/N_P$.
perOption.D: Correct. The iron core increases the flux linkage without changing the frequency.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q24.issues: Key's reason for option B (no change in flux linkage) is debatable: a smaller coil P would reduce the flux linking Q. Either way B does not increase the amplitude, so the answer D is unaffected.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q25.body:
Mean power is $V_{\text{rms}}^2/R$ for each waveform:

A (sinusoid): $\dfrac{(60/\sqrt{2})^2}{8.0} = 225\ \mathrm{W}$

B (half-wave sinusoid): $\tfrac{1}{2}(225) = 112.5\ \mathrm{W}$

C (square wave): $\dfrac{60^2}{8.0} = 450\ \mathrm{W}$

D (square wave, on half the time): $\tfrac{1}{2}(450) = 225\ \mathrm{W}$

Only C gives $450\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: A sinusoid of peak 60 V has $V_{\text{rms}} = 60/\sqrt{2}$, giving only 225 W.
perOption.B: The half-wave sinusoid gives half of 225 W, i.e. 112.5 W.
perOption.C: Correct. A ±60 V square wave has $V_{\text{rms}} = 60\ \mathrm{V}$, so $P = 60^2/8.0 = 450\ \mathrm{W}$.
perOption.D: The voltage is zero for half of each cycle, so the mean power is half of 450 W, i.e. 225 W.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q26.body:
Current from the a.c. supply flows in both directions around the circuit as the supply alternates.

However, the arrangement of the four diodes (a bridge) makes the current through R flow only upward in both half-cycles. So both halves of each cycle appear across R with the same polarity: a full-wave rectified trace.

perOption.A: Shows the unrectified a.c.; the diodes stop the current through R from ever reversing.
perOption.B: Correct. Both half-cycles pass through R in the same direction (full-wave rectification).
perOption.C: This is half-wave rectification from a single diode; the bridge conducts during both half-cycles.
perOption.D: Assumes the diodes block all current; in each half-cycle one pair of diodes conducts through R.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q26.issues: Key gives only a brief qualitative explanation. Full-wave bridge rectification is slightly beyond the 9478 outcome (single-diode half-wave).

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q27.body:
Find the speed from the kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 9.3 \times 10^{-16}$, so $\frac{1}{2}(9.11 \times 10^{-31})v^2 = 9.3 \times 10^{-16}$, giving $v = 4.52 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Then $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{(9.11 \times 10^{-31})(4.52 \times 10^{7})} = 1.6 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Too large by a factor of about 30; does not follow from $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2mE_k}$ with the given energy.
perOption.B: Correct. $\lambda = h/mv$ with $v$ found from the kinetic energy.
perOption.C: Off by a factor of about 3; arises from a slip such as omitting the factor 2 or the square root in $p = \sqrt{2mE_k}$.
perOption.D: Treats the electron like a photon, using $\lambda = hc/E$.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q28.body:
Use $\Delta x \Delta p \approx h$: $(7.2 \times 10^{-9})(\Delta p) \approx 6.63 \times 10^{-34}$, so $\Delta p \approx 9.2 \times 10^{-26}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

The uncertainty in position is the slit width, which lies along the $y$-direction, so the uncertainty in momentum is also in the $y$-direction. This sideways spread in momentum is what spreads the electrons out into a diffraction pattern.

perOption.A: Wrong magnitude (a powers-of-ten slip with the nm) and wrong direction: the slit width is along $y$, not $x$.
perOption.B: Right direction, but the magnitude comes from a powers-of-ten slip when converting 7.2 nm.
perOption.C: Right magnitude, but the position uncertainty (slit width) is along $y$, so $\Delta p$ is along $y$, not along the beam.
perOption.D: Correct. $\Delta p \approx h/\Delta y$, perpendicular to the beam.

tmjc-2025-other-p1-q29.body:
Most α-particles pass through undeflected or with only small deflections, so the chance of an α-particle getting close to the positive charge is small: the atom is mostly empty space.
