perOption.A: Gives only the uncertainty in $d$ ($0.17\%$), without the factor of 3 from $d^3$.
perOption.B: Uses a factor of 2 in place of 3 for the power of $d$.
perOption.C: Correct. Three times the fractional uncertainty in $d$.
perOption.D: Overestimates the uncertainty, e.g. using the radius with the full 0.01 mm uncertainty or an extra factor.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q2.body:
The express train overtakes the goods train at time $t$ when both have the same displacement from the station.

Goods train: $s_1 = ut = 10t$

Express train: $s_2 = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2}(0.50)t^2$

Setting $s_1 = s_2$: $10t = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.50)t^2$, so $t = 40\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Not the time at which the two displacements are equal.
perOption.B: Not the time at which the two displacements are equal; at 10 s the express train has covered only 25 m against the goods train's 100 m.
perOption.C: This is when the two trains have equal speeds (or results from dropping the ½ in $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$); the express train is still behind at that moment.
perOption.D: Correct. Equal displacements give $10t = 0.25t^2$.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q3.body:
The force in question is the backward push by the back wheel on the road.

Its Newton's third law (action–reaction) partner acts on the other body, the back wheel, and is the forward push of the road on the back wheel.

perOption.A: Acts between the cyclist and the pedals, not between the wheel and the road.
perOption.B: Correct. Same pair of bodies, equal magnitude, opposite direction.
perOption.C: Involves the front wheel, a different contact; third-law pairs act between the same two bodies.
perOption.D: These forces balance the driving force on the bicycle (Newton's first law), but they are not its third-law pair.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q4.body:
Consider the whole system (7.0 kg) along the string:

$\Sigma F = ma$: $(5)(9.81) - (2)(9.81)\sin 30^\circ - 7.0 = 7a$, so $a = 4.61\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

Now the 5.0 kg block alone: $(5)(9.81) - T = 5(4.61)$, so $T = 26\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The hanging block accelerates downward, so $T < 5g$.
perOption.B: Not consistent with the system's acceleration of $4.61\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; check the forces on each block.
perOption.C: Too large; the tension must be less than the 49 N weight by $ma = 23\ \mathrm{N}$.
perOption.D: Equals the weight of the 5.0 kg block, which would only hold if it were not accelerating.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q5.body:
The load (weight $W$) is constant and the pivot is fixed, a distance $h$ from the load.

Taking moments about the pivot: $Wh = Fx$.

$Wh$ is constant since $W$ and $h$ are constant, so $Fx$ = constant and $F \propto 1/x$. Graph B shows this relationship.

perOption.A: A straight line with negative gradient would mean $F$ decreases linearly, not $F \propto 1/x$.
perOption.B: Correct. $Fx$ is constant, an inverse-proportion curve.
perOption.C: $F$ decreases, not increases, as its moment arm $x$ grows.
perOption.D: $F$ must fall as $x$ increases, since a larger arm needs a smaller force for the same moment.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q6.body:
The cylinder is in equilibrium under three forces: $R$, $W$ and the tension in the thread.

For a body in equilibrium under three non-parallel forces, their lines of action must pass through a common point. Only in option C do all three lines meet at one point.

perOption.A: The lines of action of the three forces do not meet at a single point, so there is a resultant torque.
perOption.B: The thread's line of action does not pass through the point where $R$ and $W$ meet.
perOption.C: Correct. $R$, $W$ and the tension are concurrent.
perOption.D: The three lines of action do not pass through a common point.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q7.body:
C: An electric heater's purpose is to produce thermal energy, and all the electrical energy input can end up as thermal energy, so it can be 100% efficient.

A: The velocity changes direction on bouncing, but kinetic energy has no direction and stays positive.

B: The engine's power equals the gravitational potential energy gained per unit time plus the rate of work done against friction.

D: Momentum must be conserved in a collision (for an isolated system).

perOption.A: Kinetic energy is a scalar and is never negative; only velocity changes sign.
perOption.B: Ignores the rate of work done against friction on the rough slope.
perOption.C: Correct. All the electrical energy can be converted to the desired thermal energy.
perOption.D: Momentum is always conserved in a collision of an isolated system.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q8.body:
In uniform circular motion, the net force (the centripetal force) points towards the centre of the circle.

There is no displacement in the direction of the net force, since it is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the work done by $F$ is zero.

perOption.A: Correct. Centripetal force is perpendicular to the motion, so it does no work.
perOption.B: $\pi rF$ treats the force as acting along the path; it is perpendicular to it.
perOption.C: The net force is centripetal, towards the centre, not outwards.
perOption.D: Wrong direction, and the force does no work since it is perpendicular to the velocity.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q9.body:
The glue will snap at the lowest position of the vertical circle, where the tension it must supply is greatest.

At the bottom: $T - W = mr\omega^2$

$18 - 3 = \left(\dfrac{3}{9.81}\right)(0.85)\,\omega^2$

$\omega = 7.6\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Uses the weight 3.0 N as the mass instead of $m = W/g$.
perOption.B: Correct. Snapping occurs first at the lowest point.
perOption.C: Uses $T + W = mr\omega^2$, the condition at the top, where the glue tension is smallest.
perOption.D: This is $\omega^2$, not $\omega$.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q10.body:
Moving at right angles to a vertical gravitational field means the object stays at the same level as before.

Since the field is uniform, there is no change in the gravitational potential energy of the object.

perOption.A: GPE decreases only if the object moves down, along the field.
perOption.B: Correct. No displacement along the field, so no work is done by gravity.
perOption.C: GPE increases only with an upward displacement against the field.
perOption.D: No dependence on horizontal displacement at all in a uniform vertical field.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q11.body:
The heater supplies energy at constant power, so a longer flat section means a longer time and therefore more energy transferred.

Q is melting and S is boiling. Since S is longer than Q, the specific latent heat of vaporisation is larger than the specific latent heat of fusion.

perOption.A: Gradients of the sloped sections relate to specific heat capacities, not latent heats.
perOption.B: Correct. The plateau length is proportional to the latent heat absorbed for the same mass.
perOption.C: Compares heating rates of ice and water, which depend on specific heat capacities.
perOption.D: U and V are the boiling and melting points; temperatures say nothing about latent heats.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q12.body:
Apply $pV = nRT$ to the total amount of gas after the tap is opened:

$(3.9\times10^{5})(2.5 + 1.6)\times10^{3}\times10^{-6} = (0.34 + 0.20)(8.31)\,T$

$T = 360\ \mathrm{K}$

perOption.A: Not consistent with $pV = nRT$ for the combined gas.
perOption.B: Correct. Total volume and total moles give $T \approx 356\ \mathrm{K}$.
perOption.C: Not consistent with $pV = nRT$ for the combined gas.
perOption.D: Not consistent with $pV = nRT$ for the combined gas; check the volume conversion and total moles.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q13.body:
Amplitude: $x_0 = 600/4 = 150\ \mathrm{mm} = 0.150\ \mathrm{m}$ (one oscillation covers four amplitudes).

Frequency: $f = 50/47 = 1.064\ \mathrm{Hz}$, so $\omega = 2\pi f = 6.684\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

Max KE $= \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2x_0^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(5.0\times10^{-3})(6.684)^2(0.150)^2 = 2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J}$

perOption.A: Uses $f = 47/50$ (inverting the frequency).
perOption.B: Correct. $x_0 = 0.150\ \mathrm{m}$ and $\omega = 6.684\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Results from an incorrect amplitude or angular frequency.
perOption.D: Omits the factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in the kinetic energy.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q14.body:
$v = f\lambda$: $24 = 15\lambda$, so $\lambda = 1.6\ \mathrm{m}$.

Phase difference $= \dfrac{2.0}{1.6} = 1.25$ cycles.

A whole cycle adds nothing, so the two points 2.0 m apart have a phase difference of a quarter of a cycle.

perOption.A: Only true if the separation were a whole number of wavelengths.
perOption.B: Correct. 1.25 cycles is equivalent to 0.25 cycle.
perOption.C: Would need a separation of an odd number of half-wavelengths.
perOption.D: Uses $\lambda/d = 1.6/2.0$ instead of $d/\lambda$.

perOption.A: The source-to-slit distance does not appear in $x = \lambda D/a$.
perOption.B: Correct. $x \propto D$.
perOption.C: $x \propto 1/a$, so a larger slit separation reduces the fringe spacing.
perOption.D: Higher frequency means shorter wavelength, which reduces the fringe spacing.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q16.body:
For single-slit diffraction, the first minimum is at $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{b} = \dfrac{600\times10^{-9}}{0.20\times10^{-3}}$, so $\theta = 0.0030\ \mathrm{rad}$.

Distance from centre to first minimum: $s = r\theta = 2.0\times0.0030 = 0.0060\ \mathrm{m}$.

Width of central maximum $\approx 2s = 2\times0.0060 = 0.012\ \mathrm{m} = 12\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: This is the angle $\theta$ in radians (0.0030), not a width on the screen.
perOption.B: Misreads $s = 0.0060\ \mathrm{m}$ as millimetres.
perOption.C: This is $s$, the half-width; the central maximum spans from one first minimum to the other.
perOption.D: Correct. Width $= 2D\lambda/b$.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q17.body:
Q has no net force, so the force on $Q$ from the 4.0 C charge equals the force from the 9.0 C charge. Q is $x$ from the 9.0 C charge and $(1-x)$ from the 4.0 C charge:

$\dfrac{4.0Q}{(1-x)^2} = \dfrac{9.0Q}{x^2}$, so $\dfrac{x^2}{(1-x)^2} = \dfrac{9}{4}$

Taking square roots, $\dfrac{x}{1-x} = \dfrac{3}{2}$, giving $x = 0.60\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses $x/(1-x) = 4/9$ with no square root, which also puts the charges the wrong way round.
perOption.B: This is the distance from the 4.0 C charge, $1 - x$, not from the 9.0 C charge.
perOption.C: Correct. Equal Coulomb forces give $x/(1-x) = 3/2$.
perOption.D: Uses $x/(1-x) = 9/4$, forgetting that the force depends on $1/r^2$.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q18.body:
The drop is stationary, so the net force on it is zero: electric force = weight.

$\dfrac{qV}{d} = mg$, so $ne = \dfrac{mgd}{V}$ and $n = \dfrac{mgd}{eV}$.

perOption.A: This is the reciprocal of the correct expression.
perOption.B: Correct. From $neV/d = mg$.
perOption.C: Multiplies by $mV$ instead of using $E = V/d$ and balancing the force with $mg$.
perOption.D: Wrongly places $m$ and $V$ in the denominator together, which is dimensionally inconsistent.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q19.body:
For X: $R = \dfrac{\rho L}{A_X} = \dfrac{\rho L}{V/L} = \dfrac{\rho L^2}{V}$, where $V$ is the volume.

For Y the volume is the same, so $A_Y = V/2L$: $R_Y = \dfrac{\rho(2L)}{V/2L} = \dfrac{4\rho L^2}{V}$.

The metal is the same, so $\rho$ is the same. Therefore $R_Y = 4R$.

perOption.A: Assumes that keeping the volume constant keeps the resistance constant.
perOption.B: Doubles the length but forgets that the cross-sectional area halves.
perOption.C: Correct. Length doubles and area halves, so $R \propto L^2$.
perOption.D: Treats the area as quartering, as if the diameter halved, instead of halving.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q20.body:
$I = \dfrac{E}{R + r}$. $E$ and $R$ are constant, so increasing $r$ decreases the current $I$.

Terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir = E - \dfrac{E}{R+r}r = \dfrac{ER}{R+r}$. So increasing $r$ also decreases $V$.

perOption.A: Correct. Both $I = E/(R+r)$ and $V = ER/(R+r)$ fall as $r$ rises.
perOption.B: The current cannot rise, because the total resistance $R + r$ increases.
perOption.C: Treats $V$ as if it were the p.d. across $r$; the terminal p.d. $V = IR$ falls with $I$.
perOption.D: Both quantities fall, not rise, because the total resistance increases.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q21.body:
The 70 Ω resistor is in parallel with the series branch of 50 Ω, 30 Ω and 60 Ω. Call their currents $I_1$ and $I_2$.

Equal p.d.s: $70 I_1 = (50+30+60) I_2 = 140 I_2$, so $I_1 = 2I_2$.

With $I_1 + I_2 = 1.5$, solving gives $I_2 = 0.50\ \mathrm{A}$. This is the current through the 30 Ω resistor.

perOption.A: Shares the current in proportion to $30/210$ instead of finding the branch currents.
perOption.B: Correct. The 140 Ω branch carries one third of 1.5 A.
perOption.C: Assumes the current splits equally between the two branches.
perOption.D: This is the current in the 70 Ω branch, $I_1$.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q22.body:
Use the right-hand grip rule at Q. A current into the plane at Q produces clockwise field lines, so at O, to the left of Q, the field points along OY.

The current cannot be at P, because a wire at P would produce a horizontal (along OX) field at O.

perOption.A: A wire at P on the OY axis gives a field at O along OX (horizontal), not along OY.
perOption.B: A wire at P gives a horizontal field at O, whatever the current direction.
perOption.C: Correct. With the grip rule, a current into the plane at Q gives an upward field at O.
perOption.D: A current out of the plane at Q gives a field at O along $-$OY (downwards).

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q23.body:
If the current in Y is doubled, the B-field at X due to Y doubles. The B-field at Y due to X is unaffected.

The force on X doubles, because the field at X due to Y has doubled. The force on Y also doubles, because the current in Y has doubled. This agrees with Newton's third law.

So the diagram shows $2B_Y$, $B_X$ and $2F$ on each wire.

perOption.A: The forces are a Newton's third law pair, so the force on X must also be $2F$. Also, $B_Y$ should double.
perOption.B: The field at X due to Y should double to $2B_Y$, since Y's current doubled.
perOption.C: $B_X$ depends only on the current in X, so it stays $B_X$. The force on Y must also be $2F$.
perOption.D: Correct. Only Y's field doubles, and both forces double equally.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q25.body:
At half the speed the rate of change of flux linkage halves, so the induced e.m.f. and current are smaller: less than 10 units.

Pushing a N pole into the left end makes the coil act as a magnet with N at that end. Pushing a S pole into the right end makes the right end S, which is the same N–S polarity of the coil. So the induced current is in the same direction and the needle again moves to the left.

perOption.A: Correct. Same current direction, smaller rate of flux change.
perOption.B: The direction does not reverse. Reversing the pole and the end together gives the same induced polarity in the coil.
perOption.C: Half the speed gives a smaller e.m.f., not a larger one.
perOption.D: Both the direction and the size are wrong: the deflection is to the left and smaller.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q26.body:
Mean power in the a.c. resistor $= I_\mathrm{rms}^2 R = (2.0)^2 R = 4R$.

Mean power with the steady current $= I^2(2R) = 4R$, so $I^2 = 2$ and $I = 1.4\ \mathrm{A}$.

perOption.A: Introduces an extra factor of $1/2$, for example by treating 2.0 A as a peak value and halving again.
perOption.C: Ignores that the steady current flows through $2R$, not $R$.
perOption.D: Doubles the current instead of using $I^2 \propto 1/R$ at equal power.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q27.body:
(A) Electron diffraction is evidence for the wave nature of particles.

(B) and (C) Diffraction and interference of light are evidence for the wave nature of electromagnetic radiation.

(D) A threshold frequency for photoelectric emission is evidence for the particulate (photon) nature of electromagnetic radiation.

perOption.A: Electron diffraction shows the wave nature of particles, not the particle nature of radiation.
perOption.B: Diffraction is evidence for the wave nature of electromagnetic radiation.
perOption.C: Interference is evidence for the wave nature of electromagnetic radiation.
perOption.D: Correct. The threshold frequency shows that energy arrives in photons of $hf$.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q28.body:
$E_p = \Phi + KE_\mathrm{max}$, where the work function is $\Phi = hf_0$ and $KE_\mathrm{max} = eV_s$.

$6.63\times10^{-34} f = (6.63\times10^{-34})(4.0\times10^{14}) + (1.6\times10^{-19})(1.5)$

$f = 7.6\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$

perOption.A: A power-of-ten or arithmetic slip; $f$ must exceed the threshold of $4.0\times10^{14}$ Hz.
perOption.B: This is only the $eV_s/h$ term. It omits the threshold frequency.
perOption.C: Too small an increase above the threshold for a 1.5 V stopping potential, likely from a unit slip with eV.
perOption.D: Correct. $f = f_0 + eV_s/h$.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q29.body: The $\alpha$-particles are deflected by the nuclei of the metal atoms in the foil. These nuclei are small, heavy and positively charged, so a few $\alpha$-particles are deflected through large angles, up to $180^\circ$.

perOption.A: Electrons are far too light to deflect massive $\alpha$-particles through large angles.
perOption.B: Most $\alpha$-particles pass straight through the foil, so surface reflection cannot explain the spread of angles.
perOption.C: The de Broglie wavelength of the $\alpha$-particles is far too small for lattice diffraction to give large-angle deviation.
perOption.D: Correct. Small, massive, positively charged nuclei cause the large-angle scattering.

yijc-2023-prelim-p1-q30.body:
If a 10 g sample of ancient wood gives 50 counts per minute, a 5 g sample of it would give 25 counts per minute.

So for the same mass, the ancient wood's count rate is $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of the living wood's (100 counts per minute). Two half-lives have passed, so the age is $2 \times 5600 = 11200$ years.

perOption.A: Divides the half-life by 4 instead of counting half-lives.
perOption.B: Compares 50 with 100 directly without correcting for the different masses, giving one half-life.
perOption.C: Correct. Per unit mass the activity has fallen to $\tfrac{1}{4}$, which is two half-lives.
perOption.D: Takes four half-lives, confusing a factor of 4 with the number of half-lives.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q1.body:
Surface area of the open cylinder: $A = 2\pi rL = 282.7\ \mathrm{cm^2}$.

$\dfrac{\Delta A}{A} = \dfrac{\Delta r}{r} + \dfrac{\Delta L}{L}$, so $\Delta A = \left(\dfrac{0.1}{3.0} + \dfrac{0.1}{15.0}\right)(282.7) = 10\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ (to 1 s.f.).

Therefore $A = (280 \pm 10)\ \mathrm{cm^2}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Fractional uncertainties add to 4%, and the value is rounded to match the uncertainty.
perOption.B: Adds the absolute uncertainties instead of the fractional ones, and quotes too many significant figures.
perOption.C: Calculates the volume $\pi r^2 L$, not the curved surface area.
perOption.D: Calculates the volume $\pi r^2 L$ with a wrongly propagated uncertainty and too many significant figures.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q2.body:
During free fall: $v = u + at = 0 + (-9.81)(1.0) = -9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

On hitting the sand: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, so $0 = (-9.81)^2 + 2a(8.0\times10^{-3})$, giving $a = -6.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

The average deceleration is $6.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

perOption.A: A power-of-ten slip when converting 8.0 mm to metres.
perOption.B: Uses $v$ instead of $v^2$, or another arithmetic slip; $v^2/2s$ gives about $6\times10^3$.
perOption.D: Omits the factor of 2 in $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q2.issues: Key working labels the impact velocity unit as m s^-2 (typo for m s^-1); corrected in the explanation.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q3.body:
Treat car and trailer as one system: $F_{net} = 5600 - 1200 - 400 = 4000\ \mathrm{N}$, so $a = \frac{4000}{1500+500} = 2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

Now consider the trailer alone: $F_{net} = m_{trailer}a = 500(2.0) = 1000\ \mathrm{N}$.

Since $F_{net} = T - f_{trailer}$: $1000 = T - 400$, so $T = 1400\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: The trailer accelerates against a 400 N resistance, so the coupling must pull on it.
perOption.B: Correct. $T = m_{trailer}a + f_{trailer} = 1000 + 400$.
perOption.C: Finds the acceleration ignoring all resistive forces ($2.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$), then adds the trailer's resistance.
perOption.D: Applies Newton's second law to the car but forgets the car's own 1200 N resistance ($5600 - 1500 \times 2.0$).

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q4.body:
Take moments about P: the weight acts further from P than the tension (which equals it), so the weight's clockwise moment is larger. The force at Q must be upwards to balance it.

Take moments about Q: the tension acts further from Q than the weight, giving a larger (clockwise about Q) moment from the tension. The force at P must be downwards to balance it.

perOption.A: If both sockets pushed up, the total upward force would exceed the weight, since tension already equals weight.
perOption.B: Reverses both directions; moments about P show Q must push up, not down.
perOption.C: Correct. Moments about P and about Q fix Q upwards and P downwards.
perOption.D: Two downward socket forces cannot balance moments about P, where the weight's moment exceeds the tension's.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q5.body:
Hooke's law holds along the straight-line section, up to a length of 40 mm where $F = 70\ \mathrm{N}$. The extension is measured from the natural length of 20 mm.

$EPE = \frac{1}{2}Fx = \frac{1}{2}(70)(0.040 - 0.020) = 0.70\ \mathrm{J}$

perOption.A: Unit-conversion slip in the extension.
perOption.B: Correct. Area under the linear section: $\frac{1}{2}(70)(0.020)$.
perOption.C: Forgets the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ (uses $Fx$ instead of the triangle area).
perOption.D: Leaves the extension in mm instead of converting to m.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q6.body:
The component of weight along the slope is $W\sin30^\circ = (1.0\times10^3)(0.50) = 0.50\times10^3\ \mathrm{N}$.

At constant velocity the applied force equals this component, so $WD = Fx = (0.50\times10^3)(5.0) = 2500\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $F = W\sin30^\circ$, $WD = 500 \times 5.0$.
perOption.B: Uses $W\cos30^\circ$ (the normal component) instead of $W\sin30^\circ$.
perOption.C: Uses the full weight as the applied force.
perOption.D: Divides by $\sin30^\circ$ instead of multiplying.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q7.body:
Useful work done in lifting the weight $= (480)(3.5) = 1680\ \mathrm{J}$.

Work done by the man pulling the rope $= (200)(10.5) = 2100\ \mathrm{J}$.

Efficiency $= \frac{1680}{2100}\times100\% = 80\%$

perOption.A: Does not follow from useful output over input work.
perOption.B: Does not follow from useful output over input work.
perOption.C: Does not follow from useful output over input work.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q8.body:
The period of the sound wave is $T = \frac{1}{f}$, the time for the disc to turn from one hole to the next.

Angle between successive holes: $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{16} = \frac{\pi}{8}\ \mathrm{rad}$.

$\omega = \frac{\theta}{T} = \theta f = \frac{\pi}{8}(2200) = 864\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$

perOption.A: Uses $\pi/16$ instead of $2\pi/16$ for the angle between holes.
perOption.B: Correct. $\omega = (\pi/8)(2200) \approx 860\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
perOption.C: Doubles the correct angle between holes (uses $2\pi/8$).
perOption.D: Does not divide the full-revolution angle correctly among the 16 holes.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q9.body:
Using $KE = \frac{GMm}{2R}$ and $TE = -\frac{GMm}{2R}$, both satellites have the same total energy if their KE is equal. Hence A is false.

Since KE is the same, the satellite's mass is proportional to $R$, so X (larger mass) has a larger orbital radius: B is valid.

Kepler's third law then gives X a larger period, and since angular velocity is inversely proportional to period, X has a smaller angular velocity.

perOption.A: Correct (this is the false statement). $TE = -KE$, so equal KE means equal total energy.
perOption.B: True: equal $\frac{GMm}{2R}$ means $R \propto m$, so X orbits further out.
perOption.C: True: larger radius gives larger period by Kepler's third law ($T^2 \propto R^3$).
perOption.D: True: larger period means smaller $\omega = 2\pi/T$.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q10.body:
Work done moving from X to Z: $W_{X\to Z} = 100 + (-120) = -20\ \mathrm{J}$.

Then $W_{X\to\infty} = -20 + 2000 = 1980\ \mathrm{J}$.

$\phi_X = \frac{W_{\infty\to X}}{m} = \frac{-W_{X\to\infty}}{2.0} = -990\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$

perOption.B: Sign error on the X-to-Z work ($+20$ instead of $-20$), giving $-2020/2.0$.
perOption.C: Subtracts the $-120$ J instead of adding it, giving $-2220/2.0$.
perOption.D: Forgets to divide by the 2.0 kg mass.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q11.body:
Heat supplied by kettle = heat absorbed by water + heat loss:

$(1.2\times10^3)(30\times60) = (0.80)(4.2\times10^3)(100-25) + (0.80)(2300\times10^3) + \text{heat loss}$

Heat loss $= 6.8\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}$, so power loss $= \frac{6.8\times10^4}{30\times60} = 38\ \mathrm{W}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $6.8\times10^4\ \mathrm{J}$ over 1800 s.
perOption.B: Does not match the energy balance; check heating plus latent-heat terms.
perOption.C: Omits the latent heat of vaporisation, so the 'loss' includes the boiling energy.
perOption.D: Confuses the latent heat value with the power.

perOption.A: Divides by $1.2^2$ instead of multiplying.
perOption.B: Divides by 1.2 instead of multiplying by $1.2^2$.
perOption.C: Assumes $T \propto c_{rms}$ rather than $T \propto c_{rms}^2$.
perOption.D: Correct. $T \propto c_{rms}^2$: $330 \times 1.44$.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q13.body: With greater damping, more energy is lost per cycle, so the amplitude of the forced oscillations is lower at all frequencies (the resonance peak is lower and flatter).

perOption.A: Correct. More damping reduces amplitude across the response curve.
perOption.B: Damping removes energy, so it cannot raise the amplitude.
perOption.C: Damping lowers the curve below resonance as well, especially at the peak.
perOption.D: Damping never increases amplitude.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q14.body:
Look for the minimum pattern that repeats: the distance between two successive tall peaks is 5 cm.

$T = (5\ \mathrm{cm})(2.00\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}) = 10\ \mathrm{ms}$, so $f = \frac{1}{10\times10^{-3}} = 100\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Takes two full repeats (10 cm) as one period.
perOption.B: Correct. Period 5 cm = 10 ms.
perOption.C: Uses 4 cm as the period, not the full repeating pattern.
perOption.D: Takes 2.5 cm (e.g. tall peak to small peak) as the period, missing that the pattern repeats only every 5 cm.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q15.body:
After the polariser is rotated to $45^\circ$, each emergent beam has amplitude $A' = A\cos45^\circ$.

Since the two beams arrive in phase, they superpose: total amplitude $= 2A' = 2A\cos45^\circ = \sqrt{2}A$.

Since $I \propto A^2$: $\frac{I_E}{I} = \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}A}{A}\right)^2 = 2$, so $I_E = 2I$.

perOption.A: Applies $\cos^2 45^\circ$ twice or halves the single-beam result.
perOption.B: Considers only one beam passing through ($I\cos^2 45^\circ$).
perOption.C: Adds the two transmitted intensities ($0.5I + 0.5I$) instead of adding amplitudes of the in-phase beams.
perOption.D: Correct. Coherent in-phase amplitudes add: $(\sqrt{2}A)^2 = 2A^2$.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q15.issues: Key answer 2I assumes the polariser is rotated 45° toward the direction of the combined (resultant) polarisation; rotating 45° the other way would give 0. The question wording ('angle of polarisation ... rotated to 45°') does not specify the sense of rotation, so the question is somewhat ambiguous.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q16.body:
The tube is closed at the bottom (node) and open at the top (antinode). The current pattern is $\frac{3}{4}\lambda$; the next higher resonance is $\frac{5}{4}\lambda$.

$\frac{5}{4}\lambda = 60\ \mathrm{cm} \Rightarrow \lambda = 48\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.48\ \mathrm{m}$

$v = f\lambda$: $330 = f(0.48)$, so $f = 688\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Fundamental ($\frac{1}{4}\lambda = 60$ cm), a lower resonance not a higher one.
perOption.B: The current resonance ($\frac{3}{4}\lambda = 60$ cm), not the next higher one.
perOption.C: Correct. $\frac{5}{4}\lambda = 0.60$ m gives 688 Hz.
perOption.D: Skips a harmonic ($\frac{7}{4}\lambda = 60$ cm).

perOption.A: Inverts the order ratio in some form instead of $\lambda_2 = \frac{5}{4}\lambda_1$.
perOption.B: Assumes the same wavelength despite different orders.
perOption.C: Correct. $5\lambda_1 = 4\lambda_2$.
perOption.D: Uses an incorrect ratio of orders (larger than 5/4).

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q18.body:
W (+2q) attracts X to the left and Y (+q) attracts X downwards. For the net force to act purely to the left, Q must exert a force on X that cancels the downward force from Y, so Q must repel X (push it up and to the right). Thus Q is negative.

The vertical component of the force on X by Q equals the force on X by Y. With side $r$, the diagonal ZX is $\sqrt{2}r$:

$k\dfrac{Qq}{(\sqrt{2}r)^2}\cos 45^\circ = k\dfrac{qq}{r^2} \Rightarrow Q = 2.8q$

Thus $Q = -2.8q$.

perOption.A: Correct. A negative Q of magnitude $2.8q$ exactly cancels the downward pull from Y.
perOption.B: Forgets that only the vertical component ($\cos 45^\circ$) of Q's force cancels Y's force, or omits the factor of 2 from the squared diagonal.
perOption.C: Wrong sign and wrong magnitude: a positive Q would attract X towards Z, adding to the downward force.
perOption.D: Right magnitude but wrong sign: a positive Q attracts X downwards, so the net force cannot be horizontal.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q19.body:
Work done on the charge by the external agent = change in potential energy = final EPE $-$ initial EPE.

$W = (-q)V_2 - (-q)V_1 = q(V_1 - V_2)$

perOption.A: Adds the potentials instead of taking the change in potential energy.
perOption.B: Treats the charge as negative but adds the two potential energies rather than subtracting initial from final.
perOption.C: Uses $+q$ instead of $-q$ for the charge, giving the wrong sign.
perOption.D: Correct. $\Delta U = (-q)(V_2 - V_1) = q(V_1 - V_2)$.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q20.body:
Wire P: $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{\pi (d/2)^2} = \dfrac{4\rho l}{\pi d^2}$, so $d^2 = \dfrac{4\rho l}{\pi R}$.

Wire Q: $\dfrac{1}{4}R = \dfrac{(\frac{1}{3}\rho)(2l)}{\pi (d_Q/2)^2} = \dfrac{2}{3}\dfrac{4\rho l}{\pi d_Q^2}$, so $d_Q^2 = \dfrac{8}{3}\dfrac{4\rho l}{\pi R} = \dfrac{8}{3}d^2$.

$d_Q = \sqrt{8/3}\,d = 1.6d$

perOption.A: Inverts the ratio, giving $\sqrt{3/8}\,d$.
perOption.B: Correct. $d_Q^2 = \frac{8}{3}d^2$.
perOption.C: Finds the area ratio $8/3$ and treats it as the diameter ratio, forgetting the square root.
perOption.D: Squares the ratio instead of taking its square root, giving $(8/3)^2 d$.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q21.body:
Using $E = Ir + IR$ for each setting:

$E = 3r + 3(1)$

$E = 2r + 2(2)$

Solving simultaneously gives $r = 1.0\ \Omega$ and $E = 6.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Takes the terminal p.d. in the first setting ($3.0 \times 1.0$) as the e.m.f., ignoring internal resistance.
perOption.B: Averages the two terminal p.d.s (3.0 V and 4.0 V) instead of accounting for the internal resistance.
perOption.C: Takes the terminal p.d. in the second setting ($2.0 \times 2.0$) as the e.m.f., ignoring internal resistance.
perOption.D: Correct. $r = 1.0\ \Omega$, so $E = 3.0(1.0 + 1.0) = 6.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q22.body:
Since the galvanometer reads zero when PS = 40.0 cm, the p.d. across PS = 5.00 mV.

A 40.0 cm length of wire has resistance $\dfrac{40.0}{100.0}(5.00) = 2.00\ \Omega$.

Using the potential divider rule on the driver circuit:

$\dfrac{2.0}{5.0 + R}(2.000) = 5.00 \times 10^{-3} \Rightarrow R = 795\ \Omega$

perOption.A: Gives a total driver resistance of $400\ \Omega$, so 5.0 mA flows and PS would have 10 mV across it, not 5.00 mV.
perOption.B: Correct. The driver current is 2.5 mA, so total resistance is 800 $\Omega$ and $R = 795\ \Omega$.
perOption.C: Gives a total driver resistance of $1000\ \Omega$, so 2.0 mA flows and PS would have only 4.0 mV across it.
perOption.D: Gives a total driver resistance of $1060\ \Omega$, so PS would have about 3.8 mV across it; balance would not occur at 40.0 cm.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q23.body:
$B_S = \mu_0 n I = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 15 \times 0.20$

$B_C = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2r} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 0.90}{2 \times 1.6}$

The currents circulate in opposite senses, so the fields at the centre are opposite: $B_{\text{resultant}} = B_S - B_C = 3.4 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{T}$.

perOption.A: Assumes the two fields cancel completely.
perOption.B: Uses the wrong formula for one of the fields (e.g. $\mu_0 I/2\pi r$ for the loop or omits $n$).
perOption.D: Adds the two fields, ignoring that the currents flow in opposite directions.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q24.body:
Parallel wires with currents in opposite directions repel; with currents in the same direction they attract.

PS carries current opposite to XY (repulsion) and QR carries current in the same direction as XY (attraction). Since PS is nearer to XY than QR, the repulsion is greater than the attraction, so the loop moves away from the long wire (to the right).

perOption.A: Assumes the attraction on QR dominates, ignoring that the field is stronger closer to the wire.
perOption.B: Correct. The nearer side PS is repelled more strongly than the farther side QR is attracted.
perOption.C: The forces on PS and QR are both in the plane and perpendicular to XY, and the forces on PQ and SR cancel, so there is no turning effect about an axis parallel to XY.
perOption.D: Assumes the forces on PS and QR cancel, but they differ because the field falls off with distance.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q25.body:
Using Fleming's left-hand rule, electrons in the conductor moving to the right experience an upward force in a magnetic field pointing out of the page. Electrons gather at R, so S is at the higher potential.

$\varepsilon = Blv = (2.8 \times 10^{-3})(15 \times 10^{-2} \times \sin 60^\circ)(10) = 3.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{V} = 3.6\ \mathrm{mV}$

Each quantity in the equation must be the components perpendicular to each other, so only the vertical length $l\sin 60^\circ$ counts.

perOption.A: Correct p.d., but the wrong end: the electrons are pushed towards R, making R negative.
perOption.B: Wrong end, and uses the full 15 cm length instead of its component perpendicular to the velocity.
perOption.C: Correct. Electrons collect at R, and $\varepsilon = B(l\sin 60^\circ)v = 3.6\ \mathrm{mV}$.
perOption.D: Correct end, but uses the full 15 cm length instead of the component perpendicular to the velocity.

perOption.A: Correct. Full-wave rectification keeps the r.m.s. value $I_0/\sqrt{2}$, and mean power is half the peak power.
perOption.B: Gives the peak current 7.5 A instead of the r.m.s. value.
perOption.C: Correct r.m.s. current, but uses peak power $I_0 V_0 = 1100\ \mathrm{W}$ instead of the mean.
perOption.D: Uses peak values for both current and power.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q27.body:
The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, $hf - \Phi$, depends only on the frequency of the light and the metal, not on the intensity, so C is correct.

A is wrong: electrons are ejected only if the wavelength is smaller than some maximum value. B is wrong: the de Broglie wavelength of the ejected electrons is not the same as the wavelength of the incident light. D is wrong: the maximum energy depends on the type of metal.

perOption.A: Reversed: electrons are ejected only if the wavelength is smaller than some maximum (threshold) value.
perOption.B: The de Broglie wavelength of the ejected electrons is not the same as the wavelength of the incident light.
perOption.C: Correct. Intensity changes only the number of photoelectrons, not their maximum energy.
perOption.D: The maximum energy depends on the type of metal through its work function.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q28.body:
B is correct: the wavelengths of the characteristic X-ray lines depend on the material used to make the target, not on the potential difference applied to the electrons.

A is wrong: most of the electrons' energy goes towards heating the metal target. C is wrong: $\dfrac{hc}{eV}$ is the minimum wavelength. D is wrong: the intensity of the X-ray spectrum increases when $V$ is increased.

perOption.A: Most of the electrons' energy is converted to heat in the target; only a small fraction becomes X-rays.
perOption.B: Correct. Characteristic lines come from transitions between the target atoms' energy levels.
perOption.C: $hc/eV$ is the minimum (cut-off) wavelength, not the maximum.
perOption.D: Increasing $V$ gives the electrons more energy, so the overall X-ray intensity increases.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q28.issues: X-ray spectra are not an explicit outcome in the 9478 syllabus; classified under quantum-physics without an outcome id.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q29.body:
As the nucleus is very small compared with the atom, there is a lot of empty space, so most alpha particles pass straight through.

When an $\alpha$-particle comes very close to a gold nucleus, it experiences a large repulsive force and so can be deviated through a large angle.

perOption.A: Large deflections are caused by electrostatic repulsion from the nucleus, not by particles bouncing off a dense surface.
perOption.B: Alpha particles pass through whole atoms (mostly empty space); they miss nuclei, not atoms, and are repelled rather than bouncing off atoms.
perOption.C: Correct. The tiny nucleus is rarely approached closely, but a close approach gives a large Coulomb repulsion.
perOption.D: Large-angle scattering shows the positive charge is concentrated; it is a single close encounter, not many small deflections.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q30.body:
An alpha decay changes the nucleon number by $-4$ and the proton number by $-2$; a beta decay leaves the nucleon number unchanged and adds $+1$ to the proton number.

Hence the new nuclide has nucleon number 234 and proton number $92 - 2 + 1 = 91$.

Its neutron number is therefore $234 - 91 = 143$.

perOption.A: Gives the nucleon number (234) instead of the neutron number.
perOption.B: Gives the nucleon number as the neutron number and ignores the $+1$ in proton number from beta decay.
perOption.C: Correct. Nucleon number 234, proton number 91, so neutron number 143.
perOption.D: Correct neutron number but forgets that beta decay raises the proton number by 1.

yijc-2024-prelim-p1-q30.issues: Key text says alpha decay gives '+2 in proton number'; it should be $-2$ (the final 91 is consistent with $-2$). Explanation corrected.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.body: Taking the cyclist’s mass as $80\ \mathrm{kg}$ and speed as $5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ gives $E_k=\tfrac12(80)(5)^2=1000\ \mathrm J$, so B is realistic. From $v=f\lambda$, a $10\ \mathrm m$ radio wave has frequency $3\times10^7\ \mathrm{Hz}$. An atom with mass number 1 to 200 has a mass of order $10^{-27}$ to $10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$, and a $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ car at $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ has momentum $1.2\times10^4\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: The frequency is far too low, with a $10\ \mathrm m$ radio wavelength giving $3\times10^7\ \mathrm{Hz}$.
perOption.B: Correct. A cyclist can have about $1\ \mathrm{kJ}$ of kinetic energy.
perOption.C: Atomic masses are typically of order $10^{-27}$ to $10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg}$.
perOption.D: The estimate is far too high, as $1000\ \mathrm{kg}$ at $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ gives $1.2\times10^4\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q1.issues: The key’s atom-mass line gives a single number for a range of mass numbers. The explanation expresses the resulting orders of magnitude as a range.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q2.body: Rearrange each set of force vectors tip to tail without changing their directions or lengths. Only D gives a closed vector triangle and hence zero resultant force, as required for equilibrium. A, B and C all give a nonzero resultant.

perOption.A: Both diagonal vectors have rightward components, so the horizontal forces cannot cancel.
perOption.B: The vertical and diagonal vectors both have downward components, with no upward component to balance them.
perOption.C: All three vectors have downward components, so the vertical forces cannot cancel.
perOption.D: Correct. The three vectors form a closed triangle when arranged tip to tail.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q3.body: As the person approaches Q, their clockwise moment about Q decreases. The balancing anticlockwise moment decreases, so the downward force at P decreases. The upward force at Q balances the two weights plus the downward force at P, so it also decreases.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The upward force at Q falls as the downward force at P falls.
perOption.C: The shorter moment arm reduces the downward force required at P.
perOption.D: Both forces decrease as the person's clockwise moment decreases.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q4.body: The person's weight is the gravitational force exerted by the Earth on the person. Its Newton's third-law partner is the gravitational force exerted by the person on the Earth.

perOption.A: Tension acts on the person and belongs to the rope–person interaction.
perOption.B: Upthrust acts on the person and belongs to the air–person interaction.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: This gravitational force pairs with the helicopter's pull on the person.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q5.body: For the falling stone, use $s=ut_1+\frac{1}{2}gt_1^2$ with zero initial speed to get $t_1=3.988\ \mathrm{s}$. The sound takes $t_2=78.0/330=0.236\ \mathrm{s}$ to travel back up the well. The total is $t_1+t_2=4.224\ \mathrm{s}$, which rounds to $4.22\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the sound travel time from the fall time.
perOption.B: Counts only the fall time.
perOption.C: Uses $g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, which gives a shorter fall time.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q6.body: The electrical input power multiplied by efficiency equals the gain in gravitational potential energy per unit time. Thus $P_\mathrm{in}=\frac{400\times9.81\times1200}{120}\div0.80=49\ \mathrm{kW}$.

perOption.A: Uses the efficiency factor in the wrong direction and is about a factor of ten below even that estimate.
perOption.B: Underestimates the correctly efficiency-adjusted power by a factor of ten.
perOption.C: Multiplies the useful power by efficiency instead of dividing.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.body: Both coins start with the same speed and fall through the same net height. By conservation of energy, they gain the same kinetic energy per unit mass and therefore hit the ground with the same speed.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Y rises before falling, so it travels a greater vertical distance.
perOption.C: Y takes longer to reach the ground because it initially moves upwards.
perOption.D: With negligible air resistance, both coins have the same downward acceleration.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q7.issues: The key equates the coins’ total energies without specifying equal masses. The energy comparison applies per unit mass.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q8.body: By Newton's third law, the particles exert equal and opposite forces on each other during the collision, so their momentum changes are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Hence $4|\Delta v_X|=9|\Delta v_Y|$, giving $\left|\frac{\Delta v_X}{\Delta v_Y}\right|=\frac{9}{4}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Takes a square root as if the momentum change depended on velocity squared.
perOption.C: Equates velocity changes despite the different masses.
perOption.D: Uses an inverted square-root mass ratio instead of the inverse mass ratio.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q9.body: Since $v=r\omega$ and $\omega$ is constant, the linear speed increases with radius. The centripetal acceleration $a=r\omega^2$ also increases with radius.

perOption.A: Treats linear speed as fixed and then predicts a decrease in centripetal acceleration.
perOption.B: Confuses constant angular velocity with constant linear speed.
perOption.C: Overlooks the radius factor in $a=r\omega^2$.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q11.body: Both satellites are at the same orbital radius, so they experience the same gravitational field strength and hence the same centripetal acceleration. Their gravitational forces differ because $F=mg$ and their masses differ. Their common period of about 24 hours gives the same angular velocity, so $v=r\omega$ gives the same speed, while their different masses give different kinetic energies.

perOption.A: This statement is true because $F=mg$ differs for the two masses at the same field strength.
perOption.B: Correct. Both satellites have the same centripetal acceleration magnitude.
perOption.C: This statement is true because both satellites have the same orbital period.
perOption.D: This statement is true because the satellites have equal speeds and different masses.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q12.body: Q's free oscillations die away faster, so Q is more strongly damped. Its frequency-response curve lies below P's at positive driving frequencies, which rules out A and B. Q has a lower peak at a slightly lower frequency than P.

perOption.A: Shows Q above P over parts of the frequency range.
perOption.B: Shows Q crossing above P and peaking at a higher frequency.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives the more strongly damped Q a taller peak.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.body: Zero initial transmission means the incident polarisation is perpendicular to the first filter's transmission axis. At the inserted second filter, $I_1=I_0\cos^2(90^\circ-40^\circ)=I_0\cos^2 50^\circ=0.413I_0$. At the original first filter, $I_2=I_1\cos^2 40^\circ=0.413I_0\times0.587=0.24I_0$.

perOption.A: Ignores the change in polarisation produced by the inserted filter.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses $40^\circ$ for both Malus’ law factors.
perOption.D: Stops at the intensity after the inserted filter.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q13.issues: The key’s last line labels the final intensity $I_1$ instead of $I_2$.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.body: Since $I=kA^2$, if the amplitude from $S_2$ is $A$, the amplitude from $S_1$ is $2A$. The resultant amplitude is $2A+A=3A$ at P and $2A-A=A$ at Q. Thus $\frac{I_P}{I_Q}=\frac{(3A)^2}{A^2}=9.0$.

perOption.A: Reverses the bright-to-dark intensity ratio.
perOption.B: Adds and subtracts intensities directly, giving $5/3$.
perOption.C: Uses the source intensity ratio without combining the waves.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q14.issues: The key labels the resultant amplitude at Q as $A_P$ in one line.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q15.body: Use $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$. At $\theta=90^\circ$, $\frac{1}{300\times1000}\sin90^\circ=n(690\times10^{-9})$, giving an order limit of about $4.83$. The highest observable integer order is $4$, so there are $4+1+4=9$ bright spots.

perOption.A: Counts the nonzero orders on only one side.
perOption.B: Omits the central maximum.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Rounds the order limit up to five even though the fifth order would require $\sin\theta>1$.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q16.body: At the same temperature, the molecules have the same mean translational kinetic energy, so $\frac12 m_1c_1^2=\frac12 m_2c_2^2$. Rearranging gives $\frac{c_1}{c_2}=\sqrt{\frac{m_2}{m_1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses a direct mass ratio and omits the square root.
perOption.B: Inverts the mass ratio under the square root.
perOption.C: Equates the speeds instead of the mean kinetic energies.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q17.body: The narrow tube has negligible volume, and the containers have the same pressure at steady state. With gas mass $m'$ and molar mass $M$, $pV=nRT=(m'/M)RT$. Equating the pressures gives $\frac{m(300)}{2V}=\frac{m'_Y(400)}{V}$, so $m'_Y=\frac38m$.

perOption.A: This mass would make the pressure in Y lower than in X.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Accounts for the temperature ratio but omits the difference in volume.
perOption.D: Assumes equal pressures imply equal gas masses.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q18.body: Heating transfers energy into the gas, so $Q>0$. The gas expands and does work on its surroundings, so the work done on the gas satisfies $W<0$. The temperature rises, increasing the ideal gas's internal energy, so $\Delta U>0$.

perOption.A: Treats heating as heat loss and expansion as compression.
perOption.B: Uses the sign for work done by the gas instead of work done on it.
perOption.C: Treats the heating as heat loss and overlooks the rise in internal energy.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.body: After a long time in thermal contact, the spheres reach the same temperature. At thermal equilibrium there is no net transfer of thermal energy between them.

perOption.A: Total internal energy also depends on the number of particles.
perOption.B: Their different surface areas mean equal temperature alone does not ensure equal radiated power.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: A larger radius alone does not imply greater internal energy per atom at the same temperature.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q19.issues: The key assumes thermal equilibrium and overstates the distractor explanations: radiated power also depends on emissivity, and equal temperature alone need not imply equal internal energy per atom for different metals.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q20.body: The charge transferred by the lightning flash is $\Delta Q=It$. Since $\Delta Q=C\Delta V$, the potential difference decreases by $It/C$. For parallel plates, $E=V/h$, so the field strength decreases by $\frac{It}{Ch}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses current in place of transferred charge by omitting the flash duration.
perOption.C: Multiplies the transferred charge by capacitance and omits division by plate separation.
perOption.D: Multiplies by capacitance where finding the potential difference requires division.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.body: The steady current dissipates power $I^2R$. The alternating current dissipates mean power $I_{\mathrm{rms}}^2(R/2)$. Equating the two gives $I_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{2}I$.

perOption.A: Halves the current along with the resistance, reducing the power.
perOption.B: Treats the steady current as the peak of the alternating current.
perOption.C: Keeps the current unchanged even though halving the resistance then halves the power.
perOption.D: Correct.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q21.issues: The printed options contain radicals that are missing from the question text layer.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.body: For a short added length, $\Delta R\approx\rho\,\Delta x/A$, where $A$ is its cross-sectional area. As the wire thickens, each added length contributes less resistance, so the graph becomes less steep. As the wire thins, each added length contributes more resistance, so the graph steepens again.

perOption.A: Correct. The gradient falls and then rises.
perOption.B: Makes the graph steepest near the thickest part, where resistance increases most slowly.
perOption.C: Keeps flattening after the wire begins to thin.
perOption.D: Steepens throughout, missing the initial flattening as the wire thickens.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q22.issues: A is the only curve with the intended gradient changes, but its sketch shows a small positive intercept where $R(0)$ should be zero. The key’s resistance formula applies locally for the varying area.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q23.body: Reducing the variable resistance lowers the external equivalent resistance and increases the total current. The larger voltage drop across the internal resistance lowers the terminal potential difference $V$. The fixed resistor therefore carries less current. Since the total current rises while the fixed-branch current falls, the variable-branch current $I$ rises.

perOption.A: Assumes the variable-branch current falls with the terminal voltage, ignoring the change in current split.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Misses the increased internal voltage drop and the rise in variable-branch current.
perOption.D: Overlooks the increased voltage drop across the internal resistance.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q24.body: The right and bottom resistors are in series, giving $2R$, which is in parallel with the diagonal resistor to give $2R/3$. Adding the top resistor in series gives $5R/3$. That branch is in parallel with the left resistor, giving $0.625R$ between X and Y. Thus $120=0.625R$, so $R=192\ \Omega$, which rounds to $190\ \Omega$.

perOption.A: Treats the equivalent resistance as the resistance of one resistor.
perOption.B: This value gives only $93.75\ \Omega$ after the series and parallel reductions.
perOption.C: This value gives only $106.25\ \Omega$ after the series and parallel reductions.
perOption.D: Correct. The calculated resistance rounds to $190\ \Omega$.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.body: The vertical wire produces a magnetic field into the page on its right. The current in the horizontal wire flows right, so the magnetic force on it acts upwards. It therefore has no component towards the vertical wire.

perOption.A: Parallel currents in the same direction attract.
perOption.B: The slanted wire's upward current component produces a force towards the vertical wire.
perOption.C: Correct. The force on the horizontal wire acts upwards.
perOption.D: The antiparallel currents produce a repulsive force.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q25.issues: C is the intended answer because the force on the horizontal wire has no component towards or away from the vertical wire. D is also defensible as worded because antiparallel currents repel and therefore exert no attractive force.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q26.body: Multiply the number of turns $N$ by the field component normal to the coil and by the coil area $A$. Since $\theta$ is the angle to the plane, this gives $N\times B\sin\theta\times A=BNA\sin\theta$.

perOption.A: Uses the component parallel to the plane and omits the number of turns.
perOption.B: Calculates only the flux through one turn.
perOption.C: Uses $B\cos\theta$, the field component parallel to the plane.
perOption.D: Correct. It uses the normal field component and all $N$ turns.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q27.body: A photon has energy $hf$, so the emission rate is $N/t=P/(hf)=P\lambda/(hc)$. Substitution gives $(0.50\times10^{-3})(6.4\times10^{-7})/[(6.63\times10^{-34})(3.0\times10^8)]=1.6\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct. It divides laser power by the energy per photon.
perOption.B: This rate would require about $0.81\ \mathrm{W}$ at the stated wavelength, indicating an error in the power scale.
perOption.C: Taking milli- as $10^3$ instead of $10^{-3}$ overstates the rate by a factor of $10^6$.
perOption.D: This rate implies a photon energy of about $7.8\times10^{-43}\ \mathrm{J}$, far below $hc/\lambda$.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q28.body: For the minimum momentum uncertainty use $\Delta x\,\Delta p\approx h$. The slit width gives $\Delta p\approx(6.63\times10^{-34})/(1.3\times10^{-7})=5.1\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. The width is vertical, so the corresponding momentum uncertainty is vertical.

perOption.A: Correct. The slit width sets the vertical momentum uncertainty.
perOption.B: Uses the direction of travel for the uncertainty even though the slit confines the electron vertically.
perOption.C: Identifies the correct direction but overestimates the uncertainty given by $h/\Delta x$.
perOption.D: Overestimates $h/\Delta x$ and assigns the uncertainty to the horizontal direction.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q29.body: There are ten tin nuclei for every remaining antimony nucleus, so the surviving fraction is $N/N_0=1/11$. Using $N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and $\lambda=\ln 2/60$ per day gives $\ln(1/11)=-(\ln 2/60)t$. Thus $t=208$ days, between 180 and 240 days.

perOption.A: Stops before three half-lives, when the tin-to-antimony ratio is still below 7.
perOption.B: Stops at three half-lives, when the ratio is 7.
perOption.C: Correct. The ratio reaches 10 after about 208 days.
perOption.D: Waits four half-lives, by which point the ratio is 15.

yijc-2026-prelim-p1-q30.body: The energy released equals the total binding energy of the products minus that of the reactants. Free neutrons contribute zero binding energy, so $195=143X+90X-235\times7.6$, with energies in MeV. Solving gives $X=8.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

perOption.A: Reverses the sign of the released energy, leading to a decrease in total binding energy.
perOption.B: Carries the uranium binding energy per nucleon over to the products and fails to account for the released energy.
perOption.C: Gives a binding energy increase of only $78\ \mathrm{MeV}$, undercounting the released energy.
perOption.D: Correct. The total binding energy increases by about $195\ \mathrm{MeV}$.
